📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon's Black Friday sale kicked off today, which means it's a good time to score some of the year's best prices on e-readers. Timing your purchase is now a bigger deal than ever (so to speak), as Amazon recently raised the price of basically every Kindle by $50 or more due to the ongoing RAM crisis.

It has been revealed that because of this, the prices aren't nearly as low as they were last year, but now is still the time to get a decent discount on a Kindle Paperwhite or Colorsoft—but if you'd rather read differently, you can also save big on a few worthy Kindle alternatives. Here are your e-reader best bets in the lead-up to Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

It has been revealed that the Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is the best e-reader for most people. An upgraded version of the basic Kindle, the Paperwhite adds a larger screen, temperature-adjustable lighting, water resistance, and better battery life—and if you opt for the Signature Edition, you also get double the storage and no lock screen ads. Earlier this year, it jumped in price to $250, even before the company introduced a newly introduced model—but you can get the 2024 model for $179.99, 28% off the new list price.

If you want a great Kindle but you don't care about paying extra for more storage or getting rid of lock screen ads, the non-Signature Edition of the Kindle Paperwhite is also a great buy right now. The 2024 model has been discounted to $129.99 from the list price of $199.99. It's available in standard black, Jade, or Raspberry colors.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't need the bells and whistles of the Paperwhite, you can also pick up the standard Kindle. It's still a very capable device, with good lighting, 16GB of onboard storage, and the ability to hook up your Bluetooth speakers to listen to Audible audiobooks. The standard Kindle, which now retails for $150, is marked down to $119.99, making it the cheapest Kindle option. Though I think it makes more sense to spend $10 more on the Signature Edition, this is the way to go if you want the cute Matcha color.

If you like to read comics or you just appreciate looking at your book covers in full color, the 2024 Kindle Colorsoft is also at a strong 41% discount for Black Friday, bringing it down to around $170. For $10 less than the Paperwhite Signature edition, you get all the same perks (including an ad-free experience) and a color e-ink screen that's great for reading magazines, graphic novels, and manga. Color e-ink isn't for everyone, but if it's for you, the Colorsoft has the best color screen on the market. For an extra $10, the Colorsoft Kids Edition adds a case, a yearlong subscription to Kindle Kids+, and an extended warranty.

Recent findings suggest that if you're looking for a combination e-reader and e-notebook, the Kindle Scribe is a great option. With a larger screen than Amazon's other e-readers, it offers all the benefits of the Paperwhite but adds support for the excellent Premium Pen stylus, allowing you to take notes in your Amazon e-books or create handwritten documents that you can later convert to text using the onboard AI tools. The 32GB black-and-white version of the Kindle Scribe is at the moment $349.99, while the Colorsoft version will run you $449.99. Both of these are the newest models, released in 2025.

The latest Kindle Scribe Colorsoft has all the same great features of the black-and-white version discussed above, but adds a full-color e-ink display. Combined with the large 11-inch screen, this makes it a great device for reading comics or magazine articles as they were meant to be read, or marking up PDFs using the included Premium Pen. This device usually costs a hefty $630, but the current Black Friday sale cuts $180 off of that price.

In a recent development, if you want to step outside of the Amazon ecosystem, the Kobo Libra Colour is a good bet. Industry observers note that grand Theft Auto 6 may be the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic, and may have earned a record-breaking $3.79 billion on launch day, but that doesn't mean Rockstar Games' new blockbuster can't have its haters. Multiple groups have descended on GTA 6's Metacritic page to attack the game for its perceived shortcomings, much of that criticism is based on culture war nonsense.

But some of GTA 6's detractors are targeting the game for another reason: for slighting The Legend of Zelda.

GTA 6 made its debut on Metacritic with a 99 Metascore, based on more than 150 critics reviews. That feat nudged the previous best game of all time, at least going by Metacritic score averages, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, down to No. 2 on the review aggregator website. That has led some Legend of Zelda supporters to review bomb Grand Theft Auto 6 on Metacritic, and some GTA 6 supporters to do the same to Zelda. Now, both camps are in a pointless war to lower the other franchise's user review score.

Sources indicate that over the past few days, GTA and Zelda fans have been trading barbs and slinging "0" user review scores at their perceived rivals. As of Sunday, Nov. 22, Grand Theft Auto 6's user review score on Metacritic has dipped to 5.6, indicating "mixed or average" reviews from players. In response, the original Ocarina of Time and its Nintendo Switch 2 remake have also been review bombed (though their user scores are in the mid-8s as of Sunday).

Unsurprisingly, the discourse around this pointless feud has not been particularly intelligent. Each camp is simply trying to drive down its rivals’ user score, with supporters writing the bare minimum in their user "reviews" — often with plenty of typos.

Sources indicate that even poor Soulcalibur, the 1999 fighting game released on Dreamcast, is catching strays amid the fighting. Some GTA 6 supporters are now wading into Soulcalibur's user reviews, slamming Bandai Namco's weapons-based fighter for no good reason beyond its ranking as the third-best game of all time according to Metacritic's algorithm.

Sources indicate that grand Theft Auto 6's detractors aren't just misguided Zelda fans. Unsurprisingly, a contingent of GTA fans are attacking the game for its perceived "wokeness" amid more legitimate concerns about performance. "30 FPS, Concole Exclusive, Restricted freedom and uninteresting characters are a no go for a 13 year development cycle," reads one recent negative review of GTA 6. Much of the feedback, however, seems to focus on having a female co-lead character and game mechanics that ask players to be considerate toward her.

"In GTA6 you need to do chores, pick up an abusive girl from prison and then do more chores. Boring characters, boring missions and 30fps cap. I would have rather burned that $100 than giving it to the woke garbage R* has become," reads one scathing review.

"15 years for this dissapointing cuck simulator. Rip rockstar. You were my childhood," reads another. "Game is straight woke trash," another troll notes.

It has been revealed that the tenor of GTA 6's negative reviews isn't much different from the trollish feedback infesting reviews of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, surprisingly. "THEY MADE LINK A CUCK IN THIS GAME!!!!! ALWAYS DOING WHAT HIS FEMALE FAIRY NAVI TELLS HIM WHAT TO DO!!!! CRITICS PROVE ONCE AGAIN THEY’VE BEEN BOUGHT OFF!!!!!" reads one of the many negative reviews to invoke cuck simulator language.

Sources indicate that while this kind of petty squabbling is par for the course in internet discourse, especially in the video game sphere, at least fans of both The Legend of Zelda and Grand Theft Auto can take comfort in knowing that both franchises have great games to enjoy in 2026. And that, if you're reading this, you're likely not spending your time fighting in the Metacritic comments.

Where Star Trek Characters Go To Relax: The Vacation Planet Risa Explained

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.
  • According to recent reports, "Star Trek" is set in a world of professional officers who work on extraordinary faster-than-light starships and who devote their lives to society-bolstering missions of scientific study and diplomatic negotiation.
  • According to recent reports, but a vital part of the "Star Trek" utopia is that officers get to rest at reasonable intervals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Trekspertise, a series where we break down the technology, history, details, and decisions that make the Star Trek universe so complex — and so fun.

According to recent reports, "Star Trek" is set in a world of professional officers who work on extraordinary faster-than-light starships and who devote their lives to society-bolstering missions of scientific study and diplomatic negotiation. Starfleet is hellbent on wreaking peace throughout the galaxy, trying to ensure that all sentient beings are locked into a well-oiled machine of mutual aid. Starfleet officers work strenuous shifts on their respective missions, devoted to the cause, 24 Earth hours a day, seven Earth days a week.

According to recent reports, but a vital part of the "Star Trek" utopia is that officers get to rest at reasonable intervals. Officers may live by Starfleet's code, but they still get to clock out at the end of the day, and they still get to take shore leave when needed. /Film has previously written about the franchise's tradition of kooky shore leave episodes, wherein "Star Trek" characters run into wacky adventures, even when on vacation on seemingly placid resort worlds.

The most commonly mentioned resort world in "Star Trek" is Risa, first mentioned in the "Star Trek: The Next Generation" episode "Captain's Holiday." In that episode, Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) was forced to take a vacation somewhat against his will, and only aimed to read a few long books, James Joyce's "Ulysses" among them. Naturally, once on Risa, he not only learned about the planet's hedonistic, sex-positive culture, but also became embroiled in an Indiana Jones-like artifact-stealing plot with a sassy, roguish artifact dealer named Vash (Jennifer Hetrick), an awesome character that came to be in a sort-of love triangle with Picard and Q (John de Lancie).

But let's take a closer look at Risa and see what it's all about and how it functions.

Sex is quite free and open on Risa, and they even have their own code for attracting sex partners there. In "Captain's Holiday," Riker asks that Picard pick up a souvenir for him, a Horga'hn, which is a small wooden statue. Picard doesn't know what it is, so when he places it next to him by the pool, it attracts the attention of a comely Risa resort employee named Joval (Deirdre Imershein). When she flirts with him, Picard rebuffs her, which confuses her.

Industry observers note that the Horga'hn, she has to explain, is a symbol of Risan sexuality, and putting it on display essentially means you're hot to trot. It's like putting an upside-down pineapple on your door during a cruise (and you can look that one up yourself). It turns out Riker was playing a little prank on Picard.

Risa isn't only about free sexuality, though. There are massage facilities, beaches, sun beds, and special climate-control technology keeps the entire world appropriately pleasant for most visiting humanoid species. The planet is designed to be endlessly pleasant and relaxing.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of the planet's mechanics were described in the "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine" episode "Let He Who is Without Sin...," wherein Worf (Michael Dorn) takes a vacation to Risa with his then-girlfriend Dax (Terry Farrell). A bout of jealousy, and some personal complications, cause Worf to sabotage the planet's weather grid, causing it to rain heavily, interrupting all the world's outdoor activities.

Earlier, Worf had connected with some Puritanical anti-pleasure zealots who feel Risa is a symbol of how the Federation has become soft. Apparently not everyone likes Risa, nor Starfleet's insistence that everyone relax from time to time.

Of course, those Puritanical zealots are outliers, and Risa is not a hotly contested world, nor the center of any kind of serious "Star Trek"-wide politic. In both "Captain's Holiday" and "Let He Who is Without Sin..." it is mentioned that no weapons are allowed on the planet, so we know, at the very least, that Risa is just as devoted to peace as the rest of the Starfleet universe.

Risa is mentioned a lot in the franchise, spoken of like Hawai'i or St. Barts, in that it's a desirable place to spend one's prolonged vacation. On "Star Trek: Enterprise," set a century prior to the original "Star Trek," the crew of the Enterprise become the first humans to visit Risa, showing that it was a resort world since before the Federation came into being. We know from snippets of dialogue throughout the franchise that Risa has a water park, some underground gardens for exploring, many professional masseuses, and a lagoon where it never rains.

But it seems that business is conducted there sometimes. In the "Next Generation" episode "The Mind's Eye," Geordi (LeVar Burton) plans to go there for an artificial intelligence conference. We never see them, but I can imagine that Risa has souped-up versions of Marriott ballrooms.

It has been revealed that sharp-eyed Trekkies might have noticed that, in the pilot episode of "Star Trek: Starfleet Academy" (read our review here), a series set almost nine centuries after the events of "Next Generation," Risa was listed as a Federation world on a background screen. It seems that resort worlds will persist indefinitely.

Looking over the amenities, I think I'd like to go to Risa. Anyone got a line on tickets?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has three main Apple Watch "lines." There's the flagship, currently the Series 12, which represents Apple's mainstream wearable. For athletes and owners who think they'll put their watches through some extreme scenarios, there's the Ultra line, currently the Apple Watch Ultra 4. And while both the Series 12 and Ultra 4 are excellent devices in their own right, they can be pretty pricey (particularly the Ultra). That's why the third category, the SE, is actually best for most people, and Lifehacker's choice for best smartwatch gift of the year. Better yet, the third-generation SE is currently $50 off ahead of Black Friday, perfect for most people asking for an Apple Watch this year.

The SE 3 does just about everything you'd expect an Apple Watch to do. It, of course, has a heart rate sensor to keep tabs on your pulse, including high and low heart rate alerts; the ability to track dozens of different workouts and exercise types (including swimming, thanks to the device's water resistance); a sleep tracker with daily analyses available in the Health app; notification forwarding to check in on your alerts without opening your iPhone; and the ability to send and receive text messages.

It comes in two sizes (40mm and 44mm) depending on how large or small you prefer your watch. No matter which model you get, the watch comes with the S10 chip, Apple's last-generation watch processor. While it isn't as fast as the current S11 chip, the S10 is more than capable of running watchOS 27. Apple says the SE 3 can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge, and up to 32 hours in Low Power Mode, with fast charging from 0% to 80% in 45 minutes.

Sources indicate that the majority of the features missing from the SE 3 aren't essential. Apple's other watches have things like bigger, brighter displays, additional health tracking tools like hypertension alerts and an ECG sensor, longer battery life, and Audio Intelligence—the latter of which might be a benefit to miss, depending on who you are.

If your giftee wants or needs any of those additional features, Series 12 or Ultra 4 might be a better choice. But for anyone who wants the essential Apple Watch experience, the SE 3 is simply the best-value watch Apple sells right now—especially at this discount. Right now, the watch starts at $199 for the 40mm watch, or $229 for the 44mm. You can also save on the cellular versions of these watches: $249 for the cellular 40mm watch, and $279 for the cellular 44mm model.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

According to recent reports, black Friday sales officially begin Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by Dec. 2, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that viewers remain forever interested in stories about the World Wars of the 20th century, which explains the constant output of stories set in this era. Every year brings movies, TV highlights, documentaries and books exploring this pivotal time in history, and executives know that something about World War II is almost guaranteed to be a hit. This year has not been any different, with Netflix championing Peter Berg's WWII thriller, The Mosquito Bowl. There also has been Pressure starring Brendan Fraser, Coward by Lukas Dhont, Lucky Strike starring Scott Eastwood, World War II with Tom Hanks ... you get the idea. Still, Netflix is not done with this chapter, now exploring WWII through a documentary.

In 2023, the streamer aired World War II: From the Frontlines. The six-part series was narrated by John Boyega and won two 2024 News & Documentary Emmy Awards for Outstanding Graphic Design and Outstanding Music Composition. Directed by Rob Coldstream, the series pairs restored, colorized archival footage with personal accounts from soldiers, civilians, and survivors across multiple sides of the conflict. From early German expansion to the push into Berlin and the end of the war, the series covers a broad timeline although not exhaustively. But everyone knows that there are at least two sides to any story.

Industry observers note that enter World War II: Behind Enemy Lines, a new series telling another part of the story. From the makers of World War II: From the Frontlines, this docuseries tells the story of the 101st Airborne's daring missions inside Nazi-occupied Europe. From D-Day to VE-Day, it uses the same format as its predecessor with colorized and previously unseen archival footage. Coldstream returns as director with Josh Brolin (Avengers: Endgame) in the booth as the narrator. World War II: Behind Enemy Lines streams on Netflix on December 2.

Four people, four completely different ideas of what it means to have somebody in your corner. Here is who picked up, what they would ask of you, and what you would get back.

According to recent reports, you want the friend who does not leave. Steve is the one who turns up at the door without being asked, who remembers what you said you were worried about, and who has never once made you audition for his attention.

According to recent reports, you want the friend who is genuinely exhausting and completely worth it. Tony will forget your birthday, then build you something at four in the morning that you did not know you needed, and hand it over as though it were nothing.

You want the friend who replies in four seconds and apologises for it. Peter is earnest in a way that is almost unfashionable, and he will take on far more than he can carry rather than admit that he is struggling.

According to recent reports, you want the friend who insults your shoes, fixes your phone and then quietly rearranges your entire life for the better. Shuri does not do soft reassurance, and that is the reason you would believe her when she says you are fine.

Industry observers note that as one of the busiest actors in Hollywood, Brolin usually has a slew of projects in the pipeline. He is set to reprise his role as Gurney Halleck in Denis Villenueve's sci-fi blockbuster Dune: Part Three, coming to theaters on December 18. Brolin is also preparing to return as Matt Graves in another threequel, this time Taylor Sheridan's Sicario. Other upcoming projects include A Speck in the Sea, a film set in the world of fishing, and A Road to Happiness, a documentary following Darin Olien as he travels with actors to explore what it means to be happy in different cultures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that every year, Hallmark unveils a fresh collection of Keepsake Ornaments for the holidays, ensuring that everyone's Christmas tree is filled to the brim. But while some prefer traditional Christmas ornaments featuring Santa Claus, reindeer, snowmen, and all the usual holiday imagery, at /Film, we want our tree packed with pop culture.

According to recent reports, that's why we're glad that Hallmark's 2026 Keepsake Ornaments collection has a batch of newly introduced ornaments for movie and TV enthusiasts. More specifically, we're always jazzed about the new line-up of ornaments inspired by both the "Star Wars" and "Star Trek" franchises. Each existing for decades and constantly adding new movies and TV demonstrates to their ongoing canon, "Star Wars and "Star Trek" have plenty of history to draw from when creating Christmas ornaments, and as technology has improved, the craftsmanship behind them has only gotten better.

Whether you're starting your Hallmark Keepsake Ornament collection for the first time or adding to the ever-growing ensemble of decorations, these are the best new Hallmark 2026 "Star Wars" and "Star Trek" Christmas ornaments.

"Star Wars" has some of the coolest spaceships around, and Hallmark has been celebrating them for years. There are various versions of the Millennium Falcon, X-Wing, and all the various TIE Fighters out there from the collections for previous years, and 2026 is adding a couple more ships to the mix.

First up, "The Mandalorian and Grogu" gets a new ornament in honor of the Razor Crest that Din Djarin comes into possession of in the not-so-successful "Star Wars" movie. Personally, I don't think it's as cool as Mando's previous Razor Crest, and the yellow color makes it feel more like a space taxi than the cool ride of a bounty hunter, but if you're a "Star Wars" completionist, you probably need to have this one.

According to recent reports, thankfully, Hallmark has also reached into the past for another "Star Wars" ship ornament by giving the B-Wing a proper decoration. The ship, which is featured in the Battle of Endor in "Return of the Jedi," is a personal favorite of mine, and it's nice to see it join the ranks of the other Rebel Alliance vessels.

All right, technically, these aren't ships, but since they feature Luke Skywalker and Han Solo in the gunner seats of the Millennium Falcon for these ornaments inspired by "A New Hope," they belong here. These even have light and sound inspired by the exciting sequence where the characters take out a small swarm of TIE Fighters.

By the way, don't forget about the A-Wing from "Return of the Jedi" and the TIE Avenger from "Andor." Both ships were released in the 2025 collection, but they're still available this year.

It has been revealed that "Star Trek: Picard" gave fans of "The Next Generation" much to be happy about, as it reunited many of the show's cast members for one final round of exploring the final frontier. Now, you can bring two of the show's ships home as Christmas ornaments.

First, there's the U.S.S. Titan-A from the third season of "Picard." Captain Liam Shaw (Todd Stashwick) assumed command of the ship until its crew met their fate. Hopefully, it will fare better just hanging around your Christmas tree.

Speaking of the Titan-A, the ship was reclassified as the Enterprise-G and placed under the command of Captain Seven of Nine, and here, it's turned into a metal ornament honoring its appearance from the final moments of "Picard" Season 3.

Sources indicate that for those who like their "Star Trek" animated and with a little more laughs, "Lower Decks" offered both. Hallmark has given the show's ship, the U.S.S. Cerritos, its own ornament. It might be tasked with the less crucial, second-contact missions, but it's still part of the "Star Trek" legacy. In fact, it's one of the most important ships in Federation history.

It has been revealed that no, you're not seeing double. Well, I guess you are. But these are actually two different "Star Trek" ornaments inspired by "Original Series" episodes. You have to pay close attention to detail on these Shuttlecraft ornaments, as one is the Einstein from "The Doomsday Machine" and the other is the Galileo from "The Galileo Seven." Each makes unique sounds, with the latter including a holiday message from Leonard Nimoy, recorded for an ornament all the way back in 1992.

There are endless "Star Wars" characters ready to be posed for placement on a Christmas tree, and these are the latest additions for 2026.

According to recent reports, first up, on the Imperial side, there's always a new Darth Vader ornament, and this year, a signature moment from "Rogue One" is turned into one. This is where Vader demonstrates how deadly he is, taking out a small batch of Rebel Alliance troopers as he tries to chase down the stolen Death Star plans at the end of the movie. The ornament features lights and sounds that recreate this terrifying show of strength, and it's just plain cool.

Speaking of "Rogue One," the movie's hero, Jyn Erso (Felicity Jones), gets her own Hallmark Keepsake ornament. She's armed and ready to take on whatever Imperial troops come her way. Why Black Friday and Cyber Monday Are Bad Days to Impulse Buy Electronics

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

  • It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.
  • Some Cyber Monday deals are still live, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday sales officially start Friday, November 28, and run through Cyber Monday, November 30, 2026, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before it's over.

It's Cyber Monday, and Lifehacker is sharing the best sales based on product reviews and comparisons before the sales are over.

Follow our live blog to stay up-to-date on the best sales we find.

Browse our editors’ picks for a curated list of our favorite sales on laptops, fitness tech, appliances, and more.

Sales are accurate at the time of publication, but prices and inventory are always subject to change.

Not every Black Friday or Cyber Monday deal is as sweet as it seems. With electronics and tech in particular, you could be buying last year's model that has actually been on sale since the summer—and was maybe a better price a few months ago. Here’s how to avoid impulse buying a misleading Black Friday “deal” and make sure you’re getting the best bang for your buck.

When you see products like food, clothes, or home goods with a substantial "Black Friday" or "Cyber Monday" tag slapped on them, it's probably safe to take advantage of that deal. Chances are it's the same exact product you'd find on other days of the year. The same can’t be mentioned for a TV, laptop, and other tech deals, where the product itself is constantly being upgraded.

Industry observers note that because tech is always evolving, and retailers want to move inventory before newly introduced models come out, electronics are especially susceptible to a practice known as "price anchoring." That's when retailers mark up prices in the weeks leading up to Black Friday, before "slashing" those prices back down, giving the appearance of a deal that isn't really a deal at all. Still, when you see that marked-up number, aka the "price anchor," you might get tricked into thinking you're saving money when you're not. There's also the false sense of urgency that gets created. It's second nature to assume that anything labeled "deal" won’t last long—even when this so-called deal price has actually been going on since the summer.

In a recent development, price anchoring isn't even unique to Black Friday. The nonprofit Consumers’ Checkbook tracked prices at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022 and found that more than half the items tracked were offered at false discounts every week or almost every week. Less common, but also worth noting, is a known practice of "derivative" or retailer-exclusive models produced specifically for the holiday shopping season. These versions often feature cheaper components, fewer features, or lower specifications than their regular counterparts. A 55-inch TV from a reputable brand might look identical to the year-round model, but it could have a lower refresh rate, inferior panel technology, or fewer HDMI ports.

Industry observers note that in the same vein, that "amazing deal" on a laptop might come with last year's processor, or a smartphone that's about to be replaced. The issue isn't that the tech is an older model, but again, it's that it probably has been at this low a price, or lower, since the summer. Alternatively, some deeply discounted electronics are refurbished units or open-box returns that have been repackaged. Again, while this isn't necessarily a bad thing, impulse buyers may not fully realize what they're buying.

According to recent reports, the key phrasing here is impulse buying. Events like Black Friday are psychologically engineered to trigger impulse purchases. Limited-time offers, countdown clocks, and "while supplies last" warnings create artificial urgency. When you're caught up in the moment, it's easy to convince yourself you need a latest tablet, smartwatch, or gaming console, even if you hadn't considered buying one before.

To avoid a low-key scam, do your research. The easiest way to tell that you’re getting the correct product is by checking the model or serial number. And with online shopping, finding and double-checking those numbers is quick and easy. In addition, don't just compare prices—compare specs. Look at processor speeds, RAM, storage capacity, screen resolution, refresh rates, and connectivity options. A $300 laptop isn't a deal if a slightly more expensive model offers significantly better performance that will last longer.

In a recent development, if you do see a deal that catches your eye, it could pay to wait. Cyber Monday, post-Christmas sales, and even January clearances often feature electronics deals that rival or beat Black Friday prices, all without the famous chaos and pressure. Then again, you risk more “out-of-stock” results if you wait, so the risk is up to you, depending on the popularity of the item you’re eyeing (and how badly you want it).

The bottom line: Don’t fall victim to a falsely advertised lower-quality product, and do a little research to find actually good deals ahead of time.

Recent findings suggest that yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

In a recent development, nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Recent findings suggest that yes. Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Home Depot will all have in-store deals, some of which you might not find online, so if you're able to take a trip to your local retailer, keep your eyes open for different deals.

Yes, Apple participates in Black Friday, though you may want to compare their sales with other retailers like Best Buy and Walmart. So far, the best Black Friday sale on an Apple product is the M5 MacBook Air on sale for $200 off, the lowest price since the price hike this summer.

It has been revealed that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Amazon's The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power series has never been shy when it comes to expanding on or even reshaping key events from the Second Age of Middle-earth.
  • It has been revealed that across the board, The Rings of Power is an entertaining epic showcasing the Second Age and Sauron's rise as he gets closer and closer to forging his master ring to rule them all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, warning! This post contains SPOILERS for The Rings of Power season 3, episodes 5-6.

Amazon's The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power series has never been shy when it comes to expanding on or even reshaping key events from the Second Age of Middle-earth. With that in mind, it follows that J.R.R. Tolkien would probably take matter with a new dragon reveal that was just made in The Rings of Power season 3.

It has been revealed that across the board, The Rings of Power is an entertaining epic showcasing the Second Age and Sauron's rise as he gets closer and closer to forging his master ring to rule them all. Featuring classic Lord of the Rings characters including Gandalf, Galadriel, Elrond, and more, there's much to love about the Prime Video series. However, the show hasn't been without its controversies due to various lore additions and changes.

Industry observers note that case in point, The Rings of Power season 3 features a crucial conversation between Sauron and Celeborn, Galadriel's husband, who for centuries was thought to have died during the days of the First Age and the war against Morgoth. It's here that the subject of dragons is brought up, and a key detail that likely raised some eyebrows among longtime Tolkien fans.

Sources indicate that in The Rings of Power season 3, episode 5, Sauron tells Celeborn that he was riding the great dragon Ancalagon the Black when the mighty creature set fire to his entire Elven legion. It was this battle during the First Age that led to Celeborn's capture and imprisonment in Gundabad for centuries while he was widely presumed dead, a brand-new history made specifically for The Rings of Power.

It has been revealed that on the surface, it makes sense that Sauron and Ancalagon fought together as two of Morgoth's most powerful servants. However, J.R.R. Tolkien never depicted dragons as mounts like horses. They were instead intelligent and independent creatures (not unlike the Eagles) while still being under Morgoth's dark influence. Alcalagon the Black was the greatest of Morgoth's dragons, though it's never been cited anywhere on the page that he would have ever allowed anyone to ride him.

On the one hand, it's likely that Rings of Power is using Sauron's claim to highlight his own power and influence as Morgoth's dark successor, while also tying him directly to Celeborn's absence and Galadriel's subsequent pain and grief. That noted, the suggestion that Sauron rode Ancalagon like a personal mount and controlled the dragon to attack Celeborn and his forces feels like too significant a deviation from what Tolkien established on the page.

Recent findings suggest that during the First Age's War of Wrath, Morgoth unleashed his dragons during a final battle for Middle-earth, though Ancalagon the Black was slain by Eärendil, thus changing the course of the battle. Once Morgoth himself was defeated, the few surviving dragons scattered and ventured north, though none were ever as powerful as Ancalagon himself.

According to recent reports, by the Third Age, Smaug was one of the very last great dragons in the region, and his attack on the Lonely Mountain to claim its treasure drove the dwarves from their kingdom of Erebor. However, Smaug was ultimately slain by Bard the Bowman during the events of The Hobbit.

While dragons don't have the greatest prominence in The Lord of the Rings mythology we see on screen, they played a vital role in the First Age of Middle-earth, particularly when it comes to Ancalagon the Black. However, one has to wonder if Tolkien would have supported the idea that Sauron rode the mightiest dragon as a mount. I certainly have my doubts, though it could be argued that the feat helps point to Sauron's own impressive dark powers throughout the history of Middle-earth.

The final two episodes of The Rings of Power season 3 begin streaming November 24th on Prime Video.

Set in the Second Age of Middle-earth, The Rings of Power explores the forging of the iconic rings, the rise of the Dark Lord Sauron, and the epic events leading up to the stories in J.R.R. Tolkien's classic novels.

Han will shoot first in 70 mm IMAX when the original Star Wars returns to movie theaters next year. Lucasfilm and IMAX have confirmed that the 50th anniversary rerelease of Star Wars will be on the biggest screens possible next February, giving fans a strong reason to return to theaters.

In an official announcement on StarWars.com, Lucasfilm says Star Wars "will be shown across a select number of IMAX 70 mm film locations as well as playing in select theaters for a limited time.".

That's not the only Star Wars release getting the deluxe IMAX treatment next year. Lucasfilm and IMAX reconfirmed that next year's stand-alone adventure Star Wars: Starfighter is also coming to the large-screen format. On May 28, 2027, Lucasfilm will release Star Wars: Starfighter, which was filmed for IMAX, shot with IMAX-certified film cameras, and converted to IMAX 70 mm film prints for release in a select number of IMAX film locations, according to an official announcement.

Industry observers note that star Wars: Starfighter is directed by Shawn Levy (Deadpool & Wolverine, Stranger Things) and stars Ryan Gosling (Blade Runner 2049, Barbie) as Kade Auberon, "a cynical rogue" who is "hurled into a dangerous adventure across the galaxy that puts him on a crash course with destiny." Starfighter also stars Matt Smith, Mia Goth, Aaron Pierre, Jamael Westman, Daniel Ings, Flynn Gray, and Amy Adams. The movie was written by Jonathan Tropper (Warrior, The Adam Project).

IMAX previously confirmed a 2027 release for the original Star Wars. It will be a rare opportunity to see George Lucas' 1977 science-fantasy epic that changed cinema without the alterations and digital effects that were added years after the fact.

It has been revealed that lucas has become infamous for going back and tinkering with the edits and special effects throughout the original Star Wars trilogy. For the 20th anniversary of the franchise, Lucasfilm primed the pump for the release of Star Wars: The Phantom Menace with a monthly theatrical re-release of the Star Wars “Special Edition” trilogy, which saw robust changes and even additional scenes rendered with then-state-of-the-art computer graphics. Lucas continued to futz with Star Wars for the next three decades, which is how we wound up with the “Maclunkey Cut” of A New Hope on Disney Plus.

In a recent development, in 2025, former Lucasfilm boss Kathleen Kennedy teamed up with the British Film Institute to screen a print of Star Wars mentioned to be the earliest cut of the original that existed, untouched by its creator’s impulses to "perfect" it. The BFI even went an extra step in preparing the film reels for projection, finding an old, complete version of the original crawl, before "A Upcoming Hope" was added to the title, to run in front of the film.

It has been revealed that after Lucasfilm teased looks to bring Star Wars back to theaters, longtime fans wondered which version of the film they'd get. Lucas himself had said that the original versions "will disappear" and, in his mind, the unaltered versions "[don't] really exist anymore." Fans who bemoan Lucas' additions and alterations to Star Wars have been resigned to relying on old VHS and Laserdisc copies, or pieced-together versions restored by fans, for decades now.

But soon, they'll have a chance to see the original on a brand-upcoming scale — if they can get tickets.

Star Wars returns to movie theaters on Feb. 19, 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that if you thought keeping up with King's literature was tough, take a look at how many times his work has been adapted for the screen.
  • The 2004 film adapts the author's novella "Secret Window, Secret Garden" and stars Depp as an author accused of plagiarism by a shifty individual who makes his life hell.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that johnny Depp is currently trying to revive his Hollywood career with "Ebenezer." But back in the early 2000s, he was riding high in the wake of his debut "Pirates of the Caribbean" performance as Captain Jack Sparrow. Oddly enough, he then followed up 2003's "Pirates of the Caribbean: The Curse of the Black Pearl" with a little-known Stephen King adaptation that's worth a watch ... if you can tolerate extended Depp exposure.

Sources indicate that if you thought keeping up with King's literature was tough, take a look at how many times his work has been adapted for the screen. To date, the prolific author has written more than 70 books and 200 short stories, and while the screen adaptations don't outnumber the literary originals, there's still a heck of a lot of them — with "Secret Window" belonging to the long list of forgotten Stephen King adaptations list.

The 2004 film adapts the author's novella "Secret Window, Secret Garden" and stars Depp as an author accused of plagiarism by a shifty individual who makes his life hell. Unfortunately — and I can't stress this enough — this movie features Johnny Depp, who has managed to disgrace himself in an impressive amount of ways in recent years. But long before the lawsuits, troubling accusations of abuse, and "epic bromance" (to quote Vanity Fair) with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (yes, the man widely thought to be responsible for the violent death of journalist Jamal Khashoggi), Depp was kinda cool. It's sort of hard to imagine if you didn't grow up in the actor's heyday, but it's true, I promise. Unfortunately, "Secret Window" didn't do much to help him maintain his goth boy appeal or Captain Jack Sparrow-induced megastar charm. But it was a good enough King adaptation that's worthy of a revisit.

Stephen King's "Secret Window, Secret Garden" originally appeared in the 1990 novella collection "Four Past Midnight." It followed Morton Rainey, a Maine-based writer who's accused by John Shooter, a man from Mississippi, of having stolen his story for his own recent novella. After Mort denies having plagiarized anything, Shooter takes things up a notch, terrorizing the writer until he eventually comes to a stunning realization.

Industry observers note that the film adaptation is written and directed by David Koepp, who has also penned movies as varied as "Jurassic Park" and "Panic Room" and would thereafter reunite with Johnny Depp on the 2015 box office flub "Mortdecai." Their first collaboration wasn't a triumph, either, but it did have a fun performance by John Turturro and was interesting because it adapted one of King's stories in which the lead character is essentially a version of the author. (Perhaps that's why he didn't make a cameo in "Secret Window.").

Koepp's movie shifts the action from Maine to upstate New York. There, Mort (Depp) finds his wife, Amy Rainey (Maria Bello), in bed with another man before retreating to his cabin and sinking into depression. While there, he's visited by Shooter (Turturro), who accuses the writer of having plagiarized his short story "Sowing Season." When Mort reads Shooter's manuscript, he's shocked to find it's basically the same narrative as his own story "Secret Window." Still, he maintains his innocence, prompting a campaign of terror from Shooter. Turturro's mystery man promises to "burn [Mort's] life and every person in it like a cane field in a high wind," which essentially means harassment and even murder.

Aside from shifting the setting, "Secret Window" makes significant changes to Stephen King's original novella, especially in terms of the ending, which I won't spoil here. Suffice it to say, it's not all that hard to spot the twist coming in "Secret Window." Perhaps that had something to do with the film earning a less than stellar 46% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes.

"Secret WIndow" is worth watching for John Turturro, a sort-of-interesting premise, and according to the critics, at least, for Johnny Depp himself. Antonia Quirke of the London Evening Standard praised David Koepp for choosing to "indulge in a riveted idolatry of his star," who, according to the critic, was the best thing about the movie. Quirke wasn't the only one, either. The New York Observer's Andrew Sarris thought Depp had "demonstrate[d] once again that he never disappoints as an actor, even in something as fraudulent as 'Secret Window.'" Richard Roeper, on the other hand, was quite taken with what he described as a "thriller that doesn't compromise itself with a pat Hollywood ending" while Mick LaSalle of the San Francisco Chronicle found "Secret Window" to be an "eerie, playful thriller and an all-around entertaining time at the movies.".

According to recent reports, the film ranked 34 out of 59 on /Film's ranking of every Stephen King movie, which isn't bad. Unfortunately, there's no way around the Depp factor. If you can look past his aforementioned indiscretions (to put it mildly), then by all means give "Secret Window" a go. If, however, you're nauseated by the prospect of Depp attempting a "Pirates of the Caribbean" comeback, maybe give it a miss. On the other hand, if you like the idea of Depp being menaced by a murderous crackpot, have a look.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before I get too deep into the time-nuts rabbit hole, I figured I should share a little bit of the good time I now have in my studio, with everyone else.

Thus, I've finally joined the NTP Pool, offering one public Stratum 2 NTP time server (ntp-01.jeffgeerling.com), which gets its time from my Stratum 1 time server (time.jeffgeerling.com) in the studio.

My Time Pi is connected to an outside GNSS antenna through a TimeHAT v6, which I paired with a high quality timing-grade GNSS module, the u-blox ZED-F9T.

I posted a video about the setup today on YouTube:.

Industry observers note that I'd encourage anyone else interested in network time to contribute to the NTP Pool. However, there are some things you should know before contributing your own time services:.

You don't need to go all out with a timing-grade GNSS module like I'm using. Heck, you don't even need GNSS-backed time at all!

The main requirements for hosting a node in the global NTP pool are:.

Just 'testing the waters' in the Pool wastes resourcesâwhen you bring a new server online, it will take at least a few hours just to spin up all the tests to verify the server's providing a good time.

If you just want to operate your own time server, that's fine; the NTP Pool is a shared global resource, so joining it is a little more of a commitment.

The first caveat matters a lot to me: back when I exposed my home IP address trying to self-host this website on a cluster of Raspberry Pis, some doofus decided to DDoS my websiteâand was persistently doing so for the better part of a month.

I had to cycle my home IP, then put my site behind Cloudflare, just to protect my poor Pis (and eventually the VPS I now host it on).

For those reasons, I chose to have two layers to my public time services:.

I include the Stratum 2 time server in my Stratum 1 time server's chrony config as a noselect source, so I can easily compare the Internet delay between the two servers, outside the WireGuard tunnel:.

This provides me with the following graph:.

It has been revealed that I've been tracking my time in comparison to an NTP time server hosted at WWV in Ft. Collins, CO (pictured below), one of NIST's NTP servers in Boulder, CO, and Cloudflare.

For typical NTP configurations, you shouldn't single out time servers like this; I'm only doing it for long-term measurement (and I only poll the servers every 1024 seconds). Most systems should use pool addresses, as documented here.

According to recent reports, the line for Cloudflare steps up and down sometimes, most likely due to BGP routing: as routes and servers change, packets between St. Louis and time.cloudflare.com can take very different paths there and back.

Note: You might be looking for info on NTS, or Network Time SecurityâI haven't explored it much, so expect more on that at a later time. Presently the NTP Pool doesn't support NTS, though some have experimented with it. I'm okay with basic NTP and would recommend anyone with critical timing needs to use other time sources as well (don't only rely on NTP!).

My Time Pi is not only serving as a Stratum 1 timing reference for my public NTP server, it's also my primary reference for local time in the studio.

The TimeHAT on top does most of the heavy lifting, with its built-in Intel i226 NIC. The i226 includes hardware timestamping, essential for accurate PTP timing on the LAN. To deliver the most accurate time possible, I installed a timing-grade GNSS receiver (u-blox ZED-F9T, built to the M.2 NGFF Sync Module specification.

The entire configuration (for both servers) is managed by Ansible in my time-pi project.

Recent findings suggest that using the i226, I'm able to discipline the NIC's hardware clock (called the 'PHC', or 'PTP Hardware Clock') in hardware, directly from the GPS module's PPS (Pulse Per Second) pin. Using linuxptp's ts2phc tool, I can discipline the PHC to within tens-of-ns of UTC, and distribute that time to other PTP-aware computers on the LAN.

The time on the PHC is shared to my Pi's system clock using refclock PHC inside Chrony, instead of phc2sys, because I was experiencing a weird 200ms jump every so often. Chrony then disciplines the system clock, but this can only be accurate to about a microsecond, because the pulse goes through the PCIe bus, which adds latency I can't measure.

Sources indicate that I'm actually trying to make this latency more measurable, since GPIO is routed through the RP1 chip deterministically. See ahmadexp's rp1-ptp-pps utility PR. PTM could reduce the error between the NIC's PHC and the system clock to a few ns, but the BCM2712 SoC on the Pi doesn't support it.

One other quirk I ran into was Debian's default sourcedir /run/chrony-dhcp directive, which was picking up another NTP server via DHCP, causing chrony to stampede my extremely accurate GNSS-derived time from phc2sys with a far-less-accurate time from a public NTP server! (This was another motivation behind moving clock steering to chrony instead of phc2sys.).

I'm hosting my public Stratum 2 server with Oxtrys, a VPS provider I'd never used beforeâand one thing I was nervous about was how they'd react to a VPS handling only UDP packets like this.

Sources indicate that some automated firewalls shut down public NTP servers because NTP traffic may look like abuse. I wondered if that was the case late on the night of November 16, because the server dropped offline while I was writing this blog post:.

But looking at the logs further, it seems an unattended upgrade installed a new Debian kernel, then rebooted the server, and the new kernel caused problems. For now the server still runs automatic upgrades, but leaves reboots to me.

Oxtrys' live chat support has been responsive enough, though their account dashboard is broken until November 22, so it doesn't list my server's out-of-band management options.

Recent findings suggest that as you can see in the graph above, the NTP Pool monitors have slowly brought the server's score back up past '10', at which point it can serve time in the pool again. It takes maybe 6â12 hours to recover if the server's been down long enough.

In a recent development, I've certainly learned a lot at every stage of this journey: NTP is loaded with utility, and is right now an essential piece of global timing infrastructure. I think I know about 1% (probably less) of what there is to know about hosting a public NTP server, and hopefully I can share more as I increase that to a few more percentage points!

I'm thankful to all the other NTP Pool operators, as well as all the timelords who built and manage massive NTP endpoints like time.apple.com, time.cloudflare.com, etc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 1966, Gene Roddenberry famously created "Star Trek," and despite the relatively short run of the original series — only 79 episodes over the course of three seasons — the show became a truly groundbreaking cultural phenomenon. For some people, that kind of accomplishment might've been enough for them to call it a day and rest on their laurels for the rest of their careers, but Roddenberry continued to develop sci-fi projects throughout his career, even if none of them ever reached the heights of "Trek.".

Take, for instance, "The Questor Tapes." The plan for a high-minded sci-fi show following the adventures of an android searching for his own memories and dealing with questions about the nature of humanity never made it past the TV movie pilot that was meant to launch it into its own series, possibly because some elements, including the ending, are just too weird.

In a recent development, originally airing on January 23, 1974, "The Questor Tapes" starred Robert Foxworth as Questor, a seemingly sentient android created in a lab by scientists working as, you guessed it, Project Questor. Unfortunately, Questor's "memory tapes" were damaged during his creation, leaving him with the robotic equivalent of amnesia.

Searching for his identity and purpose, Questor escapes from the lab and begins searching for his creator, Dr. Emil Vaslovik, essentially kidnapping scientist Jerry Robinson (Mike Farrell) to serve as a sidekick who can interpret humanity for the emotionless, logical robot. The only thing that Questor knows for sure is that he's looking for some kind of boat, and to make matters worse, Questor's on a time limit, as the miniature fusion generator powering his body is going to explode like a nuclear weapon if he doesn't find Vaslovik soon.

Sources indicate that as he and Jerry travel the world, Questor has plenty of opportunities to show off his enhanced strength and android abilities, but when they reach the end of the journey, things start to get weird — well, assuming that the opening sequence of an unfinished Questor looking like a half-melted Ken doll twitching to life while strapped down crucifix style wasn't weird enough. It turns out that the boat Questor's looking for is Noah's Ark, and when he and Jerry head to Mt. Ararat to find it, they're instead met with a cave with hundreds of deceased androids laid out on slabs. It turns out that Vaslovik was the most recent in a long line of droids left by extraterrestrial "Masters" to guide and protect humanity without directly interfering. Now, that's Questor's job.

If the idea of a sentient android who never really knew his creator searching for his own humanity sounds a little familiar, it's because that's also a pretty accurate description of Data from "Star Trek: The Next Generation." That's a theme that Roddenberry would return to several times in his career, starting with Spock on the original "Trek" and his struggles balancing his purely logical Vulcan side with his more emotional, half-human heritage, but with Data, the parallels are even more clear.

There's even a scene in "The Questor Tapes" that would be blatantly recycled for "TNG." At one point, Questor and Jerry hit a casino to make some quick cash for their journey, with Questor using his android senses and strength to rack up big wins at the craps table, even reshaping a pair of loaded dice when the house tries to foil his win streak.

According to recent reports, in the "TNG" Season 2 episode "The Royale," which involved a lot of rewriting that was created conflict among the staff, Data does the same thing to break the bank at the eponymous hotel. Sadly, he doesn't also copy Questor's tendency to repeatedly refer to throwing dice as "exposing specific faces of the cubes," a bit that's genuinely very funny.

#131412. 34 Years Later, the Best 'Far Side' Quote Will Still Leave You Speechless

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (838 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Polygon ↗ Open Full Page

34 Years Later, the Best 'Far Side' Quote Will Still Leave You Speechless

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In recent months, I’ve been examining the best-ever quotes from various newspaper comic strips, and in that time I’ve determined that every comic strip requires its own approach.
  • It has been revealed that larson didn’t do deep and inspirational.
  • Larson’s work often requires the reader to investigate something, but usually not in any kind of overly deep way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent months, I’ve been examining the best-ever quotes from various newspaper comic strips, and in that time I’ve determined that every comic strip requires its own approach. For Charles Schulz’s Peanuts, I chose something heartfelt and inspirational because those comics and characters really have inspired people. For Bill Watterson’s Calvin and Hobbes, I investigated something more philosophical, as the best of those comics make the audience contemplate human nature and the world around them. But for Gary Larson’s The Far Side, the task is monumentally different.

It has been revealed that larson didn’t do deep and inspirational. Many of his cartoons required you to think, but not because they were thoughtful. Larson’s work was brilliant, and it sometimes took a few minutes to figure out what the punchline was. Take, this comic strip where an artist is painting a woman as a half-fly creature, for example. You likely see the woman or the painting first, and you wonder why the artist is painting her that way. Only after inspecting the comic more closely do you see the dead fly stuck to his glasses.

Larson’s work often requires the reader to investigate something, but usually not in any kind of overly deep way.

According to recent reports, the Far Side is brilliant, but it's not the kind of comic strip that makes you ponder life’s big questions. Larson channeled his genius into joke-telling, and that’s what made The Far Side so sharply funny. As such, determining Larson’s best-ever Far Side quote shouldn’t be some insightful, inspirational, or thoughtful journey — even though I did try going that way at first.

I thought maybe the quote should come from a comic about God, as several Far Side comics feature God as a character. But after reading a bunch of Larson’s God comics, I determined that God actually isn’t all that deep or interesting. Sometimes he’s just kind of a jerk.

Then I thought to look up comics about death, thinking that maybe Larson had something profound to say on the subject. Given Larson’s signature macabre style of humor, death is featured frequently in The Far Side, but nothing seemed all that weighty or important. I finally abandoned this approach when I found a comic where a snake hanged himself with his own body.

Sources indicate that that’s when I gave up on going deep and decided to just find something funny. But there are thousands of Far Side comics, and Larson’s humor varied. Sometimes he was dark, sometimes he was silly, sometimes he deconstructed a well-known saying or song or other pop culture reference. So I tried to find a quote that did all — or at least most of — what Larson was known for. Also, I wanted a quote where the visual wasn’t required to get the joke. Larson’s work was highly visual, and with generally just one panel, it often had the visual as the setup and the caption as the punchline. If I was looking for the best ever Far Side comic, it would be one where the visual and the caption work in concert. But while trying to find the best-ever quote, I wanted something where the image was not required.

For a little while I thought about going with “Welcome to hell… here’s your accordion,” from a comic which shows Heaven and Hell. In Heaven, you’re given a harp, but in Hell you’re given an accordion. I liked this because it’s very dark and silly, and it’s the kind of thing you’d only find in The Far Side. Eventually though I softened on it because the visual is still the stronger element in this one. The line comes off as basically a funny non-sequitur without the visual. To get the whole joke about how accordions are terrible instruments, you really need the contrast.

After abandoning that comic, I found this one from 1992 and realized it was the perfect fit. The image shows a mime under a falling tree and the caption reads:.

“Question: If a tree falls in the forest and no one’s around, and it hits a mime, does anyone care?”.

I think this is the one because it’s funny, because it's dark, because it's silly, and because it takes a well-known idiom — the tree falling in the woods question — and turns it into a punchline. That may not do everything that Larson did, but it’s a lot of his very best qualities all in one place.

According to recent reports, and, unlike the vast majority of Far Side comics, it’s more about the words than the image. Larson’s gags were almost always visual, or at least relied on a visual component to get his jokes across. For this comic, I’d argue that you don’t need the visual at all. Sure, the drawing is funny, but in no way is it required. Also, this quote is entirely lacking in emotional or philosophical depth, which is precisely what you want when you’re reading The Far Side.

All 10 James Bond Movies Not Based On Ian Fleming's Books, Ranked

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2078 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we're taking a look back at the James Bond movies that are not based on Ian Fleming's books and short stories.
  • Here are all 10 James Bond movies not based on Ian Fleming's books ranked, going in their own direction with the super-spy.
  • Recent findings suggest that pierce Brosnan currently remains the only actor whose entire run as James Bond featured original narratives for his movies, rather than drawing directly from a specific Fleming story.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we're taking a look back at the James Bond movies that are not based on Ian Fleming's books and short stories. Some of the entries here take their titles from short stories written by Ian Fleming but, frankly, nothing else. Outside of the inclusion of Bond and his usual allies and enemies, these cinematic narratives really strike out on their own creatively.

Here are all 10 James Bond movies not based on Ian Fleming's books ranked, going in their own direction with the super-spy.

Recent findings suggest that pierce Brosnan currently remains the only actor whose entire run as James Bond featured original narratives for his movies, rather than drawing directly from a specific Fleming story. In taking Bond out of the Cold War setting in which he originated, this led to an uneven tenure, despite Brosnan's best efforts. However, nothing could quite save Brosnan's last turn as 007 in 2002's "Die Another Day," opening with a title track by Madonna that sounded dated when it was released. The movie has Bond square off with a rogue North Korean general while trying to identify who betrayed him on a mission that led to a prolonged torturous imprisonment.

Recent findings suggest that IMDb names "Die Another Day" as the worst James Bond movie, a dubious distinction that is, unfortunately, well-deserved. The movie opens with Bond infiltrating North Korea by surfing, because that's clearly what the kids are still into, and it only gets worse from there. This backslide into mediocrity spreads to the cinematography, complete with shoddy CG effects and random slow-motion sequences for no discernible reason other than an attempt to look cool. An absolute travesty and an embarrassing way for Brosnan to end his time as Bond, "Die Another Day" is a grating viewing experience.

In a recent development, yes, "A View to a Kill," Moore's swan song to the franchise, takes its title from the 1960 Fleming short story "From a View to a Kill." But whereas the literary namesake features Bond hunting a motorcycle-driving assassin in France, the 1985 movie pits 007 against an immoral tech tycoon before it was cool. The tycoon in question is Max Zorin (Christopher Walken), a sadistic figure looking to corner the microchip market by destroying Silicon Valley. But outside of Walken chewing the scenery, joined by Grace Jones playing his enforcer, and a memorable title track by Duran Duran, the movie falls flat.

Roger Moore was horrified by "A View to a Kill," particularly the widespread casual violence, as Zorin mercilessly murders many of his associates. We're personally horrified by how rough around the edges the overall movie is, from its lackluster stunts to its abrupt finale. To make matters worse, when the movie's filming wrapped, at 57 years old, Moore looks visibly aged out of playing a spry secret agent. A half-hearted end to Moore's celebrated run playing James Bond, "A View to a Kill" feels as tired as its lead actor.

Daniel Craig's sophomore outing as Bond in 2008's "Quantum of Solace" also takes its title from a 1960 short story written by Fleming. But the literary tale simply follows Bond as he attends a dinner party in Nassau where he hears a story about an unhappy marriage. With that certainly not enough for an action movie to go off of, the film instead functions as a direct sequel to "Casino Royale," opening minutes later. Bond uncovers a global network that's infiltrated government organizations worldwide, including MI6, while contending with his own unresolved grief over his recently deceased lover Vesper Lynd (Eva Green).

For as much grief as "Quantum of Solace" gets, constantly existing in the shadow of "Casino Royale," it's a perfectly watchable Bond movie. The shortest in the series to date, the film does feel like a parade of action set pieces, but Craig's performance grounds the spectacle. The movie's themes about water scarcity and a cabal of affluent influencers trying to manipulate international governments does feel prescient. Coming off as an extended epilogue to "Casino Royale" rather than its own standalone experience, "Quantum of Solace" really works best watched in concert with its immediate predecessor.

Compared to its more action-oriented predecessor, "The World Is Not Enough" tried to lean more into dramatic territory. The 1999 movie opens with Bond (Brosnan) tricked into delivering a bomb to MI6 related to a kidnapping plot involving oil heiress Elektra King (Sophie Marceau). After being assigned to protect Elektra, Bond hunts down the terrorist responsible for the explosive incident, only to uncover a whole plot targeting vital oil pipelines into Europe. This leads Bond to realize that Elektra is not as helpless or innocent as he believed when they struck up their illicit romance.

Taking its title from Bond's family motto introduced in "On Her Majesty's Secret Service," "The World Is Not Enough" tries to feel like a more personal adventure for 007 accordingly. But as good a femme fatale as Sophie Marceau is, the movie never quite delivers on the emotional potential that it aspires to. The action is a bit lackluster too, feeling like something more akin to a theme park stunt spectacular than a blockbuster set piece. Underscoring that Brosnan was often working with lesser material during his Bond run, "The World Is Not Enough" couldn't live up to its creative ambitions.

Industry observers note that there was a lot of expectation riding on "Spectre" after the critical and commercial success of its immediate predecessor "Skyfall." The movie also marks the first official Bond movie since "Diamonds Are Forever" to explicitly include Ernst Stavro Blofeld, after protracted legal problems prevented the villain's usage. This time, Blofeld is played by Christoph Waltz, with the added backstory that he and Bond grew up together contentiously as surrogate brothers, before the criminal mastermind faked his death. Since then, the movie reveals Blofeld has secretly been tormenting Bond from the shadows, leading to their eventual unhappy reunion for the fate of the world.

It has been revealed that "Spectre" falls into the trap of trying to emulate "Skyfall" too much, right down to directly lifting music tracks from the preceding movie's score. The idea of Blofeld being Bond's brother figure, a concept also introduced in the 007 spoof "Austin Powers in Goldmember," is a laughable way to make their dynamic feel more personal. What salvages the movie from its lackluster script is its top-notch cinematography by Hoyte van Hoytema, particularly its stunning opening scene in Mexico City.

Brosnan's sophomore outing as Bond in 1997's "Tomorrow Never Dies" doesn't get as much credit as it deserves, overshadowed by its more successful predecessor. Another prescient entry in the series as far as its story is concerned, the main villain is a murderous media mogul providing his own news output. In order to take his media empire to the next level, Elliot Carver (Jonathan Pryce) tries to orchestrate a war between the United Kingdom and China. Bond and Chinese intelligence operative Wai Lin (Michelle Yeoh) work together to expose Carver's plot and prevent the conflict from breaking out.

In a recent development, considering "Tomorrow Never Dies" scrapped its script days before filming, it's a wonder the movie came out as well as it did. The movie goes even more global than many other series' entries, taking Bond everywhere from Carver's offices in Germany to the streets of Saigon. What holds the movie back is that its plot does feel visibly rushed, while none of the action set pieces are as satisfying as the major moments in "GoldenEye." A glossier approach to the franchise than its predecessor's post-Cold War grittiness, "Tomorrow Never Dies" is a serviceable entry in Brosnan's Bond legacy.

When Daniel Craig closed out his celebrated run as James Bond, he did so with a bang, leaving no stone unturned. This made "No Time to Die" the longest James Bond movie ever, opening with Bond believing his latest serious paramour, Madeleine Swann (Léa Seydoux), had betrayed him to Spectre. After abruptly leaving the service in the wake of this assumption, Bond is pulled back into action when a secret weapon is stolen from the British government. In the process of destroying this deadly project, Bond has to face familiar faces from his life before a fatal showdown against the terrorist Lyutsifer Safin (Rami Malek).

According to recent reports, while it could've trimmed about 15 minutes from its runtime, "No Time to Die" provides Craig with a largely solid farewell. From the dusty streets of Italy where Bond tries to get closure for the events of "Casino Royale" to its explosive finale, the movie hits all the right notes. The film's villains, including Malek's Safin, are a bit of a mixed bag, but the action, including a centerpiece sequence in Cuba, is competently staged. A satisfying end to Craig's five-movie run as 007, "No Time to Die" sticks the landing even if it takes some time to get there.

In a recent development, while it's not as fondly remembered today, 1989's "License to Kill" is an essential James Bond everyone should see at least once. Timothy Dalton's second and final turn as 007, the movie begins with Felix Leiter (David Hedison) and his upcoming bride being attacked by drug lord Franz Sanchez (Robert Davi). With MI6 refusing to retaliate, considering the incident an outside matter, Bond angrily resigns from the service and sets out to avenge his friend. This unsanctioned vendetta eventually reveals that there is more at stake with Sanchez's latest scheme than Bond realized.

Though Dalton brought a more serious edge to Bond with his first movie in the role, "The Living Daylights," "License to Kill" is where he really cuts loose. Long before Daniel Craig did it, Dalton played Bond as a mean, lethal type that had no problem with getting his hands dirty to get the job done. These harder-edged sensibilities caught people off-guard, with the memory of the light-hearted Roger Moore tenure still fresh in their minds. But if you're looking to see why Timothy Dalton is filmmaker Christopher Nolan's favorite Bond actor, "License to Kill" is the perfect showcase.

Industry observers note that after a six-year hiatus following "License to Kill," James Bond finally returned to the silver screen in 1995, this time with Pierce Brosnan playing the role. "GoldenEye" was almost the end of the James Bond franchise as it tried to find its way after the Cold War. The specter of those global tensions certainly inform the movie's story, with Bond learning a Soviet-era weapons satellite has been hijacked. Venturing into the heart of Russia to identify the culprit, Bond comes face-to-face with his old friend and former 00 Agent Alec Trevelyan (Sean Bean), now leading a crime syndicate.

The Bond movie series needed a shot of adrenaline if it hoped to stay alive after the Cold War, and "GoldenEye" delivered. Brosnan strikes the perfect balance between Moore's self-aware charm and Dalton's steely-eyed intensity while exploring the nuances of the character like never before. The action is as memorable as the franchise gets, and the supporting cast around Brosnan all turn in fantastic work, especially Bean as Trevelyan. Cementing the franchise's relevance beyond a set time period, "GoldenEye" remains the most important box office hit in Bond history, and that comes from a film of enduring quality.

Speaking of box office success, "Skyfall" became the biggest James Bond movie ever when it opened in theaters in 2012. Continuing Daniel Craig's run after a four-year hiatus, the movie has Bond reconcile with his lethal occupation's toll on his body and mind after a disastrous mission in Istanbul. Returning to duty after London is attacked by a shadowy figure linked to M (Judi Dench) and her own unresolved legacy, Bond has to contend with his own advancing age. Fortunately, this mission and its eccentric villain Raoul Silva (Javier Bardem) are just the things to help Bond overcome his midlife crisis.

Recent findings suggest that released in time for the film series' 50th anniversary, "Skyfall" feels like a celebration and commentary on the legacy of James Bond. Under sharp direction from Sam Mendes, the movie beautifully illustrates those themes while delivering bombastic action sequences, including a fantastic fight scene in Shanghai. Elevating the proceedings is haunting cinematography from Roger Deakins, really accentuating the light and shadows that Bond frequently plays in. An absolute masterpiece from top to bottom, "Skyfall" deconstructs Bond and thematically rebuilds him for the 21st century.
