#131410. Advice for Young Researchers

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3205 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Blogspot ↗ Open Full Page

Advice for Young Researchers

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Blogspot

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m currently in the process of recruiting a whole new research lab, as I’m moving to a new university.
  • It has been revealed that I’m doing this against a backdrop of things moving fast, to say the least.
  • Sources indicate that what does this mean for an incoming PhD student?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m currently in the process of recruiting a whole new research lab, as I’m moving to a new university. I’m sifting through several hundred PhD student and postdoc applications in order to hire a handful of people initially, and more soon. The quality of the candidates is excellent, and several of them have impressed me deeply in interviews. (It also makes me wonder how I ended up getting a PhD position back in 2004; I was way less prepared then than my top candidates are now.) The selection work is hard but fun, as work should be.

It has been revealed that I’m doing this against a backdrop of things moving fast, to say the least. Two years ago AI agents were mediocre at coding and terrible at maths; today they are, in some senses, superhuman at both. You can now simply give an AI agent a research idea, and it goes away and does the work and gives you a finished paper. You can even ask the damn thing to come up with the research idea itself. In my field and experience, the result is typically a fairly solid but also quite boring paper, reporting some incremental progress on some minor problem with good experimental statistics but terrible writing. Nothing that would win any awards, but the kind of work that used to be a respectable first paper from a PhD student. Now, you can get it with a prompt. And, again, things are moving fast. I’m not sure how much the writing abilities of AI agents will improve, but their ability to design and execute complex research pipelines is likely to be much better next year, and then next year again….

Sources indicate that what does this mean for an incoming PhD student? And what does this mean for a PI, responsible for hiring students and postdocs, setting research direction, managing a lab, and advising students, which means being everything from domain expert to brainstorming partner to secretary to therapist? I will try to reason about this here. My field is AI for games/creativity/open-endedness, but I guess what I say will apply to other fields to some extent.

It has been revealed that let us first agree on what a PhD is supposed to be about. During a PhD you learn to do research, meaning that you learn to produce or uncover new knowledge. New, as in new to humanity. The way you learn this is through a form of apprenticeship: you do research on your own and together with others, advised by one or more senior, experienced researchers. Typically, you are part of a research group led by a professor who is also your advisor. In my experience, your advisor and research group, and how well you get along with them, matter a lot to the quality of the research you do and your general enjoyment and mental health. Much more than the prestige of the university.

Recent findings suggest that in general, you develop skills, factual knowledge, and understanding during a PhD. As a viral tweet stated, you can outsource thinking but not understanding. I think this is an excellent observation. Understanding is what really matters. The more work AI agents can do, the more you need to understand in order to guide them. Also, understanding is arguably the main goal of science (as opposed to technology). Still, skills, factual knowledge, and understanding cannot be easily disentangled. Implementing an algorithm brings not only skill, but also a level of understanding that you cannot get from simply importing it, or having an agent implement it for you.

It has been revealed that there is a phenomenon which I call understanding debt, by analogy to technical debt. Understanding debt is when you have had your agents do a bunch of stuff for you, and you no longer really understand what’s going on. Then you’re faced with the prospect of either trying to understand in depth what’s happening, or just going on anyway. But if you go on anyway, you will notice that the quality and relevance of your inputs drop, because you no longer understand enough to make informed decisions. This is something that I think we will all need to learn and re-learn as agents get better.

It has been revealed that I’m not saying I’ve solved this for myself. I have various half-finished projects sitting around that will probably never get published because I am not ready to put in the work to understand them well enough to write them up. Writing them up is a good test; you need to really understand a project to be able to write a good paper about it. And you should definitely write it yourself, at least the first draft. If you weren’t interested enough to write it, why would anyone be interested enough to read it? Pushing slop on your peers is rude. On the other hand, using agents to critique and polish your drafts is useful.

Which brings us to a key question for a beginning researcher, just like for everyone else in a knowledge-intensive profession: When and how should you outsource your work to AI agents? The answer is not “as often as possible”.

According to recent reports, why not? Because your effort and your choices matter. You can see this in project-based classes, as well as in workplaces which use AI heavily. Even when everyone has access to the same AI tools, the quality and character of people’s contributions vary widely. (Not so much the quantity, because it’s so easy to produce things now.) Some students in my classes turn in barely adequate work, whereas others repeatedly shine. Typically, those who turn in the best work also understand it the best. Just like it’s always been; access to amazing tools does not erase the value of talent and dedication. Perhaps it even amplifies it.

Here’s another reason: Just because you can get to lots of places rapidly and easily by flying does not mean that you should never drive, or bike, or even walk. There is lots to be gained by seeing the landscape up close. If your idea of visiting a country is to go only to the major cities with international airports, you are going to get a very skewed idea of that country. Most of the US is really not like Newly introduced York, and most of Sweden is not like Stockholm. From the car window, you can see farms, factories, and small towns; you can stop to talk to people and get their views. If you walk or bike, it takes even longer to get to your destination, but you’ll notice way more details. You’ll also be able to take little detours, perhaps find new paths that aren’t even on the map yet. Perhaps you will be the ones to put these paths on the map, and lay the first stone for the airport, so that people can one day fly there. It’s exciting to be an explorer! In fact, as a researcher, it’s your job to take the roads less traveled. Anyone can buy a ticket to the significant swanky international airports and sip espresso in a lounge. It’s your job to do the uncomfortable and uncertain: make your way through the jungles/mountains/swamps/ruins so that we can go somewhere we couldn’t go before.

According to recent reports, nothing wrong with getting carried away by a metaphor. In fact, it can be a good way to ideate. See for example bio-inspired algorithms, where a lot of good ideas have come from taking biological metaphors very seriously. A lot of bad ideas as well. Luckily, we can run experiments to help us tell the bad ideas from the good ones. Running experiments is now easier than ever, and you will be doing a lot of it as a PhD student, to test your ideas and develop your understanding.

Given how easy it now is to implement and test ideas, many researchers will probably be spending their time in tight loops with agents, feeding them ideas to test, and trying to make sense of the results as they come in. I personally think it is important to also spend plenty of time offline reading and writing before handing instructions to the agents, but research and thinking styles vary. We are all learning and re-learning how to work with these upcoming tools available to us, and I think it is important to also experiment with how we work.

I think PhD programs in technical subjects are going to become more similar to art schools, in the sense that the focus will increasingly be on developing your own style of asking and answering questions. And of course your taste in questions. During an MFA (Master of Fine Arts, typically the terminal degree in an art school) the student learns to develop and express a cohesive artistic identity, a process which includes plenty of conceptual argumentation. Craft, in contemporary art, is often taken as a given, or as something that can be outsourced. Interestingly, this describes successful senior researchers as well: they are known mostly for their artistic identity, as the actual craft of their research is largely carried out by their postdocs and PhD students. The artistic identity of the PI is what gives their lab a research direction, and attracts attention, students, and funding. What has changed recently is that outsourcing of the craft of research (to AI agents) can happen further down the line; the PI might now need to spend more time and effort supporting the development of their PhD students’ researcher identities and research taste rather than technical skills.

Now, some people might disagree with how I paint research as akin to art. Science, they would say, is about truth; however great Picasso, Virginia Woolf, or Charlie Parker were, they were not searching for truth. I would rather set aside the complex question of whether art seeks truth, and instead emphasize that many of the greatest scientists and inventors operate with something like an artistic worldview, with their taste in problems rooted in visions only they fully understand, based on their idiosyncratic combinations of interests and understandings. See: Einstein, Ramón y Cajal, Lovelace, McClintock, Feynman, Tesla. Artists. But they helped uncover new truths, because they generated ideas that could be tested experimentally. With AI agents potentially automating so much of research execution, even junior researchers could have the resources to develop their unique vision.

Recent findings suggest that things will change when it comes to the rituals, norms, and technical infrastructure that govern research dissemination and collaboration. Take academic publishing. People have been complaining about the academic publishing machinery for a long time now. Well, good/bad news: AI agents seem to be pushing it to some kind of breaking point this time. As it is trivial to just generate latest papers that may or may not have scientific value, conferences and journals are getting flooded by shameless papermaxxers and jolly amateurs. Nobody wants to review this flood of slop, so people just ask AI agents to do it for them.

It has been revealed that reviewing will have to evolve, taking into account that AI agents are now very good at many aspects of the review process, including replication and fact-checking. The human part of the review process might deal more with critical commentary and judging what is interesting, perhaps with the fact that people chose to review your paper at all becoming an vital signal. Yes, this is another way in which technical research may come to resemble arts more.

Sources indicate that and yes, your papers need to be interesting. Your job as a researcher is not just to produce research, but to produce interesting research. This remark may seem trivial and obvious to some, and borderline blasphemous to others. There are those who think that human value judgment should be minimized in the research and publication process. Papers should be accepted purely on technical merits in an as-blind-as-possible process. I think we should go the other way. As more and more of the research process can be automated, the scarce resource is your own vision, narrative, and personality. There are infinitely many things you can do at any given point, and infinitely many questions you can address. Your job is to choose the next step to take towards some goal that perhaps only you understand. Then, your job is to explain to the world what you are trying to do and why that is vital.

It is sometimes remarked that you should write the novel you want to read, make the music you want to listen to, or paint the paintings you want to see. Good advice, methinks. Well, you need to be capable of doing the work as well; some authors would rather write like Shakespeare or Dostoyevsky, but find success writing teen soaps or movie tie-in novels. As for myself, I’m neither Turing nor von Neumann, but I’m doing alright in my niche. Anyway. You should write the papers you want to read. To do that, do the research you are interested in. In general, you must do work that interests you.

Sources indicate that this leads to an interesting problem: how do you develop your interest, so that you find the right things interesting? You must know things first to find upcoming things interesting. I would not be interested in measures of skill depth through agent differentiation, tradeoffs of tokenizer design, or arguments against functionalism in the philosophy of mind if I had not spent a lot of time reading, writing, thinking about, and even experimenting in those domains. Did I simply follow my own interests all the way there? No, not simply. Sometimes I’ve done and read really tiresome things because I thought it would advance my interests. And by sometimes, I mean often.

Now for the most obvious thing I’m saying in this text: to be an interesting person, with interesting interests, you must be interested in multiple different things, and be able to see the connection between them. Because that’s where the magic happens, and that’s what makes people want to talk to you at the party. (I’m talking about parties where you don’t need to shout, civilized ones where you sit in armchairs and sip good wine.) Look, there is a near-infinite number of things to know in the world. But humanity only knows a small sliver of these things, and a good LLM in a good harness knows a shockingly large proportion of that sliver. But the number of combinations of things you can know is vastly larger than the number of things there are to know (elementary combinatorics), and it is entirely possible to have a unique set of specialized knowledge, and a unique combination of interests. This means that you, by seeing the connection between your unique set of interests, can take research in a unique direction. If you only studied the standard CS curriculum and your interests are all discussed on AI Twitter, then you need to broaden your horizons. Go to a different section of the bookstore, buy some books you wouldn’t normally think of reading, and read them. Talk to people on the train about what they do at work all day (most people are very happy to talk about their work if you ask them, and their jobs are way more diverse than you think). Talk to your family.

As I’m apparently in the habit of saying obvious things, let me continue down that path. Obviously, hard work matters, just like it always did. There is a certain allure in simply sending off tasks to agents, feeling good about having “done” something, and calling it a day. But then you are not adding much of yourself. And you’re not learning much; there pretty much needs to be friction for effective learning. When I recruit for my lab, I’m looking for the people who run towards friction, those who actually like to learn and to put in the effort. People with a high need for cognition. This is as notable now as it ever was, but the AI era has led to a nice litmus test, as some people like to say things like “my work is so easy now that AI can do it for me”. Those are people I don’t want to hire as PhD students, or for any other intellectual job. Work should be hard but fun.

Let me now try to summarize what I’ve been writing as terse advice: Be yourself. Be unique. Become an interesting person by broadening and deepening your interests. Do hard work, seek out the friction that leads to learning. Do things that interest you, write things that interest others. Understand, formulate, and develop your identity as a researcher, which is much like being an artist. Seek to do the research that only you would do, in your own style. Learn how you best work with these marvelous fresh things we call AI agents by thorough experimentation, and how to manage understanding debt. Read a lot, and always write the first draft of whatever you’re writing yourself. If it’s not worth your time to write, it’s not worth anyone else’s time to read.

Note that while I very much think we should all experiment with AI-enhanced workflows, I am emphatically not saying that we should, in Gretzky’s words, simply “skate to where the puck is going to be”. Some Silicon Valley people believe they know what the future looks like, and that that future looks like us replacing our own thinking with AI systems as much as we can. Well, Silicon Valley is an incestuous monoculture; listener beware. Nobody knows where the puck will be. The puck might be like a wave function that never really collapses; there might be lots of pucks. And we are not passive observers, we can steer the puck by methodically scrubbing the ice. A bit like how we can steer an extended sports metaphor from ice hockey to curling.

It has been revealed that finally, remember that we’re all in this together. AI agents are changing things rapidly, and we are all trying to figure out, and shape, the new rules. Welcome to the club! Let’s get to work.

It has been revealed that a sip of fresh and real air in this doomed echo chamber current. thanks!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, you can cancel your Prime subscription via web browser by first logging into your Amazon account. Amazon has a Cancel Your Prime Membership button on its support page to launch the process, or you can follow the steps detailed on Amazon's page:.

Head to Amazon.com in your web browser.

Hover over the Accounts & Lists menu on the top-right of the window, then select the Prime Membership option.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

Note that Amazon requires a bunch of clicks to finalize your cancellation, giving you lots of “opportunities” to change your mind.

Open the Amazon Shopping app on your mobile device.

Click the three horizontal lines on the bottom right.

Under Shop by Category, select Prime.

On the top bar, slide all the way to the end and select Help.

Then tap the End Your Amazon Prime Membership button and finally click the Cancel Your Prime Membership orange button.

Follow the on-screen instructions to cancel your Prime subscription.

As mentioned, closing your account will immediately end your access. Amazon also offers you the option to pause your benefits and billing temporarily instead of canceling them completely. Either way, your Amazon account is still active—you simply won’t have Prime benefits.

Finally, if you have other subscriptions connected to your Prime account, those will end when your billing is up. And if you signed up for Prime through the Android mobile shopping app or the Prime Video Android app, you’ll have to go through Google Subscription to manage your membership.

Recent findings suggest that yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, and we vet our deals to make sure they’re the best ones. You can also refer to guides like our live blog that have already done all of the vetting for you. And if you have an Amazon Prime membership, make the most of it.

The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Robert Pattinson's Divisive Sci-Fi Action Movie Proves He's Perfect For James Bond

💡 Key Takeaways

  • And, as we all know, looking good in a suit is one of the main requirements to play 007, so Pattinson has already passed his first test as our newly-cast James Bond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, how good does Robert Pattinson look in a tailored suit? Damn good, is the answer.

Industry observers note that the proof is in Christopher Nolan's 2020 time-warp thriller "Tenet," wherein Pattinson sports a dazzling wardrobe of bespoke suits, knit polos, scarves, and impeccably rumpled pocket squares. The attire in "Tenet," provided by Oscar-nominated costume designer Jeffrey Kurland, are so impressive that GQ Magazine had to pause to write an article about them (even if it was just to complain that the suits look a little too good).

And, as we all know, looking good in a suit is one of the main requirements to play 007, so Pattinson has already passed his first test as our newly-cast James Bond.

Recent findings suggest that however you feel about "Tenet," one has to admit that its costumes are amazing and that Pattinson rocks every single outfit he wears. He carries himself with poise and class, playing the sidekick Neil to the film's protagonist, The Protagonist (John David Washington). Poise and class are the bedrocks on which James Bond is built, and Pattinson can certainly handle those qualities with skill.

Industry observers note that "Tenet" is Nolan's lowest-rated directorial effort among critics on Rotten Tomatoes, and in his own review for /Film, Chris Evangelista pointed out that no one will be able to figure out what the heck is going on in the film. Having seen it, I agree and can confirm that I have trouble grasping the physics of its sci-fi rigmarole. The movie centers on a machine that can cause people and objects to travel through time in "reverse," yet they continue to exist in regular space. As a result, humans and items that have been "inverted" seem to be moving in reverse. To them, though, it's the rest of the world that appears to be going in the wrong direction.

Sources indicate that by the time-travel conceit of "Tenet," effect precedes cause. That means an inverted person can point a backward-moving gun at a target and, somehow, a bullet is sucked out of the wall and pulled back into the gun's chamber. How an inverted person caused that to happen is unclear to me. There is likewise a scene wherein the regular-moving Protagonist has to fight someone who is inverted and while Christopher Nolan's use of reverse photography is ingenious here, I couldn't help but wonder how one lands a punch when one is moving backward through time.

Sources indicate that and if the time-travel physics are hard enough to fathom, there's also a twisted plot laid on top of them. The average sci-fi fan will likely be unable to remember all the details after just one go-through. Really, one will likely only recall a few fascinating visuals from "Tenet," and a very, very general sense of what's happening.

Sources indicate that in short, Kenneth Branagh plays a dying Russian oligarch who has decided to destroy the world, with Robert Pattison and John David Washington playing the agents sent to foil his efforts. In addition, the oligarch's estranged wife (Elizabeth Debicki) is tragically mixed up in all this. The film even climaxes with armies of soldiers moving alternately forward and backward through time, and the apprehension of an oblique doomsday device. Truly, "Tenet" is a rather confusing movie.

Again, some of the imagery in "Tenet" is elaborate and fascinating, and the scenes of Neil and the Protagonist discussing things have a breezy tone. Even if their conversations are oblique and unmemorable, one gets the vibe that Pattinson is wholly at ease. He has a 007-like confidence.

As mentioned, "Tenet" might be Christopher Nolan's least beloved film. It's too hard-to-follow to be a super crowd-pleaser, and it wasn't as well-loved by the Academy as some of Nolan's other movies (despite winning the Oscar for Best Visual Effects). Some critics were downright savage to the film, including Mick LaSalle. Writing for the San Francisco Chronicle, he gave the film one star out of four, arguing that it was confusing yet didn't really inspire a viewer to try to understand it.

According to recent reports, brian Tallerico, writing for RogerEbert.com, was kinder, giving the film three stars out of four and drawing parallels to the James Bond franchise. He noted that Kenneth Branagh's destruction-hungry Russian oligarch is straight out of the Bond playbook, adding:.

It has been revealed that "[T]here's never been a Bond movie so stuffed with expository dialogue. 'Tenet' spends roughly two hours of its 150-minute run time explaining what is happening, why it is happening, and what might happen next. And yet even with that it's still incredibly difficult to follow because Nolan goes so far down his own rabbit hole of time travel that one almost needs to take notes to keep up (and I still think it arguably wouldn't all add up if they could).".

Still, Tallerico noted, "If 'Tenet' can be a hard movie to engage with emotionally or even comprehend narratively, that doesn't take away from its craftsmanship on a technical level." It is, many might agree, an impressive feat, even if it is opaque.

Robert Pattinson, meanwhile, has said that "Tenet" is not about time travel. Of course not. As we now know, the movie is just as much about spy vibes and nice suits as it is time inversion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After landing his breakthrough Hollywood role as the blood-weeping baddie Le Chiffre in "Casino Royale," it seemed like Mads Mikkelsen would be a go-to villain for years to come. He was horrifyingly seductive as Dr. Hannibal Lecter in the NBC series "Hannibal," at which point it was hard to see mainstream viewers accepting him as anything other than a straight-up monster.

Industry observers note that I don't know that he's turned the corner with American audiences, but there's ample evidence out there for moviegoers willing to go off the beaten path that Mikkelsen is terrifically effective as a hero. He can even be downright lovable, as he is in Thomas Vinterberg's booze-drenched comedy "Another Round" (where he gets to show off his hoofing chops).

Mikkelsen is not anywhere close to loveable in Kristian Levring's 2014 Western "The Salvation," but he is brutally compelling as a Danish combat veteran who settles east of the Mississippi River in the 1860s, and goes to war with a malevolent crime boss played with vicious glee by Jeffrey Dean Morgan. It's a different kind of role for Mikkelsen, and a departure for his "Casino Royale" co-star Eva Green as well. Whereas she was glamorous and wounded as Vesper Lynd, she's just flat-out wounded as Morgan's serially abused sister-in-law.

Levring conjures the widescreen majesty of Sergio Leone (replete with an Ennio Morricone-esque score), and depicts the violence with a matter-of-fact bluntness. Alas, despite receiving mostly good reviews (it holds a 72% Fresh rating at Rotten Tomatoes), it got unceremoniously dumped into U.S. theaters in 2015. It's right now available to stream on multiple services, so now is the time to catch up with it!

Industry observers note that mikkelsen stars as Jon, who leaves Denmark with his brother Peter (Mikael Persbrandt) to start anew in America. Eventually, Jon's wife (Nanna Øland Fabricius) and son (Toke Lars Bjarke) join him, and the trio sets out on a stagecoach to begin the American chapter of their lives. Their hopes and dreams are immediately shattered when two criminals eject Jon from the stagecoach. The rape and kill his wife, and also murder his son.

Jon tracks down the coach, and kills the two men. That's revenge served piping hot, but it causes fresh troubles for Jon, as one of the murderers was the brother of ruthless gang leader Henry Delarue (Morgan). Delarue flies into a rage and begins killing townspeople, hoping to intimidate them into helping him capture Jon. Delarue's savagery knows no bounds, and he's especially fond of inflicting his cruelty on Green's mute Madelaine.

Levring isn't out to reinvent the genre. He just wants to make a good-and-bloody Western where the truly nasty bad guys get theirs before the credits roll. If you're a fan of the genre, this is a solid programmer filled with superb performances. So saddle up and get your gunslinging fix. (And then catch up with one of Mikkelsen's finest performances in "The Hunt").

The weight of the role impacts Scott and puts real pressure onto this young character who never expected to be a hero. As he grows in his own abilities, Scott finds a way to haphazardly balance his two lives, but it's never the same as before. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, nicholas Evans' "The Horse Whisperer" was a publishing phenomenon in 1995. The novel is about a young girl who's involved in a horseback riding accident that kills her best friend and their horse, leaving her and her own horse seriously injured. When she falls into a deep funk, her mother whisks her off to rural Montana. There, they try to heal her horse emotionally via a horse whisperer. And while she is married, the mother finds herself falling in love with the handsome, deeply sensitive animal shrink, something which, according to many critics, transformed the narrative into a shamelessly sentimental romance à la "The Bridges of Madison County.".

Sources indicate that the novel sold millions of copies, which meant a film adaptation was inevitable. Like "The Bridges of Madison County," the pedigree didn't make it immediately attractive to A-list directors. But Robert Redford saw something more in the material and took it on as his first directorial effort since his brilliant 1994 drama "Quiz Show." For the first time in his filmmaking career, Redford took the lead in his own movie. He also assembled a sensationally talented cast that included Kristin Scott Thomas, Dianne Wiest, Sam Neill, Chris Cooper, and Cherry Jones. For the role of the young girl, he and the casting team of Ellen Chenoweth and Gretchen Rennell went with up-and-comer Scarlett Johansson, who gave a moving performance that wound up being her breakthrough role.

"The Horse Whisperer" isn't quite on the level of the movie version of "The Bridges of Madison County" (a lovely film that Clint Eastwood saved from production limbo), but the screenplay credited to Eric Roth and Richard LaGravenese is nuanced in a way that maybe the novel isn't. And though it's not one of Redford's best movies, it's a strong piece of work that deserves more attention.

Recent findings suggest that "The Horse Whisperer" holds a 72% Fresh critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes and grossed $187 million at the worldwide box office upon hitting theaters. That was a decent result for Touchstone Pictures, but it didn't come close to matching the runaway success of its source material.

It has been revealed that robert Redford rarely failed to strike up chemistry with his leading ladies ("The Great Gatsby" being a notable exception), so it's hardly a shocker that he's perfectly paired with Kristin Scott Thomas. This is not, however, a heated attraction, as Redford's character is still mourning the end of a previous romance where the woman chose the city over him and the country. Thomas is from the city, too (and, again, married), so he's worried that another heartbreak is around the corner.

As for Scarlett Johansson, she captures the grief of a young woman whose life has been irreparably changed. Her leg was partially amputated, which she fears will make her undesirable to romantic partners as she gets older. This gives rise to the most overpoweringly emotional scene in the movie when, after a row with her mother, Johansson's character tearfully asks, "Who's going to want me?" If that doesn't switch on your waterworks, go straight to the doctor, because your heart isn't properly functioning.

"The Horse Whisperer" is available to rent via streaming, but the film is badly in need of a digital restoration. Hopefully, Disney will commission one at some point, although I'm not sure if the movie is a popular enough library title to merit such treatment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that not everybody is convinced Robert Pattinson is the right choice to be the next James Bond. Some are complaining Bond should be played by someone less famous, like he has in the past. Others feel he’s not masculine enough, or good-looking enough, or charismatic enough. Most of all, though, it seems many people don't love the idea that “the Twilight guy” is playing Bond.

Industry observers note that honestly, I do think there is some merit to the idea that Bond should be played by an up-and-comer, if only because that’s been the tradition. (Clearly Amazon, which took over the franchise in 2025, has other ideas.) As for the more cosmetic complaints, I guess those all come down to personal taste.

As for the Twilight-related concerns, I understand them because, when Pattinson was confirmed as Batman back in 2019, I thought​​​​​​​ “Oh no, the Twilight guy? How could this guy, who seemed so…soft, be the Dark Knight?” I hated the idea. Then, a few months after the announcement, I saw the Robert Eggers film The Lighthouse and completely changed my mind.

According to recent reports, the Lighthouse, which is at the moment streaming on HBO Max, is generally described as a horror film or as psychological horror with some fantasy elements, but I found it to be more of a comedy than anything else. I honestly think that, up until The Lighthouse, I’d literally never seen Pattinson in a movie before. Literally nothing I’d heard of with him had appealed to me, so it wasn’t Pattinson that lured me to The Lighthouse. Part of the reason I went to see The Lighthouse was Willem Dafoe, who I love. Another factor was a review I’d read by film critic Tim Grierson, who described​​​​​​​ the movie as “a terrific comedy about having a terrible roommate.” As a fan of The Odd Couple who regularly laments a lack of comedies in theaters, that was enough to convince me to check it out.

The Lighthouse really is just about two guys in a lighthouse dealing with the loneliness of the job, which requires them to be stuck at sea for weeks at a time. Dafoe plays a grouchy old sea-dog, while Pattinson is his young apprentice. The movie is a laugh riot, with lots of drinking, some wild singing, and both men becoming increasingly unhinged. One dreams he has sex with a mermaid, the other masturbates all the time, and both are brought to their breaking point by the end.

It has been revealed that to be clear, nothing about Pattinson’s character in The Lighthouse made me think that he would be the perfect Batman. His character is a young man who’s green to this profession, but he’s a bit jaded from past failures and secretive about his personal life. He's fairly serious at the beginning, but he jumps into a rage more and more as the film progresses. I guess there’s some overlap with Bruce Wayne/Batman there, but not very much.

The reason why The Lighthouse convinced me of Pattinson's ability to be Batman was that he completely disappears into the role. Mere minutes into the movie, I entirely forgot who I was watching and any skepticism I ever had about the guy. Of course, the mustache and 19th-century New England accent helped with that, but it was more than that. Robert Pattinson is just one of those actors who can completely disappear into a role without any trace of the guy you thought you knew. As much as that’s the desire for any acting role, it doesn’t really happen quite that often, but Pattinson does it in The Lighthouse and I’ve seen him do it in several films since.

Of course, with Pattinson in the news right now, a lot of his movies are being recommended, and while I love him in The Batman, The Odyssey, Tenet, and others, all of those movies have a lot of plot and action going on. In contrast, The Lighthouse​​​​​​​ is pretty bare-bones. You get to see two guys just acting without much else to distract from it.

According to recent reports, the chemistry between Pattinson and Dafoe is also just fantastic. Those two are so funny and interesting together, especially when they are at each other’s throats. It kind of makes me hope for a Lighthouse reunion in one of Pattinson's​​​​​​​ Bond films, with Dafoe cast as a Bond villain. I mean, Dafoe feels like a guy who would make a perfect Bond villain anyway, and, given his chemistry with Pattinson, I think that would be really exciting to see.​​​​​​​.

Perhaps I’m getting ahead of myself a little bit there, but if you, like I did, think of Pattinson as nothing more than that Twilight guy, I’m telling you, you’re wrong, and you only need to see him have sex with a mermaid to wipe that impression clean from your mind​​​​​​​.

The Lighthouse is available to stream on HBO Max.

That means they only have one mentor, the alcoholic Haymitch Abernathy (Woody Harrelson), unlike other Districts' tributes that have two mentors each.

It has been revealed that "Hunger Games" author Suzanne Collins told the story of the first District 12 victor in "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes" — Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), who won the 10th Hunger Games decades before Katniss was born and then vanished. Now, "Sunrise on the Reaping" tells how Haymitch won his own Hunger Games.

Recent findings suggest that haymitch was at a disadvantage before he even entered the arena, since there were no District 12 victors available to mentor him. To address this concern, the Capitol "borrowed" victors from other districts and assigned them to mention Haymitch and his fellow District 12 tributes. Those mentors are Mags Flanagan (Lili Taylor) and Wiress (Maya Hawke), younger versions of characters who first appeared in the second "Hunger Games" film/book, "Catching Fire.".

Recent findings suggest that wiress (played by Amanda Plummer back in "Catching Fire") isn't in the movie much, but "Hunger Games" fans will likely recognize the actress playing her. The daughter of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman, Maya Hawke is one of the more charming "nepo babies" to come out of recent Hollywood.

Hawke has been acting in film and television since 2017, when she played Jo March in a BBC production of "Little Women." In 2019, she not only appeared in Quentin Tarantino's "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" as "Flower Child," a member of the Manson family; she also got her big break. Hawkey joined "Stranger Things" in its third season as Robin Buckley, working alongside Steve Harrington (Joe Keery) at mall ice cream store Scoops Ahoy.

The season seems to set up Robin and Steve as a newly introduced romantic couple ... until she reveals she's not into guys! Despite the show taking place in the 1980s, though, Steve is cool with it. While Season 3 of "Stranger Things" tends to be remembered as one of its weaker outings, Robin was a great addition to the ensemble and Hawke returned as part of the main cast for the subsequent two seasons.

Hawke has also worked alongside her father. In historical miniseries "The Good Lord Bird," where Ethan Hawke starred as radical abolitionist John Brown, Maya Hawke played Brown's daughter, Annie. When Ethan Hawke directed the Flannery O'Connor biopic "Wildcat" in 2023, he cast Maya as the famed author.

Maya Hawke's other film roles include parts in Wes Anderson's "Asteroid City," Pixar sequel "Inside Out 2" as the voice of Anxiety, and a part in the upcoming "Magic: The Gathering" film. Hawke is also a singer-songwriter and has released four studio albums ("Blush," "Moss," "Chaos Angel," and "Maitreya Corso") as of 2026.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is now in theaters.

HBO released on November 8, 1972, and has since produced some of the finest shows in television history. It has also produced plenty of swiftly forgotten and overlooked curios, many of which are actually quite good. The Dustin Hoffman-led "Luck" was, according to critics at least, one example. This horse racing drama looked set to be another ongoing hit for the network until it was canceled following the deaths of three horses involved in production, bringing a tragic end to the show despite the fact it had already been renewed.

David Milch began his career on "Hill Street Blues" before co-creating one of the best shows of the 1990s in "NYPD Blue." That alone would be enough to make him a TV legend, but Milch wasn't done. He managed to steer clear of the ill-advised "NYPD Blue" spin-off "Public Morals," which was canceled after one episode, but he did oversee his share of short-lived crime series in "Brooklyn South," "Total Security," and "Substantial Apple." It wasn't until 2004 that he struck gold again with the HBO series "Deadwood," arguably the best Western TV show ever made. After that, however, Milch's career involved creating little-known series that came and went without making much of an impact.

His 2006 series, "John from Cincinnati," was a strange affair that lasted just one season. "Luck," on the other hand, looked as though it could break the trend and go the distance. Set in the world of horse racing, the Hoffman-fronted series also benefited from the directorial talents of none other than Michael Mann, and became a critical hit, earning a second season renewal. But that second season never materialized after some unfortunate on-set events which forced HBO to cancel "Luck" despite the fact filming had already started on Season 2.

"Luck" was somewhat of a passion project for David Milch, who told the Los Angeles Times, "I've been thinking about doing a show like this for 25 years." The creator explained how his father had taken him to horse racing events since he was age five or six, and how he saw the horses as "heart-stopping beautiful." All of which just makes the story of "Luck" even more tragic.

According to recent reports, dustin Hoffman plays Chester "Ace" Bernstein, a gambler who after coming home after a three-year stay in federal prison immediately concocts a plan for revenge against those who helped put him away. His bodyguard, driver, and right hand man, Gus (Dennis Farina) acts as front for Ace's investment in race horse Pint of Plain. Meanwhile, Hoffman's gambler sets out to restore the failing Santa Anita racetrack as part of his plan for retribution. Nick Nolte also appears as a veteran trainer who now owns his own colt.

It has been revealed that "Luck" premiered in January 2012 to positive reviews and looked as though it might have the potential to become one of the best HBO shows of all time. By the end of that month, the show had already earned a second season renewal. On January 31, 2012, the Los Angeles Times reported that HBO had ordered a further 10 episodes that were set to debut in January 2013, with production on the new season set to get underway in February. According to the outlet, the debut episode brought in 1.1 million viewers and the renewal was "hardly shocking" given Hoffman and Nolte's involvement. What was shocking, however, was that on March 14, 2012, the Los Angeles Times once again reported on the show, this time to announce it had been canceled altogether.

"Luck" Season 1 earned an 82% certified fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with critics praising the cast and writing in particular. But behind all this success, there was trouble brewing. People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) had been on top of HBO and "Luck" since January 2012, the month in which the show debuted. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the organization had written to the channel to enquire as to the treatment of horses used in the show, and had followed up on numerous occasions thereafter.

It has been revealed that as a report from PETA explains, two horses were euthanized during production of the first season. According to the group, "older, arthritic horses had been used in dangerous (and deadly) racing sequences" leading to the two euthanizations. What's more, the report cites "insiders at Santa Anita Race Track" as having provided information about a third horse that died on-set. Rather than push on, HBO pulled the plug and "Luck" was added to the expansive list of the best shows canceled after only one season.

A statement from HBO (via the LA Times), read, "It is with heartbreak that executive producers David Milch and Michael Mann together with HBO have decided to cease all future production on the series 'Luck.'" The network claimed to have maintained "the highest safety standards throughout production," but acknowledged that "accidents unfortunately happen and it is impossible to guarantee they won't in the future." "Luck" Season 1 continued to air, but production on Season 2 was brought to an end despite plenty of footage having already been shot. Today, Season 1 remains available on HBO Max.

A Classic Twilight Zone Episode Is Like A Sci-Fi Version Of An Agatha Christie Mystery

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (869 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The second season of "The Twilight Zone" has some of the series' greatest twist endings, as the show proved unafraid to push into even more out-there science fiction and fantasy.
  • Somewhere in the rural United States, on a dark winter night, a UFO crashes out of the sky.
  • "You've heard of trying to find a needle in a haystack?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The second season of "The Twilight Zone" has some of the series' greatest twist endings, as the show proved unafraid to push into even more out-there science fiction and fantasy. One absolutely outrageous ending I haven't forgotten since childhood comes at the end of "The Twilight Zone" Season 2 Episode 28, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?", written by series creator Rod Serling.

Somewhere in the rural United States, on a dark winter night, a UFO crashes out of the sky. Two state troopers investigate and track the missing pilot to a roadside diner, where a bus trip to Boston has stopped over for food and rest. The bus driver (William Kendis) remembers picking up six passengers, but there are seven in the diner — and he can't remember which of the six faces are the ones who boarded the bus with him.

"You've heard of trying to find a needle in a haystack? Well, stay with us now, and you'll be part of an investigating team whose mission is not to find that proverbial needle, no, their task is even harder. They've got to find a Martian in a diner," says Rod Serling in the episode's opening narration.

Writing about "The Twilight Zone" for /Film, Valerie Ettenhofer compared "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" to an Agatha Christie novel. That comparison stands up quite sturdily. The episode is a closed circle mystery in the vein of "And Then There Were None" or "Murder on the Orient Express," complete with a twist ending that denies the simple answer of one suspect being the guilty person. But instead of looking for a murderer like Hercule Poirot would, the detectives are searching for an alien invader disguised as a human.

Like the best Agatha Christie mysteries, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" winds up the tension by trapping the characters together, because the bridge the bus was meant to cross is out of order. The winter setting complements this; cold weather amps up stress while forcing people to huddle together. Watching the episode decades later, it reads like an ancestor of John Carpenter's "The Thing" — both are about groups of people trapped in the cold and trying to find an alien hidden among them.

In a recent development, but unlike the many Agatha Christie books and movies out there, "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" has to do the setup, mystery, and payoff in only 24 minutes. There's no "characters get picked off one by one" plot structure here, because with the episode's tight timeframe and seven suspects, there's just no way to do that. The episode still manages to capture escalating paranoia, like when even the two married couples among the bus passengers begin to suspect each other. The bug-eyed Mr. Avery (Jack Elam), who keeps laughing at the situation and prodding the others, is the obvious red herring in the ensemble.

There's also never any doubt the Martian is real and rejecting the pretense of ambiguity keeps the episode focused. There's physical proof in the footprints leading out of the pond where the UFO crashed to the diner, and as the episode goes on, inexplicable phenomena like lights flashing and sugar canisters exploding open plague the diner. Rod Serling's intro narration promises a real Martian, too. If this was all a misunderstanding, then it wouldn't be "The Twilight Zone.".

Sources indicate that the real Martian is the curt businessman Ross (John Hoyt), and you can spot an impressive amount of foreshadowing. Ross is one of three passengers traveling alone, leaving him without an alibi for his identity. (The POV panning shot when the troopers enter the diner shows him pointedly sitting alone. He also turns his head away as if trying to escape notice.) Avery jokes Ross is "the most suspicious of the bunch" and probably doesn't realize how right he was.

It has been revealed that at the episode's denouement, the bridge is cleared and everyone departs without getting an answer. But then Ross saunters back into the diner, alone, telling the clerk Haley (Barney Phillips) that the bridge collapsed and everyone else died. That's when he reveals a third arm hidden underneath his coat, mixing his coffee as he explains his fellow Martians are coming to colonize Earth.

According to recent reports, rod Serling doesn't end on that semi-predictable note. Ross' reveal sequence includes close-up reaction shots of Haley, suggesting mounting terror as he finds himself alone with an alien invader. But then Haley agrees. "This is an extraordinary place to colonize. We folks on Venus had the same idea," taking off his cap to reveal a third eye. Haley was beneath both the audience and the troopers' suspicion — he wasn't on the bus, and he technically wasn't the Martian they were looking for, either. The ending avoids feeling like a cheat, too, because the whole mystery rests on there being an alien invader; if one of the diners is a Martian, is it that significant a stretch that another is a Venusian?

The "Will The Real Martian Please Stand Up?" twist may not be more than a clever parlor trick, but what a trick it is.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tracker may have outdone itself this week by pairing Colter Shaw (Justin Hartley) with an unlikely ally who couldn't be more different from our hero on paper. "That's The Job" brings newcomer Josh Holloway into the picture as bounty hunter/gun-for-hire Luke Kelso, who finds himself on the wrong side of Colter's latest job. Just after our favorite rewardist united with his entire cast last week, the CBS program introduces a one-off character who we hope to see again.

Sources indicate that this week's episode picks up in Gray Haven, South Carolina, where bed and breakfast owner John Iddo (Tinpo Lee) closes everything down for the night. However, upon seeing someone outside, he goes out to investigate, only to be suddenly attacked. The next day, Colter is on the road when he gets a call from his latest flame, Jenna Nova (Gillian Bolt), who is on a job collecting a vintage car with her father, Mario (Daniel Edward Mora). The pair rapid-fire some banter about drinks and darts, reminding us why this pair work so well together. It's a sweet little moment as Colter pulls into his next job, and quite the juxtaposition with how the episode ends. Arriving at the B&B, Colter speaks with Eliza (Ruby Jay), John's employee and daughter figure who is concerned about his disappearance. Colter presses her to tell him everything, and Eliza reveals that he takes sleeping pills for insomnia. Walking outside, he finds some blood and evidence of a struggle, as well as what looks like a kill switch for a water sports vehicle. It's then that Eliza reveals that John had gotten into a recent confrontation with some jet ski guys who may have stolen credit card information from B&B guests.

Tracker works because the case changes every week and the four people solving it never do. Here is which of them you are, what it says about you, and the case for yours being the best of the four.

According to recent reports, you would rather handle it yourself and you are usually capable of doing so. Colter is a survivalist who lives in an Airstream and takes reward money for finding missing people, which is a premise that only works because he is clearly running from something of his own.

It has been revealed that you know somebody, and that somebody owes you a favour. Reenie is the lawyer Colter calls when a case needs a door opened legally, and she is the only person on the show who can get further with a phone call than he can on foot.

In a recent development, you are two steps ahead and you rarely mention it. Bobby is the one who finds the thing that unlocks the case, usually from a desk, usually about ninety seconds before anybody realises they needed it.

You turn up, change the temperature of the room, and leave people arguing about you. Russell is Colter's brother, ex-military, and the show has never once let the audience settle on whether he is a help or a problem, which is exactly why he keeps coming back.

When Colter goes to confront the parties responsible, he finds himself surrounded by two guys — which really just means that they're outnumbered. Colter pushes back, pinning one of the jet ski bums and pressing him for more information about John. He’s told that another employee, Lenny Remy (Dylan Kenin), is the man to talk to. Apparently, Lenny went by John's place to send a message, but they hadn’t heard from him since. So, Colter calls Randy (Chris Lee), and it seems like Lenny is bad news. The tech whiz sends our hero to the last pinged location: a trailer park on the other side of town. Entering a condemned manufactured home, Colter finds Lenny beaten and tied up in the closet. According to Lenny, “some psycho” beat him up after he attacked John, knocking him out before he woke up there. When Lenny finally came to, he heard an argument between John and the mystery man — this was a few hours ago. That mystery man? None other than Josh Holloway's Luke, who drops John off at some location after telling him none of it is personal.

Industry observers note that colter continues to look around and finds a few security cameras nearby. Typically, this is when he dials Randy and gets all the footage he needs, but according to Tracker's resident tech guru, it appears that the camera went blank for an hour or so. Colter theorizes that the hired man ran a jammer, which Randy discovers came from a laptop, which is then tracked to the local Dogwood Motel. When Colter arrives, he breaks into a nearby room next to Luke, who readies a firearm of his own. After blasting through the door, Colter narrowly avoids being shot. The man runs, and Colter follows. The result is probably the best fight sequence we've seen this season, maybe on the show period, before Colter gets Luke to talk. From what the bounty hunter knows, he simply dropped John off at a lawyer's office. With the police on the way, Luke decides to go with Colter, albeit as more of a prisoner than a partner.

In a recent development, as Luke soon reveals, he was paid $100K to grab John and not ask questions. This leads to a quick debate over the ethics of their respective professions, where Luke eventually reveals that John’s real name isn't John at all. Rather, he was told that he was really David Watanabe, a man who previously harmed the lawyer in question by supposedly ripping off a Japanese hotel, killing a man, and escaping to the United States. This rattles Colter a little, but a phone call from Reenie (Fiona Rene) puts all the facts back in order. As it turns out, John didn’t kill anyone at all, but rather saved a woman from her abusive husband, Hiro Tanaka (Sonny Saito). After the ex-wife, Mika (Chika Kanamoto), escaped, she turned over evidence of Hiro’s crimes, sending him to prison for decades. Now that Hiro is back, he's itching for revenge.

Although unsure about it at first, Luke eventually agrees to help Colter, who tells him that he needs to make things right. Upon arriving at Hiro's offices, they head inside to find the place empty. It seems as if, after Luke delivered John to the former gangster, he took him and ran. They even find John’s fingernails ripped off and littered on the floor. At this point, it seems as if the pair have hit a dead end, only for Tracker to lay down the tragedy quite thickly this week. After Colter notices a broken lock to a nearby dumpster, they find John dead inside. Although Luke at first wants to take a step back from it all, Colter gives him a choice: either let John die for nothing or use this to help him find and save Mika. Of course, Colter's heroic charm is quite convincing, and Luke agrees to help, tracing Hiro’s number to a local library.

It has been revealed that at the library, Mika closes up for the night only to be surrounded by Hiro and his men. The criminal reveals that he killed John, only for Mika to fight back, killing one of the two goons and escaping into the nearby bookshelves. It isn't long before Colter and Luke arrive, splitting up to cover more ground. This was the right call, as Hiro corners Mika, ready to deliver the final blow when Luke stops him. Unfortunately, Hiro gets a shot off and wounds Luke pretty bad — but before he can finish the job, Colter shoots the gangster dead and stabilizes his newfound partner. With all this fast-paced gunplay, we need to get Colter, Luke, and Jensen Ackles' Russell Shaw in a room.

In a recent development, the next day, Colter runs into Mika at the hospital, who stuck around to thank Luke when he woke up — it turns out that the bounty hunter is out of surgery and is in recovery. Colter dips in to check on Luke, who wonders if our favorite rewardist has a "walk-away number" when it comes to the job. Of course, Colter doesn't. “I like what I do,” he explains. “I like fixing things. I like bringing people back together.” For Colter, the job gives him purpose and others hope, and so, despite all the profit he makes, it’s never been about the money. But "That's The Job" doesn't end here. True to the title, Colter now has to go and do the hard thing by informing Eliza about John's death, and it's a heartfelt, intimate moment that reminds us that, sometimes, not even Colter Shaw can bring about a happy ending.

Tracker goes beyond Colter Shaw's abilities as he partners with an unlikely ally to see things through.

Breaking: Verifying formal models of Raft implementations

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antithesis

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.
  • At Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems.
  • In this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 19, 2026 | Rohan Padhye, Research fellow | Hillel Wayne, Developer educator.

At Antithesis, we love finding bugs in distributed systems. But Antithesis can also help eliminate certain classes of bugs by using a combination of AI and formal methods to prove the correctness of complex design choices.

In this post, we demonstrate the paradigm on two Raft implementations, production libraries from etcd and HashiCorp. Although theyâre implementing the same protocol, there are significant differences in the approaches the two use. We used AI, TLA+, and Antithesis to formally model the two libraries with trace validation. We iterated between model checking, Antithesis testing, and proof attempts, each of which exposed bugs in the code or gaps in the model. We patched bugs and refined the model until it was provable, and until every test run was conformant.

Our model handles several extensions to the core Raft algorithm including pre-votes, snapshots, leadership transfers, and, for etcd-raft only: read indexes for linearizability, async storage writes, and membership changes (where etcdâs implementation intentionally deviates from the Raft paper).

The final proofs establish core Raft safety properties such as Election Safety, Leader Completeness, and State-Machine Safety. In other words, our process established that once we applied the workarounds and fixes needed, the specific designs (scoped to the features we modeled) embodied in HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft actually offer the same guarantees that the Raft paper does. We make the artifacts available for open review:.

Industry observers note that earlier this year, we wrote about how we keep finding bugs in every major Raft implementation we test with Antithesis. This was surprising, because the underlying Raft protocol has been extensively studied, formally specified, and rigorously proven correct (under a set of assumptions). In that post, we pointed out that many implementations subtly deviate from those assumptions, re-design the algorithm for performance, and/or extend the core Raft protocol with unverified extensions â thereby introducing bugs.

According to recent reports, since then, advances in AI have made automated theorem proving and formal verification of complex systems much more scalable, making it feasible to connect a specification to its implementation. So we set out to formally verify not just the core Raft protocol, but the specific designs implemented by production Raft libraries, incorporating custom data structures, different modes of concurrency, and various extensions such as pre-votes, leadership transfers, snapshots, and (in the case of etcd-raft) membership changes.

According to recent reports, A key challenge in applying formal methods is to identify a level of abstraction that both allows us to reason mathematically about desired properties, and bridges the gap between specification and implementation. We are not yet at the point of reasoning directly at the level of assembly instructions or even programming language semantics in order to verify distributed safety properties in production systems.

Both Anthropic/Theoremâs OSS-Verify and Google DeepMindâs AlphaProof Code only model single-threaded assembly code; whereas distributed systems are concurrent.

According to recent reports, the most widely used approach models the software as a state-transition system in a specification language such as TLA+, and checks invariants over these transitions for finite state spaces. TLA+ models can either be hand-written by experts, or these days, inferred directly from the code using AI. This approach has its own limitations, but is increasingly popular. The next challenge, then, is showing that the TLA+ model corresponds to the actual software that will run in production.

For our demonstration, we used Claude Fable 5.2 to automatically infer TLA+ models from the implementations of HashiCorp Raft and etcd-raft and then manually reviewed the safety properties declared in the specifications.

The etcd-raft repository has a TLA+ model crafted for trace validation that is now out of date, and is not designed for ease of proof. The Specular project produced models of etcd-raft and hashicorp-raft, but those models are designed for trace validation, not ease of proof, and the TLAPS leaderboard indicates that they remain unsolved as of 20 Nov 2026.

It has been revealed that we had to manually provide guidance on which features to model or leave out, what scenarios to specify for model checking, and make one refinement to the auto-generated safety properties. While AI is generally bad at inferring properties, in this case we simply instructed the agent to express the core safety properties defined in the Raft paper.

Thatâs where Antithesis helps.

Sources indicate that we used the recently debuted Antithesis plugin to automatically set up a test cluster, an input-generating workload designed to handle all the features captured in the model, and assertions that correspond to the modelâs safety properties. The software was then tested under fault injection while being fed random inputs, exercising various code paths and thread / message interleavings.

Recent findings suggest that for this demonstration, we developed a lightweight trace validation kit that allowed the software running in Antithesis to emit structured log events that correspond to state transitions in the TLA+ specification. Any test execution that produced a trace that did not conform to some path in the model got flagged. A non-conformant trace could indicate incorrect instrumentation of the trace logging itself, or more seriously, a modeling error or a real bug in the system. We instructed our AI agent to diagnose which one of these it might be, using Antithesis as necessary, and continue iterating until the traces and the inferred model converged.

For both Raft models, the specification expresses the following safety properties, taken directly from the Raft paper:.

Before trying to prove anything, we verified that these invariants hold on bounded instances using TLC, the standard TLA+ model checker. These instances, also synthesized by our AI agent, specify various bounds: clusters are usually three nodes, a single client value, at most a couple of terms of leader election, logs that are limited to a few entries, with only a handful of network messages in flight. These bounds sound tiny, but theyâre sufficient to create several interesting cases: competing elections, a deposed leader still replicating, log entries overwritten and re-replicated, crashes in the middle of an operation, etc. We also model checked various configurations of the Raft libraries, e.g. with pre-vote or snapshotting features enabled and disabled. These âsmallâ instances can reach a state space of over 1.6 million states, which TLC explores exhaustively. We also included some larger problems which were only checked via random simulation. If model checking triggered a safety violation, we attempted to reproduce it as an assertion failure locally or in Antithesis; if the software couldnât exhibit the behavior, the model had to be tightened.

Overall, our process was an iterative loop consisting of model checking (flagging invariant violations), trace validation (flagging deviations), model refinement (to fix design flaws or conformance), and software patching (to fix bugs).

Recent findings suggest that in some ways, this approach is similar to and inspired by Specular. However, given their goal of finding bugs, Specularâs approach involved using AI to identify buggy scenarios before writing models, which meant that static analysis was doing a lot of the heavy lifting. In contrast, our models are intended to be more general and prove safety of the full design.

According to recent reports, along the way, we encountered bugs in both systems, including previously known open problems such as hashicorp/raft#695 and etcd-io/raft#551, as well as fresh ones such as hashicorp/raft#746 and etcd-io/raft#558. In our internal repository, we applied a total of 7 patches across the two implementations. In each case, our goal was to make the system and model pass both verification and validation.

We also encountered a few additional crash bugs, but those donât violate safety.

Recent findings suggest that but bounded model checking only shows the absence of bugs in a small state space. The only way to get assurance for unbounded input sizes is via rigorous mathematical proof.

Industry observers note that there are two good techniques for proving invariants correct for the whole specification: using a theorem prover integrated into TLA+ called TLAPS, or by translating the model into Veil, a library for the Lean proof assistant for modeling state-transition systems. We used both, delegating the task of proof construction to Claude Fable 5.2.

We used Veilâs official tla-to-veil LLM skill for the model translation, and the recommended approach of validating this via bounded equivalence checking, using TLC and Veilâs own model checker, on our previously stored instances.

Ideally, a TLAPS proof provides the best assurance, since it can attest to safety properties defined on the TLA+ model itself. However, we decided to translate TLA+ to Veil and attempt proofs in Lean. Why? As described in the previous section, our process was extremely iterative, involving several steps of model refinement. We wanted to use the proof engine as additional feedback in that process, feeding it any candidate specifications on which bounded model checking and trace validation both succeeded. We found Leanâs interactive tactic paradigm, predictable performance, and persistent kernel-checked proof terms to be key benefits in this iterative process.

On one occasion, a model of etcd-raftâs membership change as implemented could not be proven correct, revealing a complex bug whose trigger was beyond the state space that bounded model checking explores. In such situations, we could use the Antithesis plugin to attempt to synthesize a workload to reproduce the counter-example.

Antithesis also helped in the proof construction process. When working on challenging parts of the proof, Claude hypothesized several intermediate invariants which if true would lead to a straightforward proof strategy. The agent then used Antithesis to rapidly check if those invariants held true in test runs, and discarded them if run-time assertions failed. Antithesis thus made the proof construction phase more efficient.

Once we converged on a state where the safety properties were fully provable in Lean and the model was passing trace validation with Antithesis, we froze the specification and asked agents to prove the same invariants on the TLA+ spec directly with TLAPS. This last step wasnât strictly necessary, but eliminated any shadow of doubt concerning the Lean proofs and the TLA+ spec.

End-to-end, the work on each library cost less than $1,200 in Claude Fable tokens and approximately 2000 Antithesis compute-hours.

Less, we should note, than the prepaid allowance in a single month of Antithesis Teams.

In a recent development, note that our final proofs verify formal models of the implementation, not the code itself. However, we can gain confidence about the modelâs fidelity based on the trace validation performed with the extensive test coverage that Antithesis provides, including fault injection such as network partitions and node crashes. To strengthen assurance even further, our iterative process involved several steps of mutation testing, including: mutating the specification to check that the proofs fall through, mutating stored test logs to ensure that trace validation fails, and mutating the software itself to ensure that everything breaks.

Sources indicate that the models still make several assumptions about the environment, which limits the reach of verification. For example, both Raft libraries provide pluggable interfaces for local persistent storage. In our test workloads, we use BoltDB for storage and the models assume that no single write (e.g., a log entry or tuple of raft state) is ever torn or corrupted, which BoltDB guarantees. A crash can still fall between two writes.

Our work also leaves out several library features which we have not modeled, such as lease-based reads for etcd-raft (because it depends on wall-clock timing), async heartbeats for hashicorp-raft (because it is known to be very very buggy; really), and membership changes for hashicorp-raft (because we were exhausted from patching bugs in the simpler core). Finally, we only verify safety properties and ignore liveness in this prototype. A comprehensive list of assumptions and limitations is provided in the associated artifactâs README.

Given our reputation as âa fuzzing companyâ, formal methods might seem like an odd direction for us to explore. But we see ourselves less as âa fuzzing companyâ and more as a correctness manufacturer. We need a wide range of different approaches if we want to build truly robust systems. Each technique compensates for the weaknesses of the others. Moreover, they amplify each otherâs strengths. The first property-based testing framework, QuickCheck, derived test inputs from a functionâs static type. Many of our customers use both testing and formal methods, so we want to make the two techniques work better together.

It has been revealed that the biggest weakness of formal specification is that it proves the design correct, but doesnât guarantee that the code we implemented actually matches the design. Trace validation uses the strengths of tests to compensate for the core weakness of formal specification. Validation works best if our tests can reach wildly unusual system states, which aligns well with our core technology.

How formal specification can help testing is relatively less explored, but there are some opportunities here too. We often find that newcomers to property-based testing struggle to describe the properties for their system. But they can describe a high-level outline of what the system essentially does. With trace validation, we can potentially turn that outline into a property to test!

Sources indicate that all that said, this is an early research project. We could easily map trace logs to spec behaviors because the code and spec were at roughly the same level of abstraction, with a close correlation between lines of Go and lines of TLA+. Most real-world specs, though, are two levels of abstraction above the code they model. This is because 1) TLA+ can do things impossible in a real system, like make truly arbitrary nondeterministic choices, and 2) the spec can simplify implementation details that donât affect the essential design. These features make specification more powerful, but also make trace validation harder.

Sources indicate that think of this as us demonstrating a medicine works on mice, but we havenât yet done a human trial. More work is needed, work which weâre now doing at Antithesis. Stay tuned to see where it ends up.

In a recent development, in formal specification (like with TLA+), we write highly abstract blueprints, or specifications, of systems and find bugs in those blueprints directly. Once weâve found and fixed all the bugs, we can be confident our real system isnât going to have certain design problems.

But how do we know that the code we write actually corresponds to the design we verified? This is one of the substantial unsolved problems of formal specification, and the solution we used here trace validation (also called âtrace checkingâ). This was first publicly described in the MongoDB paper eXtreme Modeling in Practice. The authors took logged events in the production system, converted them into a sequence of states, and checked if that sequence was possible in the blueprint. If not possible, then the implementation must be doing something forbidden by the blueprint, so there is a divergence between the implementation and spec.

According to recent reports, itâs easier to see this with a concrete example. Say we have this pseudocode as our specification:.

By either-or, I mean that exactly one of the two will happen each iteration, but the decision logic is an implementation detail I donât care about. This spec also has the property that, after every loop iteration, passed + failed == i.

Now hereâs one conforming implementation:.

Industry observers note that while the practical way this works is very different than just arbitrary incrementing variables, itâs still the same thing in essence, and we should expect that every sensor either gets added to the set or marked as broken. To do trace validation, we first add some logs to the code:.

We run this program and it prints âloop passed loop failedâ. We can convert that to a behavior of the spec. If we denote a state as (i, passed, failed), the corresponding sequence of states would be [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (1, 1, 0), (2, 1, 0), (2, 1, 1)]. That is valid under the behavior, so this trace conforms to the spec.

Now if we make a diverging change like this:.

According to recent reports, itâs now possible to run this and see the logs âloop loopâ. The corresponding behavior, [(0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), (2, 0, 0)] is impossible in the spec, so this would fail trace checking and reveal a divergence between the code and spec.

Thatâs how it all works in principle, anyway. Thereâs a lot of technical challenges with getting this working practically. For example, how are we supposed to know that a network timeout may give us an invalid trace, and how are we actually supposed to trigger it? And the answer to that is a combination of the techniques that we use in Antithesis: deterministic simulation testing and fuzzing. But those are things that we talk about in detail in other articles.

5 Best Performances In The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping, Ranked
