  • As Haymitch competes in the already-dangerous Hunger Games — made much more dangerous thanks to the fact that it's the second Quarter Quell, meaning it's an extra "special" (demented) version with double the child tributes — he encounters dozens of characters, some of whom we've met before in different timelines and some of whom are brand fresh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Major spoilers ahead for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.".

Recent findings suggest that the newest movie in the "Hunger Games" franchise, subtitled "Sunrise on the Reaping," is here, and as I wrote in my review for /Film, it's a worthy addition to this genuinely excellent film series. Directed by Francis Lawrence, who has helmed every single Hunger Games movie except for the inaugural outing "The Hunger Games" in 2012 (which was directed by Gary Ross), "Sunrise on the Reaping" starss Joseph Zada as a younger version of Woody Harrelson's character, Haymitch Abernathy. Haymitch is one of the only known victors of the titular Games who hails from the downtrodden District 12 in the dystopian nation of as Panem. (Some housekeeping: District 12 is the mining district and impoverished enough that its child tributes for the Hunger Games almost never win; Panem is the redesigned totalitarian North America led by the oppressive Capitol, which is located in what we know as the Rocky Mountains.).

As Haymitch competes in the already-dangerous Hunger Games — made much more dangerous thanks to the fact that it's the second Quarter Quell, meaning it's an extra "special" (demented) version with double the child tributes — he encounters dozens of characters, some of whom we've met before in different timelines and some of whom are brand fresh. So which actors deliver the very best performances in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping?".

It has been revealed that it's a stacked cast and it's legitimately tough to choose, but ultimately, I've picked five performers who build upon the previous movies and performances from storied actors who defined these roles originally ... and do so beautifully.

Recent findings suggest that the only real beef I have with Elle Fanning's performance as Effie Trinket in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping," such as it is, is that she doesn't get nearly enough screen time for my liking. Effie Trinket, who appears in this film as a sort of assistant stylist and District 12 prep team member who saves the sartorial day after her boss Magno Stift (Billy Porter) falls down on the job, is a character we know from the original "Hunger Games" movies; in those, she's played by Elizabeth Banks.

It has been revealed that effie is a larger-than-life character whose journey is, I'll be honest, sort of disjointed. When she's the chaperone for Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark (Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson) during the original stories alongside Woody Harrelson's grown, downtrodden Haymitch Abernathy, she seems slavishly devoted to the Capitol, but also becomes part of the rebellion in the two-part finale "Mockingjay." In "Sunrise on the Reaping," Effie seems to be a willing ally to Haymitch, but her loyalty still lies with the Capitol. (We also get to meet her younger sister Proserpina, played by Iris Apatow, for the first time in the series, expanding Effie's world just a little.).

Industry observers note that fanning, a recently minted Oscar and Emmy nominee for her sensational projects "Sentimental Value" and "Margo's Got Money Troubles," is unsurprisingly great during her unfortunately limited screen time, particularly her delivery of Effie's most memorable line from the novel ("I confess to having a moment!"). Honestly, there are so many prequels possible in the wider Hunger Games world, and if Suzanne Collins ever wanted to a deep dive on Effie's whole "deal" and give her her own story, I wouldn't hate that. But she'd need to convince Fanning to return to really make the movie sing.

It has been revealed that I love Kieran Culkin, and I bristle when people accuse him of delivering the same performance over and over again. From where I'm sitting, that couldn't be further from the truth! Two of his most well-known and well-regarded performances — Roman Roy on "Succession" and Benji in "A Real Pain," the former of which earned him an Emmy and the latter of which earned him an Oscar — are very different. Roman is a broken man-child desperate for love that escapes him and that he does nothing to earn. Benji is a walking raw nerve, who is loved by complete strangers but is still desperately striving to make his own family accept him. Culkin's role in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" skews more towards Roman, but it's still a fun departure for the actor, and he's great.

According to recent reports, culkin plays TV host Caesar Flickerman. He's the second actor to play this specific character (Stanley Tucci originated the role in the original "Hunger Games" films) and the third actor to play a Flickerman TV presenter (Jason Schwartzman played Caesar's ancestor Lucky in the prequel "The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes"). We know next to nothing about Caesar's psyche or inner life, and that's fine — he's just the guy who helps make a spectacle out of child murder. In any case, Culkin's bombast matches Tucci's wearier but still explosive host. When he's not snarling at assistants, he's Cheshire Cat-grinning at the doomed tributes. Across the board, he fits into this role perfectly. Culkin is not only a great casting choice, but a worthy addition to the franchise, and he delivers one of this prequel's best performances.

Ralph Fiennes is on what the kids might call a "generational run." In 2022, he played the sadistic and vengeful chef Julian Slowik in "The Menu," followed that up with a stunning performance as a troubled, grieving cardinal in "Conclave," and a two-film turn as the kindly and offbeat Dr. Ian Kelson in "28 Years Later" and "28 Years Later: The Bone Temple." Now, Fiennes has become the third actor in Hunger Games (and cinematic) history to play Panem President Coriolanus Snow. He follows Tom Blyth, who played a young and mostly unspoiled version of the future tyrant in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes," and the late, great Donald Sutherland, who portrays the oldest version of Snow that we see in the original films.

In a recent development, it shouldn't be news to anybody that Fiennes delivers an exceptional performance in "Sunrise on the Reaping." He is one of the finest actors of his generation and has consistently proven that across multiple decades. What was news to me, though, was how perfectly Fiennes bridged the gap between Blyth and Sutherland. Blyth's Snow begins his journey as a teenage boy desperate to prove his worth, and "Songbirds and Snakes" ends with him newly embittered by heartbreak and driven by ambition. Meanwhile, Sutherland's Snow is comfortable with being a source of pure evil and confident in his actions.

Industry observers note that fiennes' Snow sits beautifully in the middle as a man who seems like he still has an ounce or two of sympathy and regret left — he even asks Haymitch about the fate of Lucy Gray Baird (Rachel Zegler), the woman who loved and left him in "The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes" — but is still ruthless enough to replace a tribute tragically killed in a pre-Games accident with a brainwashed lookalike. He's excellent.

Industry observers note that without a perfectly cast Haymitch, the entirety of "Sunrise on the Reaping" fails. Woody Harrelson's Haymitch is deep in the throes of an alcohol addiction when we meet him in "The Hunger Games," and he's a disaffected, purposefully withdrawn man who clearly avoids getting close to District 12 tributes he views as doomed. Joseph Zada's Haymitch, in contrast, begins his journey as a young man with a lot to live for and a lot to love about his life. He loves his mother and younger brother and is besotted with his girlfriend Lenore Dove Baird (Whitney Peak), a member of the Covey. Everything changes when Haymitch is randomly chosen to participate in the Games — he's not reaped, but chosen as a hasty replacement when the kid who was reaped makes a run for it and gets sniped in the head. Even then, Haymitch puts on a brave face, reassures his family, and even comforts the youngest District 12 tribute, Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), on their journey to the Capitol.

As Haymitch makes allies, forms a potential plan to blow up the arena alongside his mentor Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and Beetee's tribute son Ampert (Percy Daggs IV), and eventually allies with the other District 12 girl, Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), he suffers setback after setback. Zada manages to chart every single reaction and emotion we see from Haymitch in a way that feels real and earned. As he takes hit after hit in his quest to win the Games and return home — even though he'll only find more tragedy there — we feel every hit along with him. Zada is magnetic as Haymitch, and he's got a long career ahead of him thanks to this performance.

Every time I see a casting announcement involving Jesse Plemons, I'm excited. The dorky guy from "Friday Night Lights" — Mr. Kirsten Dunst himself — has become one of the entertainment industry's most reliably excellent actors. I'm struggling, as I write this, to think of a time where Plemons was actively bad in anything, and I'm coming up short. He can do absolutely anything, based on the fact that he's hysterically funny in "Game Night" and the most terrifying guy I've ever seen in "Civil War." I'm sure it was a daunting ask for Plemons to step into the role of Plutarch Heavensbee in "Sunrise on the Reaping" for one big and tragic reason: Philip Seymour Hoffman, who originated the role, passed away in 2014. I commend Plemons for taking the role, and I feel like I need to say that he bears a somewhat uncanny resemblance to the late Oscar winner (and even played Hoffman's son in 2012's "The Master"). He's also incredible.

According to recent reports, hindsight isn't always a gift for an actor, but in the case of Plutarch, Plemons clearly utilized everything we know about the character's future in "Sunrise on the Reaping." Plemons' Plutarch is a mere Capitol cameraman (Hoffman's Plutarch had been elevated all the way to Gamemaker), but he's shrewd, a favorite of Snow, and already a rebel ready to pursue a full takedown of the Capitol. Knowing that this comes to fruition across both parts of "Mockingjay" makes this look at Plutarch's early days of rebellion all the more satisfying, and Plemons is pitch-perfect as a man who's absolutely fascinating on the inside. It's the best performance in the movie.

"The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" is in theaters now.

The concert series for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 will get an encore performance next year with a global tour including the first ever performances in North America. The world tour was unveiled today with tickets going on sale Sept. 15. It will include Europe, the United Kingdom, and the United States. In a recent development, the concert series brings Lorien Testard's critically acclaimed and award-winning score for the 2025 RPG to life. Having attended video game concerts in the past, I can attest to the power of hearing a good soundtrack performed live. It'll be a show worth attending.

According to recent reports, the concert's French and other European dates will all be performed by Orchestra Curieux alongside Testard and lead vocalist Alice Duport-Percier. In the U.S., Daniel Sicard will conduct the Wordless Music Orchestra. Here are all the dates and locations for the 2027 Painted Symphony tour.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that marvel’s Midnight universe only has a few books out right now—Midnight Fantastic Four, Midnight Spider-Man, and Midnight X-Men—and only one of them has made good on the publishing line’s core premise as being horror-centric. These are all stories reinterpreting or retconning traditional Marvel Comics lore, of course, but the promise alone of uniquely scary or ominous retellings was the hook that they were all supposedly going to abide by, and there’s an argument to be made that Midnight Spider-Man is far scarier than Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men, with it not being a close race in the slightest.

Of course, these books have barely taken off, and it’s likely that genuine horrors are in store throughout the next couple of years. Indeed, Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men have spent a lot more time on worldbuilding, and their payoffs could be extraordinary. That mentioned, challenges of Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men also aren’t taking advantage of one of their greatest horror tools, whereas Midnight Spider-Man is: Marvel Comics’ cloaked covers.

Sources indicate that it’s disappointing that Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men haven’t dove fully into horror because the Midnight publishing line is deliberately meant to be a horror-centric continuity. It may be unrealistic to expect that every single concern will have something scary in it, but Midnight Spider-Man has successfully achieved that in the two issues that have been released thus far. Ultimately, it seems to boil down to the fact that Midnight Fantastic Four is more of a sci-fi mystery story, and Midnight X-Men is more of a fantasy love story. Still, it’s jarring that Midnight Spider-Man leans wholly into horror while the others don’t, or haven’t.

Even odder is that Midnight X-Men is specifically rooted in Earth-616 X-Men lore and history, while Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight Spider-Man are completely distinct. Midnight X-Men’s holy war between mutantkind, vampires, and empyres has the makings of a phenomenal story, especially given how Cyclops and Jean Grey’s relationship has evolved via problem #2, but it’s difficult to argue that it’s a horror story. Likewise, Midnight Fantastic Four’s cosmic horror has laid foundations for a particularly atmospheric and eerie dread, though there hasn’t been anything particularly frightening about the series yet. Meanwhile, Midnight Spider-Man wasted no time delving into gruesome body horror.

Issue covers have the potential to illustrate how horrifying these books can be, and cloaked covers further emphasize how much scarier Midnight Spider-Man is than Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men. Midnight books cloak their main covers in order to obscure or mask the full artwork, “only revealing themselves to readers daring enough to pick them up on stands,” as per Marvel, but Midnight Spider-Man is unsurprisingly the only one to truly capitalize on the shock and awe that the presentation of the cloaked covers permits them.

It has been revealed that for instance, the main, cloaked cover for matter #2 merely depicts Midnight Spider-Man’s Felicia Hardy in a state of fear, and it’s teased that something lurks behind her. The revealed cover shows that she’s right to be afraid, as Peter Parker’s terrifying Spider-Man is creepily nestled into the corner of the ceiling. Neither Midnight Fantastic Four nor Midnight X-Men has any such reveals yet, at least none that are anywhere near as scary, or that utilize the format as well.

It has been revealed that plus, Midnight Fantastic Four awkwardly always needs Reed Richards, Sue Storm, Johnny Storm, and Ben Grimm to be positioned vertically so that they can all be seen in this cloaked format, and X-Men’s massive ensemble has the same problem. Chiefly, it seems to boil down to Midnight Spider-Man being scarier and having the horror legs to stand on. That doesn’t mean Midnight Fantastic Four and Midnight X-Men are lesser, but it’s weird that they aren’t indulging in horror as much as they could be.

Midnight Spider-Man #3, Midnight X-Men #3, and Midnight Fantastic Four #3 are scheduled to be released on December 16, 2026.

What Happened to Silicon Valley?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, with the O’Reilly learning platform, you get the resources and guidance to keep your skills sharp and stay ahead. Try it free for up to 14 days.

Join a live online event on the O’Reilly platform to learn from the experts shaping tech.

From value creation to value extraction.

By Tim O’Reilly November 20, 2026 • 32 minute read.

On October 16, 2026, I delivered the second Annual Margaret Levi Lecture in Political Economy  in conjunction with the AI and History conference at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. This is my original lecture as written, which incorporates material from many pieces I’ve written over the years. As delivered, I departed significantly from the script, as you can see from the embedded video below or the transcript that you can see at the link above.

Sources indicate that it’s an honor to give a lecture in Margaret Levi’s name. I’ve been asked to reflect on the changes in the political economy of Silicon Valley throughout my 40-plus year career in and about it, and I can’t imagine a better framing for my remarks than Margaret’s vision.

Margaret understood that advances in our ability to work together are essential to a better future. Cooperation is the human superpower. She also asks what happens when the systems of cooperation we have constructed over time stop holding up their end of the bargain.

Recent findings suggest that that is very much the question that Silicon Valley is facing today. An industry that pioneered advances in collective intelligence at scale used to engender love from its customers because of the way it solved latest problems in their lives. It now too often inspires fear and loathing. How did things go so wrong?

Recent findings suggest that but let me start with my own history. I started my tech giant more than 40 years ago with a $500 initial investment. We took in no venture capital, and we built a business that now generates hundreds of millions of dollars in profitable annual revenue, funded by customers who love our products and pay us for them. We got there the slow way, through steady organic growth. That is quite anathema to the rush to the top of whatever appears to be the latest hill that seems to characterize Silicon Valley today. Even when climbing that hill traps a company at a local maximum, the hope is to get to payday before the industry moves on to the next hill.

It has been revealed that my original corporate goal was stated as simply “Interesting work for interesting people.” That evolved into two principles: “Change the world by spreading the knowledge of innovators,” and “Create more value than you capture.” Those principles shaped not only my company but what I expected the internet to be. When we introduced GNN, the Global Network Navigator, in 1993, it was the first web portal and the first ad-supported site on the World Wide Web, and for two years it was the place people went to find other sites. What we built was a machine for pointing you at the best of what other people had made, and then getting out of your way.

Even our idea of advertising was not what you think of today. It was inspired by direct mail advertising, where you’d read articles in a print magazine or look at accompanying ads, and then you’d call an 800 number or circle a number on a “bingo card” that you’d send in to the publisher so that the advertiser could send you a brochure. I realized that the web would be a good replacement for that awkward system, that every company ought to have its own website that provided more information about its products and services. What we invented was not the “grab your attention” kind of advertising. It was all about utility, and sharing information that customers really wanted and needed. In short, it was the commercial web, which no one any longer thinks of as advertising, even though it is the most durable and useful kind.

The commercial web was only a small part of what the web became. The web was the playground of amateurs, not entrepreneurs. It was a marvelous collective work of human imagination, creativity, sharing, and ultimately (though that became toxic only later), competition for attention. Our hand-curated catalog of the best websites was soon surpassed by algorithmic solutions like those provided by Google. The amount of content produced was far larger than purely human curation could manage. It was an early example of what Richard Sutton was later to call “the bitter lesson” in his analysis of AI training.

In my 2005 essay “What Is Web 2.0?” I described how the companies that survived the dotcom bust had all, in one way or another, figured out how to help people navigate the resulting information explosion at scale. As Herbert Simon noted in 1971, an abundance of information leads to a scarcity of attention. In the face of increasing information abundance, he predicted that we would use machines to help us better allocate our time and attention. And so it has transpired: Information has become so abundant that it defies manual curation. Instead, powerful, proprietary algorithmic systems use the data they collect to match people with the answers, news, entertainment, products, applications, and services they seek. Today’s AI is in many ways a continuation of this arc.

I called this “harnessing collective intelligence.” All of it was, in economic terms, a set of remarkable advances in networked, data-enabled market coordination. It felt like a public good even when it was privately owned.

It has been revealed that hal Varian, formerly Google’s chief economist, once told me that only about 6% of Google search result pages carry any advertising or are otherwise monetized by Google. The other 94% were served up by search in a glorious demonstration of abundance, the surplus of value created over value captured. And while many of the pages themselves were commercial, even more were the product of the joyful exuberance of humanity, people creating and sharing for the joy of it. Google’s algorithm matched that creation to the people who wanted it, with no price involved anywhere in the transaction. Forty thousand times a second, Google’s organic search algorithms were performing the coordination that twentieth-century economists thought could only be done by self-interested actors haggling over prices. And for Google’s first decade and a half, the priced market of advertising ran alongside organic search as a sidecar, not the engine.

That’s the Silicon Valley I signed up for. Some of this is nostalgia. The early web had plenty wrong with it, its share of greedy hustlers and hypesters. But value creation for both users and suppliers was the winning strategy. Companies won by solving real problems for their customers. Investors won when the manufacturer delivered on their promises. Unfortunately, that didn’t last.

Sources indicate that google, a company once known for “Don’t be evil,” now faces the same surveillance-capitalism charges as Facebook, a company that never made any such promise. On Google, advertising now pushes organic search far down the page. Especially on mobile, you often scroll through pages of ads from national chains before you reach the site that has the best answer to your question. And in today’s AI-mode search, even the content is served up directly by Google, with far less traffic sent on to the sites that provide it. Likewise, Amazon, which used to call itself the most customer-centric company on earth, now puts sixteen ads and four organic results on a typical search results page. Sometimes, it may take scrolling past three screens of results to reach the first organic search result. And by “the first organic search result,” I mean “the best guess of the company’s smartest algorithms for what the user is actually looking for.” In former times, that was the top result. No more.

The reason isn’t that good people turned bad. It’s in the overriding economic incentives of today’s shareholder capitalism. The extractive behavior the tech giants exhibit has been the norm for modern companies since Milton Friedman reset its objective in 1970, in a sentence that became doctrine: “The social responsibility of business is to increase its profits.” Harvard Business School, through the work of Meckling and Jensen, enshrined that view not only into corporate law but executive compensation. Whatever people’s original motives, the logic of the market eventually prevails, except in extraordinary cases. In his recent book Incorruptible, Eric Ries describes a set of institutions, norms, and guardrails that can help to safeguard the values of a tech giant, but you can count on your fingers and toes the high profile companies that have successfully deployed them to resist the market. Even tax policy rewards capital appreciation by taxing it at a much lower rate than labor income.

Our corporations and the financial markets that govern them and reward them are a kind of machine, what the science fiction writer Charlie Stross calls a “slow AI.” We built it. We set its objective function to reward shareholders and ignore everyone else. And then we tell everyone that it is a marvelous self-correcting system. This is an illusion. As I put it in “We Have Already Let the Genie Out of the Bottle,” an essay I wrote for a Rockefeller Foundation workshop on regulating AI:.

It has been revealed that attempts at governance are futile until we recognize that we have built a machine and set it on its course. Instead, we pretend that the market is a natural phenomenon best left alone, and we fail to hold its mechanism designers to account. We need to tear down and rebuild that machine, reprogramming it so that human flourishing, not corporate profit, becomes its goal.

If the problem were just villains, you could fix things by firing them or shaming them or suing them or otherwise holding them to account. But if the problem is the design of the entire system, everyone is eventually incentivized to seek the same result. The machine rewards outsized growth of revenue and profit and brutally punishes any slowdown. Not only that, stock options tie every employee’s fortune to that reward.

Criticizing a tech giant for turning extractive isn’t really about the values of a company or the character of its executives and employees, it’s about the incentives that have been given to them.

Silicon Valley is a mirror of what’s wrong with our economy and our corporate governance, not the cause of it, and not even the worst exemplar. Tobacco, oil, pharma companies, and far too much of Wall Street vie for that spot. But Silicon Valley is a great place to study what went wrong, because companies rise and fall so quickly, making them the equivalent of laboratory mice or flatworms, where patterns can be quickly identified and followed across generations.

A few years ago, I found a useful language for describing what I was seeing in the theory of economic rents.

It has been revealed that the essential idea is that when the reward accruing to an actor is larger than their contribution to value creation, the difference is rent. To the classical economists, to Smith and Ricardo and Mill, living in a world of inherited privilege, rents were not a temporary aberration on the way to equilibrium. They were both a persistent consequence and a persistent source of inequality. Joseph Schumpeter had a different idea, that disproportionate profits can be a reward for innovation. An innovator can earn outsized profits during the expansive phase of a newly introduced technology, when it’s solving new problems and creating value not just for consumers but for a whole ecosystem of suppliers and intermediaries and even competitors.

When economists talk about rent-seeking today, though, many of them mean what George Stigler called “regulatory capture” and what the public choice school built into its doctrine: rents extracted through government intervention at the behest of those who lobby officials and bureaucrats to get their way in despite the free market.

Industry observers note that the rents I want to talk about are a different animal. They are collected in the market, not around it, by private firms with enormous power, whose power is unchecked precisely because the government has stepped back.

For my purposes here, speaking about the rents that accrue to Silicon Valley companies, I divide them into two rough categories.

Industry observers note that the first is what I call rising tide rents. This fits with the classical idea of rent as a reward accruing to an actor that is larger than its contribution to value creation, but it is a virtuous kind, a kind of communal value creation, often the result of positive government interventions. Consider the rise in home prices that accrues to a homeowner who lives in a neighborhood that is improved by better schools or improved roads, which then may lead to newly introduced shops and restaurants or the home improvements made by neighbors. This is also a kind of unearned income. Everyone shares the improvements in quality of life. But homeowners get something bigger, the unearned income from the appreciation in home value.

In a recent development, in a similar way, leading companies make massive improvements to the neighborhood, so to speak, and we all benefit. I should point out that government plays a significant role in these improvements. It’s easy to forget the NSF grant that funded the research that became Google, the loan guarantees that made Tesla possible, and government as the founding customer for SpaceX’s commercial launch services. It’s a rising tide that lifts all boats, and the fact that the market leader takes the biggest share of it is not, to my mind, a scandal. But Schumpeter thought those outsized profits would eventually be competed away as knowledge diffuses through society. What is a scandal is the way that Business Strategy 101 and corporate governance today teach companies to build moats and barriers to keep profits high even when the firm stops earning rewards by innovating and better serving customers.

Companies do this by turning to the second category of rents, which I call robber baron rents, the income above a competitive rate that gets collected because of asymmetries in power, the way the medieval baron’s troops collected their share of the harvest whether or not the baron had contributed anything to growing it.

The same organization can collect both kinds of rent at different stages in its lifecycle. As far as I can tell, the shift from one to the other is close to a law of the technology business cycle. The rising tide doesn’t last. Once the growth of a newly introduced market slows, the now-powerful incumbents can no longer rely on new people and a vibrant ecosystem to sustain their extraordinary profits. So they turn to extraction. They use their market power to hold on to their now-customary level of profit in the face of competition that ought to be eating it away. Cory Doctorow came up with a catchy name for this. He calls it enshittification.

There’s another problem with Silicon Valley and the economy writ large.

At one point in early 2021, when Elon Musk first became the richest person in the world, Bernie Sanders tweeted about it, contrasting Musk’s fortune with the frozen federal minimum wage. Bernie was right that the comparison was shocking. But he was wrong to imply that Musk’s wealth came from profits extracted at the expense of Tesla’s workers. The median Tesla worker makes considerably more than the median American worker, and up to that time, Tesla had few profits to extract. Musk didn’t hoard Tesla’s profits like a robber baron of old. He won a different kind of game.

Musk was paid in what the financial writer Jerry Goodman, writing under the pseudonym Adam Smith, called “supermoney.” The essence of Goodman’s insight is that any company that has been financialized through stock issuance is valued today as if it were already delivering the decades of future earnings reflected in its stock price. This is another of those ideas that help you to see the world in a newly introduced way. Once you realize that owners of capital are literally living in a different economy from those who earn income from their labor, you start seeing two different economies operating under two completely different sets of rules.

There’s the operating economy, where companies make and sell products and services and earn a profit by, as Nick Hanauer and Eric Beinhocker put it, solving human problems. And there’s the betting economy, where wealthy people bet on which companies will win the beauty contest that the stock market has become. In the operating economy, a dollar is a dollar. The neighborhood dry cleaner earns one dollar of profit and has that one dollar to spend. In the betting economy, a dollar of profit becomes many dollars of market value. At the time when Musk first became the world’s richest man, a dollar of Tesla profit turned into roughly $600 of stock market value. A dollar of Amazon profit at that time was worth about $67. A dollar of Google profit, about $34. The local business that isn’t financialized gets only $1.

That gap is one of the biggest unacknowledged drivers of inequality in this country, and it’s why one slice of society has gotten so much richer in recent decades while everyone else languished. Most rich people—and really, all holders of capital assets—live in the supermoney economy, where our assets are valued as if the future had already arrived and can be borrowed against, tax-free, today. This is the ultimate unearned income, or rent. Most everyone else lives in the dollar economy. If you’re a public-tech giant executive paid in stock, or a venture capitalist, or an entrepreneur lucky enough to place in the financial horse race, you live in the other one, and you get a large interest-free loan from the future.

According to recent reports, the betting economy, within reason, is a good thing. Speculative bets on the future are how we fund innovation and build infrastructure ahead of the prosperity it will bring. Tesla is a real tech giant building real factories and real charging networks, and it kick-started a genuine transition to renewable energy. SpaceX and Starlink likewise required massive amounts of capital. And now AI has dwarfed even those bets.

Carlota Perez has shown that bubbles are a normal part of how revolutionary technologies get adopted. I’m not against betting. I’m worried about what we bet on, and what will be left over when the bubble pops.

If your biggest lever for wealth creation is not in the market for real goods and services, but in the market for future expectations, it’s easy to continue down the slippery slope to making money by manipulating those expectations. And that’s the road Silicon Valley has charged down.

Sam Bankman-Fried captured the zeitgeist with his line “Number go up.” Silicon Valley has gotten addicted to value capture without value creation. Think about it: 75 to 80% of IPOs are for companies without any profits. Add in acquisitions of pre-IPO companies and the numbers are likely even worse. It’s like a horse race where bettors can collect their winnings when the horse has rounded the first or second turn.

There are still venture capitalists who look for companies that succeed by delivering real value to customers, but the prevalence of the profitless IPO has turned the venture-backed manufacturer into a kind of financial instrument. Much as the bankers who invented the derivatives that nearly sank the global economy in the 2009 financial crisis eventually ran out of real mortgages to collateralize and turned to “liar loans” so they could keep the game going a little longer, the measure is no longer whether a company has a chance of living up to its promises but whether it can convince the investor in the next round that it can. Most startups are built to be refinanced all the way to the exit rather than to turn into sustainable businesses.

This dynamic is essential to the current AI infrastructure buildout. Data centers are built to meet expectations of massive future demand. But much of that demand is from companies that have not yet, as Silicon Valley used to describe it, found “product-market fit.” That is, they have not yet found customers willing to pay more than the product costs to deliver. In short, the future cash flows with which data center builders are expecting to pay back the trillions they have borrowed or invested are dependent on those customers’ ability to raise their next round at an ever-increasing valuation.

According to recent reports, AI is the real deal, a transformative technology like the internet. And its leading company, Anthropic, looks to be turning into an actual business with cash flow and profits. But others, even those like OpenAI with enormous revenues, are still dependent on massive additional capital infusions to survive. But it’s OK, as long as “number go up.”.

Sources indicate that A structure like this does not need demand to collapse. It only needs the hype to recede enough that it is no longer possible to raise more capital at ever more stratospheric valuations. That’s why we see hype in increasingly desperate amounts.

I first started thinking about this turn to hype in Silicon Valley in the days of Uber and Lyft. The innovation of using GPS and smartphones to create crowdsourced taxis on demand using people’s personal cars was real and important. But building the matching marketplace of riders and drivers took enormous subsidies, and it wasn’t terribly profitable. So Travis Kalanick, the CEO of Uber, told investors that Uber wasn’t out to replace taxis, but the private automobile. Then in the run-up to the IPO, he started talking about self-driving cars, presumably to suggest that Uber would be much more profitable once it was able to get rid of the cost of drivers. Meanwhile, Waymo kept its head down and did the hard work of actually building out the technology, which is only now coming to fruition.

Sources indicate that that kind of hype continued through the next one of Silicon Valley’s dry spells. There wasn’t much real innovation to talk about, so the masters of capital sold “the Metaverse” and eventually “Web3.” As the person who defined “Web 2.0,” I was asked frequently to opine on Web3. I tried to avoid answering. Most prognostications about the future turn out to be wrong. What we can do is ask questions that help us see the present more clearly. So finally, I laid out my reservations in a piece called “Why It’s Too Early to Get Excited About Web3.”.

I explained how Carlota Perez and Bill Janeway distinguish productive bubbles from unproductive ones. In a productive bubble, speculative excess builds lasting infrastructure the future can capitalize on. The dotcom bubble was, in that sense, productive. When it popped, it left behind billions of miles of high-speed fiber and the data centers and the know-how that the next decade’s boom was built on. The 2009 mortgage bubble, on the other hand, left behind mostly wreckage.

According to recent reports, the glitch with Web3 wasn’t that the prices were crazy, since prices are always crazy in a bubble. It was whether anything was being built that would outlast the crash. What Silicon Valley delivered in that period mostly turned out to be betting with only the barest nod towards actual product. You probably all remember the craze for “bored apes.”.

Even when there is real substance to an investment bubble, Silicon Valley has learned to lean into hype as an instrument for drawing investment. For example, when Tesla’s stock began descending from the stratosphere, Elon Musk started touting humanoid robots as the future of Tesla and pitched SpaceX not on the basis of its actual business of commercial space launches and Starlink’s huge network of communications satellites, but on AI, and on promises of a self-sustaining city on Mars housing at least one million people, travel to any point on earth in 30 minutes, and a possible enterprise value of $100 trillion!

It has been revealed that not everyone can be as bold and imaginative as Elon Musk. But there’s one pretty sure bet that gets the investors to pile on, and that’s the promise of a monopoly.

Look no further than that race between Uber and Lyft. When they went toward their IPOs, neither was profitable, and their enormous valuations rested entirely on the premise that if you grow significant enough and fast enough, profits will follow. Most monopolies and duopolies used to develop slowly and were understood as dangerous to competitive markets. Now Silicon Valley decided they are something to seek from the start, as the holy grail for investors. Reid Hoffman and Chris Yeh called this strategy Blitzscaling, a term they cheerfully derived from the Nazi blitzkrieg. Their argument is that you need to move fast enough to seize a market before anyone else can, even when you don’t yet know how you’ll make money. If you can promise a monopoly, you can raise a great deal of money.

I don’t have a blanket objection to moving fast. But do I think blitzscaling is a morally bankrupt idea, a game that defines winning as extracting value rather than creating it.

Sources indicate that the saddest part of blitzscaling is that it has turned the original genius of the competitive market on its head. It’s now a kind of oligopoly of capital. Instead of customers choosing the winners, the VCs do it up front. Sunil Paul, the inventor of the technology and business model that Uber and Lyft soon dominated, raised only $35 million for his manufacturer Sidecar, which was soon crushed when Uber and Lyft raised and spent billions on marketing and subsidized fares to promptly gain consumers.

If I had to name a villain in this transition, it would be Andreessen Horowitz. The firm was founded in 2009, at the start of the era of cheap capital I’ve been describing, and it built a media and narrative operation from the start. Benedict Evans, who worked there, later described the firm as “a media manufacturer that monetizes through VC.” The story that a company will win because of how much money it has raised becomes part of how it actually wins. But I don’t think it allocates capital anything like as effectively as a well functioning market where customers pick the winners.

Recent findings suggest that what connects the enshittification of search, the supermoney economy, the blitzscaling of Uber, the narrative machine of a16z, and the crypto casino is not a run of bad actors. It’s shareholder capitalism reaching the late stage of its own logic. In its youth, that system was oriented, however imperfectly, toward creating value. In its endgame it has reoriented toward extracting it.

Sources indicate that we are standing at the beginning of the next turn of the cycle. This time, AI is the technology driving the boom. And once again, it represents the possibility of huge advances in human collective intelligence. Like the web was 25 years ago, it’s a latest creative frontier enabled by technology.

The pattern I described earlier usually has a rising-tide youth that comes before the extractive turn. However, in some ways, AI has been enshittified from the very beginning. It skipped the youth. The AI labs have taken in hundreds of billions of dollars, with trillions committed to data center buildout, and capital on that scale doesn’t wait for a business to grow into itself. It demands a return, and the pressure to repay it will inevitably push these companies toward value capture before they’ve finished creating value.

In a recent development, AI also breaks the old bargain in a way even the enshittified web did not. Google, at its best, sent you somewhere else. It read the commons and pointed you back into it, 94% of the time without even trying to monetize it. AI doesn’t send you elsewhere at anything like the same rate. It offers a replacement for what you would once have gone out and found, an answer in place of the referral.

We’ve been told, again and again, that the secret of future prosperity is to create enormous, disproportionate rewards for innovators and their backers. The kind of people that tech companies used to serve as their customers don’t really matter. They are necessary casualties on the road to an unimaginably better future.

This is profoundly short sighted. An economy is a circulatory system. In The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, the visionary poet and painter William Blake (writing during the first Industrial Revolution) put the circulatory logic perfectly: “The Prolific would cease to be prolific unless the Devourer as a sea received the excess of his delights.” In other words: Output has to be consumed. The system has to flow.

It has been revealed that today, many AGI narratives assume that the “prolific” can keep producing and the broad mass of customers (“the devourer”) somehow continue to buy, even as more and more human labor is displaced and labor income and bargaining power collapses. That’s not a future of abundance. It’s a recipe for a kind of congestive heart failure for the economy.

Industry observers note that if the AI labs wish to be architects of a prosperous future, they must work as hard on inventing the new economy’s circulatory system as they do on improving model capabilities. They need to measure success by diffusion, not just capability. They have to ask always how their customers are going to make money, not just how they themselves will. They have to treat the labor transition as a core problem to be solved, not just studied. They have to be willing to win in the marketplace, not through artificial moats. That means committing to open interfaces, portability, and interoperability. General-purpose capabilities should not become a private toll road.

It’s an economy crying out for mechanism design. Mechanism design is a term that I’ve shamelessly stolen from the economists and redefined to describe what I think is missing from the AI economy. It’s a branch of microeconomics that studies how to design the rules of a market in such a way that even self-interested actors who have private information are more likely to produce outcomes that are better for everyone. Leonid Hurwicz, the founder of the field, called it “reverse game theory” because it works backward from a desired outcome to develop the rules that will produce it.

Industry observers note that they give Nobel prizes in economics for advances in the theory of mechanism design. But it seems to me that many of the most successful mechanism designs happen in the real world. They evolve. They are discovered. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie weren’t trying to invent the marvelous open-ended game that we now call open source software when they designed Unix. They were just trying to build a portable operating system able to run on multiple hardware architectures. That also happened to mean that you could only distribute software via its source code rather than just the binaries. And their breakthrough design of a protocol-centric operating system with a small kernel surrounded by cooperating, communicating utilities created what I call “an architecture of participation.” Anyone could add to the system, or easily replace one of its standard parts with an alternative.

That was a very different marketplace design than the proprietary operating systems of the day, which were created to tie software developers to specific hardware platforms. It led to a vibrant software sharing economy that is still going on today and that transformed all of software development.

It has been revealed that you can see the same kind of evolution in AI. I don’t know that David Soria Parra and his colleagues at Anthropic meant to change the market structure of AI when they developed MCP, but that’s what happened. Rather than a winner-takes-most market in which developers call the APIs of the dominant, centralized platforms (as had happened previously with Windows for the PC, and iOs and Android for mobile), the agentic web began to take on the shape of the participatory economy of open source software and the web. People can bring their own models and infrastructure to the table as an alternative to the big centralized players. And that story is far from over. In fact, it is just beginning.

Industry observers note that every major technology wave arrives in two stages. The first stage is the development of the technology itself: the personal computer, the World Wide Web, the smartphone, and now, generative and agentic and physical AI. The second stage involves the development of fresh economic mechanisms that enable transformative business models to take advantage of the technology. The earliest business models often imitate what went before and encode the business ambitions of the old technologies the creators grew up with. As the technology matures, the problems with the original business models become apparent, and eventually, through a process of trial, error, and invention, new mechanisms enable new business models.

The web was invented in 1991. But the web advertising economy didn’t really take off until Google figured out PageRank, and then perfected pay-per-click advertising and the ad auction. Ecommerce didn’t take off until companies like PayPal made it safe to type your credit card number into a stranger’s website, and until Amazon built the warehousing and delivery networks that made rapid delivery possible. The smartphone put GPS in everyone’s pocket, but it wasn’t until Sunil Paul envisioned and built the first real-time location matching marketplace for ride sharing that Uber and Lyft and DoorDash were able to turn that capability into a huge on-demand economy. YouTube didn’t become the engine of the creator economy until it answered the takedown notices and lawsuits of the music industry not with stonewalling or settlements, but with Content ID.

It has been revealed that it’s easy to look at the winners, and think the path to get there was obvious. It wasn’t. There were all kinds of failed approaches to solving the problems that only became apparent during the technology diffusion and adoption period. I don’t have time to chronicle the graveyard of failed search, advertising, and ecommerce experiments and standards. But you don’t need to look back. Just look around. How many proposals there are today for managing rights, blocking or allowing bots, enabling agents to cooperate, and payment. There are at least six competing agent payment protocols alone. We’re in the exploratory phase of mechanism design for AI.

According to recent reports, that’s where I come back to the idea of mechanism design as reverse game theory. Rather than asking ourselves the rules of the game we are now playing, it calls us to ask “What game ought we to be playing?” And that question leads me imperatively to my answer: “The game of human flourishing.”.

We have been told that the game is the quest for superintelligence. We have been told it is a winner-takes-all game that will bring untold riches to the winners and impoverish everyone else. And we have seen mechanisms designed to support that game: massive investments in data center capacity such that only the well-capitalized can play, colonialist appropriation of existing intellectual property, closed model weights with terms of service that forbid others from learning from them, memory that locks our context inside one provider’s walls, and PR stunts like dumping millions of dollars of compute to solve high-profile math problems, or hyping the cybersecurity risks of their offerings, for which only their latest, most powerful models are offered as the only remedy.

If the game we want to play instead is human flourishing, we need to design mechanisms that lead us to that outcome. We need mechanisms that provide a circulatory economy of value exchange, for and by humans in partnership with AI, rather than replaced by it. And in my experience, those mechanisms look like open source, open protocols, open memory, because these are things that give the freedom for people to shape and control this most wonderful upcoming technology wave for ourselves.

Henry Farrell, Alison Gopnik, Cosma Shalizi, and James Evans argued in Science last year that large models are best understood not as independent intelligences but as a fresh kind of cultural and social technology, one that lets us take advantage of the information other humans have accumulated, in the lineage of pictures, writing, print, and internet search. AI may be the most powerful means of harnessing collective intelligence yet. The commons isn’t incidental to AI, it’s the material AI is made from.

Industry observers note that in the world I see coming, AI is a medium, like painting or writing or music. If we get this right, everyone will get the same paints and brushes, the same words, the same notes, but some people draw more out of them than others, or do it better. We won’t decide up front that those who raise the biggest pool of capital are due all the rewards.

In a recent development, our job is to draw something more, something better, out of the ocean of possibilities in the collected knowledge inside the model. AI was built from our collective intelligence. It should not be designed to replace us. It depends on us to create its value.

  • The story has since taken on a mythical status, and was adapted for the big screen with 1969's "​​Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here," which depicted events mostly from the perspective of Robert Redford's lawman.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2014, Jason Momoa co-wrote, directed, produced, and starred in "Road to Paloma," a drama thriller designed to highlight the lack of justice for sexual abuse victims on Native American reservations. Momoa, who is of Native American descent on his mother's side, made his directorial debut with "Road to Paloma," which managed a sort of okay 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. Eight years later, he helped oversee another film centered on Native American heritage, this time in the form of a retelling of the legend of Willie Boy.

This "legend" is actually based on the true story of a member of the indigenous Chemehuevi people who fell in love with a woman named Carlotta in the early 20th Century. The pair absconded but were found and separated by their families. After Willie Boy moved to Banning, California, Carlota soon followed. But her father, William Mike, disapproved of the couple reuniting. He ended up dead, possibly due to having been intentionally shot by Willie Boy or as the result of an accident. After this began what's been called "the last Western Manhunt" in which Willie Boy was pursued by a Sheriff and his small posse over roughly 600 miles.

The story has since taken on a mythical status, and was adapted for the big screen with 1969's "​​Tell Them Willie Boy Is Here," which depicted events mostly from the perspective of Robert Redford's lawman. It was ultimately overshadowed by the actor's other Western from 1969: "Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid." In 2022, however, Momoa, writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett, and director Christian Camargo took another shot at adapting the same story in a very different way with "The Last Manhunt." If you'd like to see how it turned out, the film is presently streaming for free on Tubi.

In a recent development, jason Momoa has a few underrated projects, but "The Last Manhunt" seemed more personal. According to Variety, the "Aquaman" star heard the story of Willie Boy while in the Joshua Tree area, where he owns a home. He and writer Thomas Pa'a Sibbett then developed the story, even meeting with direct descendants of Carlotta's family. The result was a version of the legend based on the Chemehuevi's oral tradition. As Sibbet told Variety, "This is a living story for the Chemehuevi people. It has a special place for them. So we can honor their oral traditions by just listening to them.".

Momoa brought in Christian Camargo to direct, with whom he starred in the Apple TV series "See." Camargo previously wrote and directed 2013's "Days and Nights," which was based on Anton Chekhov's play "The Seagull" and boasted an impressive cast including Mark Rylance, William Hurt, and Ben Whishaw. Unfortunately, Camargo failed to do the Russian playwright's source material proud. "Days and Nights" currently sits at 0% on Rotten Tomatoes with critics ripping into the drama for having nothing to say.

All of which makes "The Last Manhunt" seem like an absolute triumph in comparison. The film stars Martin Sensmeier as Willie and Mainei Kinimaka as Carlotta, who trek across the desert after the death of Carlotta's father. They're pursued by Sheriff Wilson (Camargo) and a small group of indigenous people who want Willie to face justice for the killing. As the manhunt goes on, the ever more tragic consequences pile up. Momoa also appears in the film as Big Jim, a Native member of the posse. But he's only in a handful of scenes and isn't given much to do.

Industry observers note that "The Last Manhunt" didn't make much of an impact upon its 2022 release. After debuting at the first ever Pioneertown International Film Festival, it received distribution by Saban Films. But its limited theatrical release in November 2022 came and went and the film has just sort of languished on digital platforms ever since.

Thankfully, it's now on Tubi and is worth a watch if you're a Western fan. A 20% Rotten Tomatoes score probably isn't the best selling point, however. Luke Y. Thompson of the AV Club gave "The Last Manhunt" credit for "great visuals and the best of intentions" but ultimately found it to be little more than "a basic posse movie" that's "not exciting enough to just do that well." Catey Sullivan of the Chicago Reader, on the other hand, praised the film for "reclaiming the narrative of a Native hero" and delivering a story that "is at once an epic romance and gripping thriller." There's also plenty of acting talent on display. Alongside Martin Sensmeier and Mainei Kinimaka as the leads and Jason Momoa's brief appearances, there's Lily Gladstone as Carlotta's mother Marie, Zahn McClarnon as her father, William Johnson, as well as Wade Williams and Raoul Max Trujillo as trackers in pursuit of the couple.

In a recent development, so, while "The Last Manhunt" is far from one of the best Westerns of the 21st Century, there's enough here for fans of the genre. Those interested to see whether Momoa and his cohorts managed to finally do justice to the Willie Boy legend should also find "The Last Manhunt" worthwhile. The film is available to stream on Tubi right now.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it's been a tough decade for fans of fantasy television.
  • It has been revealed that based on the book trilogy of the same name written by Lev Grossman and created for television by Sera Gamble and John McNamara, The Magicians is often described as Harry Potter, but in college.
  • According to recent reports, we'd be here all day if we were to list everything there is to love about The Magicians.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it's been a tough decade for fans of fantasy television. Despite the early, world-shattering success of Game of Thrones and the prestige fantasy boom that followed, the last few years have seen a severe drop-off in quality for many promising projects. After the abrupt cancellation of The Wheel of Time, the disappointment of Season 2 of both The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power and Game of Thrones spin-off House of the Dragon, fantasy television hasn't hit another peak yet. Thankfully, fantasy fans don't need to look too far for a more reliable television experience, as there's one series that has never released a single bad season: The Magicians.

It has been revealed that based on the book trilogy of the same name written by Lev Grossman and created for television by Sera Gamble and John McNamara, The Magicians is often described as Harry Potter, but in college. It's a subversive take on high fantasy that infuses the awe of learning magic on Earth with all the hilarious misadventures of maturity. The Syfy series follows Quentin Coldwater (Jason Ralph), an awkward fantasy fan himself, whose dreams come true when he learns that magic is real and is invited to attend Brakebills, a college for the magically gifted, as a graduate student. Over the course of five seasons now available to stream on Prime Video, Quentin subsequently realizes his favorite fantasy series is real, becomes schooled in the true meaning of magic, and goes on all sorts of hilarious adventures alongside an equally unhinged supporting cast.

According to recent reports, we'd be here all day if we were to list everything there is to love about The Magicians. Not only does the series feature a talented cast of performers who consistently nail their roles, impressive special effects, and a unique message about the origins of magic, but by and large, The Magicians is an excellent example of how to adapt rich source material for the screen. Grossman's novels are already engrossing and filled with relatable characters, lore, and tragic backstories, but Gamble and McNamara take advantage of their long-form format to flesh out the trilogy's supporting players and make the world their own in a way that still honors the wayward spirit of the original. The result is a strong foundation for a series that only finds fresh ways to entertain, devastate, and enthrall you over time.

Industry observers note that some of The Magicians' best changes involve its main cast. Not only does the series greatly expand on characters like Margo (Summer Bishil) and Kady (Jade Tailor) — both of whom are based on characters who go by different names in the novels — but it also upgrades Fen (Brittany Curran) from a sidenote in the books to one of the show's most hilariously chaotic mainstays. Furthermore, the series honors the queerness of characters like Eliot (Hale Appleman) and Quentin with heartbreaking storylines that go beyond the teases and more ambiguous circumstances of the original trilogy. This earnest focus is what allowed The Magicians to release its most beloved and iconic episode, Season 3's "A Day in the Life," and also consistently deliver some of the show's most beautiful moments between the two in later seasons.

According to recent reports, aside from expanding Grossman's world and honoring his characters, these additions are also what allow The Magicians to sustain its level of high quality across all five seasons. Although the series stretches its source material to more or less encompass its full run, the reality is that the show could have wrapped things up in at least three seasons if its creators had opted for a more straightforward adaptation. The reason The Magicians never experiences a sudden shift in quality or narrative drop-off is that the show's storytelling never becomes dependent on the books.

Industry observers note that unlike Game of Thrones, which found itself in serious trouble once the show caught up to George R.R. Martin's series, The Magicians developed so many fresh takes on Quentin and his friends that it had plenty of additional material to explore, allowing The Magicians to come into its own over time rather than stray from the conventions of someone else's world.

Sources indicate that between the show's exploration of the underworld, multidimensional antics, and depiction of morally disturbed gods, The Magicians partially maintains its narrative momentum through largely original storylines, but it also keeps things refreshing for fans of the show and books alike. With constant pop culture references dropped by one of television's most underrated duos, it's no exaggeration to say Margo and Eliot's mere presence makes every one of their scenes better, and The Magicians' spontaneous musical numbers are another great example of how the series takes full advantage of its talented cast while also honoring the irreverent tone of the novels.

Featuring creative episode formats involving split perspectives, alternate universes, and time loops, The Magicians also takes a page out of the narrative playbook of less fantastical shows like Community, allowing innovative approaches to the show's unique medium to complement the self-sustaining power of its adaptation.

Recent findings suggest that as with any fantasy series, there are some changes The Magicians makes that don't quite land. Despite the power of Julia's (Stella Maeve) journey and some welcome tweaks the showrunners introduce to her character, her short-lived ending in the series is conflicting, to say the least. Nevertheless, the heights The Magicians hit are far more memorable than its misses, and it is through the show's strengths that it manages to remain compelling throughout all five of its seasons.

Sources indicate that A decision to kill one of the main characters, for instance, exemplifies how Gamble and McNamara were willing to deviate dramatically from their source material to move their story forward in a refreshing way. This absence allowed The Magicians to double down on its changes without relying on the novels' original protagonist, opening the door for upcoming heroes and villains to literally steal the show.

It's not for nothing that The Magicians still feels like it has even more story to tell after its Season 6 cancellation, and it's this level of success that makes the series the perfect roadmap for the future of fantasy television. At a time when series are either buckling under the weight of their source material or making changes that undermine the underlying narrative, The Magicians' ability to both respect and surpass its inspiration should be studied by streamers and other creatives in the industry.

By keeping what works, expanding ideas that deserve more screen time, and being willing to kill someone else's darlings to do what's best for the story, The Magicians delivers five seasons of phenomenal television that never misses a beat.

Apple TV's offbeat spy thriller "Slow Horses" just completed its sixth season this past October, and it won't be calling its quits anytime soon, having since been renewed for several more seasons. The vast majority of critics and fans believe the show hasn't lost a step (even with the departure of original head writer Will Smith at the end of Season 5), and its Mick Herron-penned source material still has meat on the bone. Thus, "Slow Horses" will likely run as long as Gary Oldman wants to keep chopping and literally stinking it up as Slough House chief Jackson Lamb.

The narrative arc of "Slow Horses" Season 6 was particularly gripping, as its team of misfit spies found themselves being unceremoniously liquidated. Lamb can't protect his operatives, so they're all forced to go into hiding. It's a perilous state of play for River Cartwright (Jack Lowden), the series' underdog protagonist who demonstrates flashes of Lamb's spycraft expertise but can't quite put it all together. He needs help, and he receives it from seemingly beyond the grave when Olivia Cooke's agent Sidonie "Sid" Baker turns up in River's grandfather's house.

Sid was presumed dead in Season 1, but she's back in action in Season 6, and she throws a charge into the proceedings as the romantic spark between her and River threatens to burst into a white-hot flame. We should expect nothing less from Cooke because she's been superb throughout his career, and that extends to her crucial role in Darius Marder's 2020 critical darling "Sound of Metal.".

In a recent development, in what might be her best work to date, Cooke stars in Darius Marder's Oscar-winning drama as a singer whose drummer boyfriend (Riz Ahmed) is dealing with rapidly encroaching deafness. Cooke could've easily been relegated to a stand-by-your-wounded-man role in "Sound of Metal," but she branches out and, via Marder and Abraham Marder's screenplay (and a story co-credited to Derek Cianfrance), locates the sadness in a woman trying to save the person she cares about more than virtually anyone else in the world. Unfortunately, as the film progresses, it becomes clear that her character no longer serves a function in her lover's life. It's a painful thing to watch, but they're on different journeys now, and while healing is entirely possible, they just can't heal together.

Industry observers note that cooke has never been better, but she's still one plum role away from transcendence. I can't wait to see how that plays out.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.
  • It has been revealed that the manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator.
  • Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.

It has been revealed that the manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator. It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command transcript, or Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction. Then it checks your work, sends corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.

Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed NDA and a speech due this week are one rm away, and every shift his home folder holds something newly introduced to lose.

When the shift ends you can share your review as a link.

Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).

With no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI Gateway key in .env:.

Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:.

In a recent development, for UI work, run npm run dev:web alongside npm run mock. Vite proxies /api to the server.

It has been revealed that the manager can run on your own model server: Ollama, llama.cpp's llama-server, vLLM, or anything else with an OpenAI-compatible API. Point LOCAL_LLM_URL at it and pick Local under "Your API key"; no key is asked for, and its models are listed as the server names them.

It has been revealed that the manager works through tool calls, so pick a model that supports them (Qwen 3, Llama 3.1 and newer, Mistral Small). Small models give up or loop more often; that is part of the fun, up to a point. In Docker, reach a server on the host at http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1 (--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway on Linux).

It has been revealed that the container listens on 0.0.0.0:8755 and keeps shared reviews in /data. Behind Cloudflare, set TRUST_PROXY=1 so the limits see real client addresses.

deploy/compose.yaml runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.

Everything is optional. See .env.example.

The manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see server/src/manager.ts. Each mission has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work ("Times the manager was wrong"). SPEC.md is the full design.
