📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that amazon MGM is shaking things up with their upcoming James Bond movie, and why the heck not? The end of Daniel Craig's Bond tenure in "No Time To Die" left the franchise in a sorry state of affairs and it's time to rejuvenate the saga with some fresh blood and upcoming ideas. Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond suggests things are on the right track. The British actor is the first major star to debut in the tux, breaking more than 60 years of tradition and suggesting Amazon and director Denis Villeneuve are ready to try new things.

For now, however, we're yet to learn who will surround this A-list Bond. The supporting cast provides yet more opportunity to refresh the series, and while he might not be as crucial to the 007 formula as, say, the Bond girls or M, Felix Leiter presents a particularly exciting opportunity in that regard.

It has been revealed that the character, first introduced in the inaugural Bond novel, "Casino Royale" in 1953, has traditionally been a CIA agent and Bond ally. Since the first 007 movie, 1962's "Dr. No," we've seen various iterations of Felix and multiple actors in the role. Some have been older and avuncular, some have been younger American 007 counterparts, and some have been boring bureaucrats. But for the most part, the character of Felix Leiter is yet to be fully explored. As such, the upcoming "Bond 26" presents a chance to do something completely new with Felix, and we think we have the actors for the job.

In a recent development, in 2017, James Bond's greatest ally got his first solo mission in comic books. The "Felix Leiter" comic book mini-series, from writer James Robinson and illustrator Aaron Campbell, gave the titular CIA agent his own story and missions separate from his British counterpart. The story saw him leave the foreign intelligence service and become a private detective, but that's beside the point in this instance. What could be really interesting is if Amazon MGM uses "Bond 26" to introduce a version of the character who could similarly carry his own on-screen spin-off. Aaron Pierre would be perfect for the job.

Pierre is fresh off a great performance in HBO's "Lanterns" and previously delivered a memorable turn in Jeremy Saulnier's gripping 2024 actioner "Rebel Ridge." As such, he's proved he has leading man chops. "Lanterns" also saw him convincingly play an ex-Marine, which just so happens to be part of Felix's background — at least in the books. With DC Studios now reportedly being dismantled by real-life Bond villain David Ellison, Pierre might be looking for a job and Amazon MGM should give him one.

Why not turn Felix into an action hero of his own? Everyone is surely expecting Bond spin-offs now that Amazon owns the IP, and as the comic book series proved, Felix is an ideal candidate. Of course, the character can't overshadow Bond in the upcoming film, but that doesn't mean you can't build him up over time to be a worthy competitor to Robert Pattinson's MI6 sleuth. Whether he remains a staunch Bond ally or there's some competition between the two it would make for a fresh dynamic in keeping with Amazon and Denis Villeneuve's upcoming direction for the franchise.

Sources indicate that everybody knows that Jack Lowden almost became the new face of the James Bond movies, before missing out on the lead role to Robert Pattinson. The "Slow Horses" star would have made an excellent 007 and regardless of how exciting it is to have Pattinson in the tux, it's also a shame we won't see what Lowden would have done with the part. But that doesn't mean he can't play another role in Amazon MGM's new Bond-verse, and Felix Leiter seems like an interesting option.

It could, I suppose, be seen as a bit of an insult to hand a Bond hopeful a supporting role. But it shouldn't, given the aforementioned potential for spin-offs and exploring Felix Leiter's character more extensively. Things could get really interesting if Denis Villeneuve and "Bond 26" writer Steven Knight made Felix into more of a rival to Bond. With Lowden and Pattinson's Bond audition history, there's a built-in tension there already. If Lowden were to play an American Bond counterpart who clashes with Pattinson's agent, that would be a hugely compelling on-screen rivalry to watch play out.

Industry observers note that yes, Felix has historically been a Bond ally. But with the franchise entering a newly introduced era why not switch things up? Have Lowden play a version of Felix who gives Bond a run for his money. Capitalize on the Pattinson/Lowden audition history and watch the dollars roll in. With "Slow Horses" being as good as it is, it only feels right to bring Lowden into the fold in some capacity and this could be a really interesting way to do so.

Industry observers note that if you haven't seen "Lioness" you might be wondering who this dashing stud of a man is. Well let me tell you. Thad Luckinbill is one of the most charismatic, endlessly watchable actors in Taylor Sheridan's spy thriller series. As CIA senior case officer and all round hardman Kyle McManus, Luckinbill brings a mix of smarmy charm and ruthlessness, deadly efficiency that would make for an exciting compliment to Robert Pattinson's Bond.

Kyle is, in many ways, the opposite of 007. He's loud, brash, and outspoken. But he shares much in common with Bond in that they're both supremely confident and solipsistic. If Luckinbill could bring some of that Kyle energy to Felix Leiter, the character could become either a wonderful foil to Pattinson's more urbane spy, or perhaps even pose a bit of a threat.

When he first appeared in "Casino Royale" back in 1953, Felix Leiter was a former Marine working for NATO's Joint Intelligence Staff who allied with Bond. He and 007's connection was a way to represent the United Kingdom and United States' "special relationship." With Pattinson so easily exuding the public school boy aura of Bond (it's one of the reasons he could be the best Bond yet) and Luckinbill effortlessly encapsulating the more traditionally brash American approach, these two side-by-side could make for a brilliant Trump-era representation of the somewhat strained yet still resilient "special relationship.".

"Tenet" was full of confusing moments, to the extent that the entire thing was arguably one massive confusing moment. What wasn't in doubt, however, was the fact that Robert Pattinson and John David Washington had chemistry.

Sources indicate that fittingly, Washington played a CIA agent known only as The Protagonist in Christopher Nolan's confounding thriller, alongside Pattinson as his handler, Neil. Together, they were an American and British spy team who brought very different energies to their roles. Neil was quite prepared to blow a freeport sky high, while Washington's Protagonist remained wary, making for a fun dynamic between the pair. Neil always seemed to be one step ahead and ready to do whatever was needed to get the job done, while The Protagonist remained constantly surprised by his cohort's knowledge and boldness.

In a recent development, if Washington is cast as Felix Leiter in "Bond 26," we could see a similar dynamic between the pair, which wouldn't be the worst thing in the world — especially if it were given more space to develop outside of Nolan's narrative machinations. Or, we could see a reversal of the dynamic, whereby Felix is even more of a daredevil rogue than Bond. Either way, the duo have proved their on-screen chemistry and would make a great Bond/Felix pairing.

Recent findings suggest that you can chart Robert Pattinson's transformation from teen heartthrob to versatile character actor mostly via his portrayal of freaky little weirdos. The man just has a knack for playing off-kilter and slightly creepy types. But he's far from the only actor in Hollywood who seems to have that dark, subversive energy simmering below a relatively calm exterior.

Jesse Plemons is arguably just as exciting an actor as Pattinson. He's been consistently delivering compelling performances over the last decade or so and while his particular energy might work well as a villain, it could also be really interesting to see him working with, or at least alongside, Pattinson's James Bond. Both actors are capable of fully inhabiting their characters and simply seeing them bounce off of one another would surely make for some of the most interesting scenes in "Bond 26." Or, Plemons could bring the same "Civil War" energy that previously made his co-star cry to the role and give Bond a real run for his money.

Casting an actor of Plemons' talents in the role also allows the producers to really lean into a Felix spin-off in the future. Plemons has the chops to make a character study of Bond's favorite ally work, and I for one would watch the heck out of a Plemons-led Felix Leiter miniseries. Otherwise, the actor is yet to play a character like Felix, and it would be an interesting change of pace for him.

Forget Taylor Sheridan, This is the Master of the Modern Western

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (978 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Westerns have continuously trickled down in numbers as a genre for film and TV through the decades.
  • Sources indicate that the character actor of directors, S.
  • According to recent reports, aside from Bone Tomahawk, Zahler has also quietly flexed his Western skills by both being the uncredited screenwriter of last year's underrated Frontier Crucible, and by being a prolific novelist, with his two most famous being A Congregation of Jackals and Wraiths of the Broken Land, which, combined with Bone Tomahawk, are thematically linked to make a twisted Western trilogy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Westerns have continuously trickled down in numbers as a genre for film and TV through the decades. While neo-Westerns seem to get a lot of traction, with a filmmaker like Taylor Sheridan having a filmography filled almost completely with entries in the genre—including his epic American Frontier Trilogy—there are few traditional Westerns that still get released to a wide audience. An argument could be made that there isn't much of a market anymore, or maybe that a lot of people just don't like Westerns, but that's about as much a blanket statement as saying you don't like action movies or chick flicks. That's fine if you don't like Nicholas Sparks knockoffs, but if you besmirch The Princess Bride or When Harry Met Sally by lumping them in with that sort, you best prepare to have a donnybrook on your hands. Rather, when it comes to traditional Westerns, short of homages or parodies, very few directors seem to have a deep desire to make them. That is, of course, except for the man with no first name given, and that's S. Craig Zahler.

Sources indicate that the character actor of directors, S. Craig Zahler continues to work under the radar of general audiences, even though the movies he's made have been widely well-received by critics. He's a writer/director with a succinct style—bordering on niche—that's recognizable for its lockdown visual style, methodical pace, and engrossing, stage play-like dialogue, contrasting against viciously brutal violence and inhuman villains. All of this was established with his debut film, Bone Tomahawk, which is about a group of cowboys in the Old West, led by Sheriff Hunt (Kurt Russell), working to save the town doctor, Mrs. O'Dwyer (Lili Simmons), from savage, cannibalistic troglodytes. To put it into context, if you've ever heard the Mark Twain quote where he compared masterful writing to wine, and his to water...well, Zahler's movies are like the film-making equivalent of a White Monster Energy Drink (i.e. not for everybody, but the ones who like them will REALLY like them).

According to recent reports, aside from Bone Tomahawk, Zahler has also quietly flexed his Western skills by both being the uncredited screenwriter of last year's underrated Frontier Crucible, and by being a prolific novelist, with his two most famous being A Congregation of Jackals and Wraiths of the Broken Land, which, combined with Bone Tomahawk, are thematically linked to make a twisted Western trilogy. Wraiths of the Broken Land will also forever live as a "What could have been" scenario since it was declared back in 2016 to be adapted by Ridley Scott and Drew Goddard, but has since languished in the fires of Development Hell. Presumably because of how dark the novel gets and Zahler's distinct style being hard to sell to general audiences.

Sources indicate that if spaghetti Westerns were considered subversions of traditional Westerns, Zahler's stories are subversions of spaghetti Westerns. Zahler's biggest strength as a storyteller is his ability to craft his stories into twists and turns that you're not expecting, and to go hard with wherever the story leads him. His method is to write each day until he shocks himself with what comes out, working from the idea that if he surprises himself while writing, the audience won't see it coming, either. That's probably how he came up with the horrid things that can be done with fishhooks, dead baby turtles, rifle barrels heated over an open fire, and everything about the "Wishbone" scene in Bone Tomahawk.

Sources indicate that there's a blunt harshness to his action and violence, and especially the depiction of life on the frontier. He doesn't play favorites, and isn't afraid to shock and abhor his viewers or readers under the guise of telling the stories the way he wants to tell them. Sometimes, that means the lead characters are just as cruel as the villains, and almost without fail, that means the villains are pitiless and verge on being inhuman entities. It's like Zahler read Blood Meridian before writing A Congregation of Jackals and thought Judge Holden was too affable and normal looking, so he came up with Quinlan and his gang. And then he put Blood Meridian down because Cormac McCarthy's lack of quotations and speech tags around dialogue can be hard to follow sometimes . . .I'm guessing.

What makes Zahler's stories so good is that even though their content might be too disturbing for some, his characters are consistently very fleshed-out and captivating to follow. And for every morally gray character, there are a few, like Sheriff Hunt in Bone Tomahawk and Merrick Beckford (Myles Clohessy) in Frontier Crucible, who feel like they could've come right out of a John Ford Western just for how noble they are. And in some cases, what actually makes the more disturbing things even more upsetting is it's happening to characters you like. Bone Tomahawk in particular is interesting, because—unlike something like From Dusk Till Dawn, which does a complete genre flip from crime film to vampire movie—it gradually devolves from a traditional-looking Western into a cannibal horror film. Almost as if the characters are traveling from one genre and entering into another (which is made clearer through the changing landscapes).

It has been revealed that S. Craig Zahler is a unique writer and filmmaker who's able to tell stories across different mediums, but one never usurps the other when it comes to quality. When it comes to his takes on Westerns, the stories feel uniquely his own, but they don't seem like he's trying to deconstruct the genre or emulate the style with a modern twist (or have them take place in a modern setting). They feel like stories that he wanted to tell that just happened to take place in the Old West and didn't feel the need to go the way of paying homage.

Stephen King’s R-Rated Sci-Fi Series Is Officially Darker Than His Book

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, most Stephen King novels dabble with incredibly grim subject matter.
  • While MGM+'s The Institute does not match the extremes of Frank Darabont's The Mist, it does push the darker elements of the original story to a new level.
  • From a visual standpoint, even The Institute season 2 is not too different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, most Stephen King novels dabble with incredibly grim subject matter. Owing to this, it is an impressive feat when an adaptation manages to push the boundaries of darkness even further. Quite a few movie and TV adaptations of the author's work have managed to defy expectations and deliver even bleaker stories. Case in point, 2007's The Mist leaves viewers with a completely hopeless ending.

While MGM+'s The Institute does not match the extremes of Frank Darabont's The Mist, it does push the darker elements of the original story to a new level. In season 1, The Institute felt more like a watered-down version of the original. It stayed true to the original themes and character beats of the book but featured less graphic violence and psychological horror.

From a visual standpoint, even The Institute season 2 is not too different. Despite its TV-MA rating, the show rarely pushes its disturbing imagery to match Stephen King's writing. In terms of storytelling, however, the show has officially exceeded the darker aspects of the book, which makes it even more compelling than it initially seemed.

In Stephen King's The Institute, the main young characters overcome the overarching evil forces towards the end. They take down the very facility that tortured them and emerge victorious in their battle for freedom. The Institute season 1's ending portrays something similar, where Luke and his friends destroy the titular facility, albeit with a few big losses.

However, in season 2, their victory is completely stripped. They soon realize that they are dealing with far bigger forces. The facility they destroyed was a mere pawn in a far bigger conspiracy. After jumping out of the proverbial frying pan in season 1, they realize they are now on the fire with powerful people deadset upon finding them.

In a recent development, the main character, Luke, also came off as a steadfast hero. He always took a stand against the people running the Institute and did not hold himself back from going all-out against them. In season 2, he is cursed with the power of foresight. His precognition abilities improve, allowing him to see how his decisions could even get his friends killed.

Industry observers note that as a result, instead of throwing all caution to the wind, he makes some moral compromises and plays safe. He even betrays his friends, believing that it would help him save them from their imminent doom. Speaking of doom, The Institute season 2 also does not shy away from killing off one of season 1's main heroes, Wendy, in the very beginning.

These developments instantly establish the high and incredibly bleak stakes The Institute's main characters are now dealin with.

Expanding the original story of a complete book can always be a tricky endeavor. Even some of the greatest adaptations, like Game of Thrones, have suffered after extending beyond their source material. Fortunately, for The Institute, it followed a fairly generic and derivative storyline in season 1 while introducing some intriguing ideas.

Industry observers note that this paved the way for the series to become all the more compelling in season 2. So far, The Institute has been doing an incredible job of expanding ideas surrounding precognition, free will, and determinism in season 2. This allows the series to be even more thought-provoking than the original Stephen King book. It almost feels like a Philip K. Dick adaptation in its ongoing story beats.

Hopefully, moving forward, The Institute season 2 will only get better. Instead of treading the same path as its predecessor and relying on familiar ideas from the sci-fi genre, the Stephen King adaptation should take more creative risks and not shy away from being as dark (if not more) as the original book.

The Institute, released in 2025, follows 14-year-old genius Luke Ellis, who is kidnapped and wakes up at a mysterious facility filled with children possessing unusual abilities. Meanwhile, Tim Jamieson, a former police officer, seeks a fresh start in a nearby town, inevitably intertwining his fate with Luke's.

Sources indicate that these two files are the whole claim. Statements.lean defines four propositions. Main.lean proves them, and Mathlib's own RiemannHypothesis, by citing theorems from the other 175,185 modules. Point at a symbol to see how to say it and what type it has.

Industry observers note that in words: every zero of the Riemann zeta function, other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … , has real part ½. For every Dirichlet character χ, every zero of L(s, χ) with real part strictly between 0 and 1 has real part ½.

Recent findings suggest that each rectangle is one module. Modules are grouped by directory, and a larger rectangle means more of the chosen size measure.

Scroll over the map to zoom, drag to move, click a module to read its code.

Terms come from Alpöge's announcement and from standard number theory. A module is counted if the term's identifier appears in its text, not counting import lines.

Where each step appears to live in the Lean code, according to a blueprint of the proof by GitHub user jae-63. ● found clearly   ◐ names and position fit   ○ weak evidence. The number is how many modules match. Point at a step to see it on the map; click to keep it highlighted.

Each module's field is predicted by a classifier from the Mathlib and project identifiers it uses. The prediction agrees with a language model's reading of the module about half the time (details under Sources and method). Point at a row to see where that field sits on the map.

The line under each field lists objects and theorems named in the labels that a language model gave to each of 746 directories after reading a digest of its identifiers. Treat them as a guide, not a census.

A comment on Hacker News reported 204 modules "not referenced anywhere", without a list or a method. In the import graph no module is unreferenced: every module except Main.lean is imported by at least one other module. The comment may be counting something that imports do not show, such as declarations that nothing uses.

Scroll the graph sideways to see all of it.

Colour the map by numeric literals per 100 lines or by share of characters that are the digits 0–9.

Point at a bar to see what the tactic does and which modules use it.

According to recent reports, what each of these public pages reported when read on 23 November 2026. None of the checks were run in building this page.

The Lean statements cover the Riemann zeta function and Dirichlet L-functions. They do not cover Dedekind zeta functions or automorphic L-functions.

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.].

In a recent development, paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of fresh love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Rian Johnson Leaves the Door Open to Star Wars Return: ‘It’s a World I Deeply Love’ Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Crucial Franchise.

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy Fresh York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.).

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its Newly introduced York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

According to recent reports, winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Percy Jackson & the Olympians is a series of novels by American author Rick Riordan which was a massive success.
  • The series is perhaps most famous for its stellar Disney+ TV adaptation, as well as its disastrous early 2010s movies starring Logan Lerman.
  • It has been revealed that tristan Strong Punches a Hole in the Sky is, admittedly, a bit of a mouthful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Percy Jackson & the Olympians is a series of novels by American author Rick Riordan which was a massive success. The story is about Percy, a young boy who discovers he is a demigod, i.e. that his father was the Greek god Poseidon. He is then whisked away to a secluded camp in the wilderness, where other demigods train and learn to fight the ravenous monsters from Greek mythology that prowl the world, unseen by ordinary human eyes.

The series is perhaps most famous for its stellar Disney+ TV adaptation, as well as its disastrous early 2010s movies starring Logan Lerman. If you're a massive fan of the book series and how they seamlessly blend 21st century life with mythology, there are plenty of other books out there that you might also wish to check out.

It has been revealed that tristan Strong Punches a Hole in the Sky is, admittedly, a bit of a mouthful. Lengthy title aside, this novel by Kwame Mbalia was actually presented and approved by Rick Riordan himself, basically linking the book with the legacy of Percy Jackson. The "Rick Riordan Presents" branding basically focuses on similar stories that feature mythological elements from various cultures that intersect with real life, and this tale is no exception to that rule.

Sources indicate that instead of being about Egyptian, Greco-Roman, or Norse mythology, which are arguably the most popular, this one features West African deities and folklore. This is combined with Black American folktales as well, creating a fascinating blended universe. The main character, the eponymous Tristan Strong, is actually incredibly likable. Plus, the story deserves points for bringing a mythology to life that rarely gets the chance to. Representing a rich, yet overlooked culture, combined with tween-friendly plotlines and lovable characters make this novel a real diamond in the rough. It's no wonder it was approved by the massive man himself; you just can't beat that.

Caytlyn Brooke's Among the Hunted is the first novel in the Skyglass series, which is all about Greek mythology. It doesn't serve as a retelling of an existing narrative established in the mythos. Rather, it crafts a fresh story that is seamlessly integrated into the existing mythology, so that nothing feels out of place. As of yet, no other Skyglass books have been published, but it is implied that there are more on the way.

According to recent reports, among the Hunted centers on Kaitani, a nymph warrior who serves Olean. She has fallen in love with Hermes, the messenger of the gods, and is shouldering an unbearable guilt following the death of her closest friend. It's a horrible existence, made even worse by the fact that Zeus begins actively hunting Kaitani's sister. This causes her to embark on a quest for revenge, finally releasing the emotions she's been bottling up for 100 years. Now, she has just one goal: kill an immortal. This book is a bit more mature than typical YA novels, but it's still appropriate for teens and adults alike. If you're in this age group, and you love Percy Jackson and need some more Greek mythology, this is definitely something you should check out.

It might sound like a broken record to recommend this one, but Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone is still a great book for Percy Jackson fans. This is mainly due to the fact that Harry Potter basically revolutionized the whole YA genre, creating a market boom of similar stories, of which Percy Jackson was part of. However, the similarities go beyond surface-level trends, and go right down to the bones of each story.

Each series features a reluctant hero for a protagonist; a secluded, specialized academy for magical individuals; quippy dialogue; and various monsters from mythology. Both series have their fair share of adventure and comedy in equal measure. While Harry Potter doesn't feature any gods or deities from mythology, it has enough in common with Percy Jackson that it is often the next thing readers move on to when they've finished with Percy's story. In fact, many Potter fans also move straight on to Percy Jackson once they're finished.

Industry observers note that the Serpent's Secret is the first in a series called Kiranmala and the Kingdom Beyond, a YA trilogy based on Bengali folklore. The eponymous protagonist, Kiranmala, is an ordinary 12-year-old living in Upcoming Jersey, who has been repeatedly told by her parents that she comes from a place outside this Earth, and that she is secretly an Indian princess. Though she never believes the stories, it turns out they were right, as she finds herself confronted by a horrifying rakkhosh demon, which abducts her parents. This is made more convoluted when two princes arrive and whisk her away to an alternate dimension.

Rather than being about Hinduism as a whole, the novel draws inspiration from lesser-talked about Indian traditions, imbuing its narrative with winged horses, talking birds, and a vengeful Serpent King. It's one of the most thematically interesting worlds told in a YA novel, and it fits in perfectly with the massive YA boom that began in the late '90s and peaked in the late 2000s/early 2010s. Fans of Percy Jackson will absolutely love this one, especially since it features ancient traditions and stories blending with aspects of real life in the 21st century.

In a recent development, wolves is Book One of I Bring the Fire by C. Gockel. The book is primarily about Loki, the Norse god of trickery, and opens up with Loki waking up in a prison cell. This time, he has no idea what he's actually done to land himself there, but he does know one thing: his dear father, Odin, and brother, Thor, are up to something. Loki isn't sure what that something is, but he is sure that he doesn't like it one bit. Meanwhile, in a sleepy American Midwest town, a girl is on her way to her grandmother's house when her fate becomes intertwined with Loki's.

Recent findings suggest that this hidden gem is perfectly suited for fans of Percy Jackson. After all, it has gods from a dead religion interacting with ordinary people and existing in the real world. The series also features the signature sass and chaos that Percy Jackson became famous for, alongside a cast of memorable characters and a grand adventure. It might not be the best book ever written, but it's something that fans of Percy Jackson will absolutely want to check out.

Sources indicate that the Song of Achilles is a stand-alone novel that became a major hit with audiences. Written by Madeline Miller, this novel is a retelling of the Trojan War through the eyes of one of its most famed warriors, Achilles. Alongside Achilles is his lifelong friend, Patroclus, both of whom are trained by Chiron the centaur in the arts of warfare. When Helen of Sparta is kidnapped and the Greeks lay siege to Troy, Achilles and Patroclus answer the call. However, their relationship blossoms into something beyond friendship.

Indeed, the two do end up forming a romantic relationship, which was actually fairly commonplace in Ancient Greece. This book has a little bit of everything: there's romance, war, action, and adventure in equal measure, providing a fresh spin on an age-old story. The Song of Achilles won quite a few awards, including the Orange Prize for Fiction, one of the UK's most prestigious literary awards. If you're a teen or an adult, this book is an excellent recommendation for fans of Percy Jackson and the Olympians.

The Odyssey is the quintessential Greek myth, initially penned by Homer nearly 3,000 years ago. Rather than a novel, the book is formatted as an epic poem, which was a common storytelling medium at the time. While it wasn't technically considered fantasy when it first came out, it certainly fits the bill in hindsight. The story became so popular, even for the time, that it eventually became part of the official Greek canon, meaning it is an official part of Greek mythology.

Since the poem is one of the most famous things ever written, as well as one of the oldest surviving works of fiction, pretty much everybody knows the story by now. It's about a warrior named Odysseus who is returning home to Greece after spending years fighting in the Trojan War. This journey home is no easy feat, though, as Odysseus and his crew encounter numerous beasts and beings as they sail across the Greek islands. This is such an ideal pick for Percy Jackson fans because it's one of the main works that inspired it all in the first place. Fans will definitely recognize some of their favorite featured creatures from Riordan's series in the Odyssey, and will come to understand the origins of Greek epics.

What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell.
  • To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

According to recent reports, “Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a fresh idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”.

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro stated. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”.

It has been revealed that hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro stated the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro noted. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Sources indicate that hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a fresh design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”.

In a recent development, in addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro remarked. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”.

In a recent development, during one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and stated, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

It has been revealed that “He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that all 62 episodes of Prime Video's acclaimed sci-fi masterpiece deliver gripping interplanetary warfare, extraordinary characters, and epic storytelling. Released back in 2015, this dystopian sci-fi series spanned six seasons on Prime Video until it concluded in 2022, based on a series of celebrated novels that began with 2011's Leviathan Wakes. Praised for its elite world-building, science-backed mechanisms, and great visuals, this is one sci-fi series that all fans of the genre must check out, as all 62 episodes are truly perfect from start to finish.

Sources indicate that the Expanse is a true sci-fi masterpiece on Prime Video, given its 95% Rotten Tomatoes score across 62 episodes and 6 seasons. The series delivers peak dystopian sci-fi on streaming and still sets the gold standard for the genre 11 years after its premiere on Prime Video. Critics and audiences agree that it is, somewhat quietly, one of the greatest sci-fi series of the 21st century, with The Ringer saying of its final season, "For all the worthy comparisons to Game of Thrones, there's one thing The Expanse achieved that its HBO counterpart couldn't: This show stuck the landing." For a complete sci-fi binge that's worth the investment, The Expanse can't be beat.

The Expanse has one of the most intriguing premises with a massive scope in all modern sci-fi set between conflicting communities on Earth and in outer space. With each competing for political power and cosmic influence, The Expanse is set several centuries in the future, when humans have colonized several areas of the solar system, including Mars and the Asteroid Belt between Mars and Jupiter.

Industry observers note that when the series begins, Earth remains the most dominant force within the solar system, but a newly advanced society and military presence on Mars threatens to disrupt that order. Earth's key vulnerability, however, is its dependence on off-planet resources from far-off colonies.

Much like the distribution of power between nations on Earth, colonies each import, export, and trade resources, which become the driving forces behind power and control in this newly introduced dynamic. This is one of the ways that The Expanse feels reality-based and plausible given the circumstances, while also maintaining modern science elements that never lean too heavily into the fantasy genre.

Sources indicate that even the battles that take place in outer space are based on realistic physics, separating it from other epic space franchises such as Dune and Star Wars. This emphasis on political considerations and resource allocation resembles the most crucial and basic foundation of human civilization and conflicts between world superpowers.

While The Expanse carries a vast scale across planets and colonies, the heart of the series throughout all six seasons is the crew of the Rocinante spaceship. Featuring members from Earth, Mars, and the Belt, the crew forms an unlikely bond and allegiance despite their cultural differences, which forms the emotional core of the series. Several key figures include James Holden (Steven Strait), an ex-military officer and captain of the ship, Naomi Nagata (Dominique Tipper), an engineer from the Belt, Amos Burton (Wes Chatham), a mechanic from Earth, and Alex Kamal (Cas Anvar), a pilot from Mars.

These four begin on the Canterbury, a freighter ship transporting water from Saturn's rings to the Belt, which is destroyed in season 1. James, Naomi, Amos, and Alex must work together to survive and discover who destroyed the Canterbury and why. As their journey continues, they eventually come into possession of a Martian gunship they rename the Rocinante, a reference to the famous 1605 novel Don Quixote. All this only scratches the surface of the characters and story in The Expanse, which has a fresh prequel series set to be released in 2027. It's truly a modern sci-fi masterpiece that is perfect from start to finish across all 62 episodes on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

According to recent reports, there was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

Chris Columbus directed the original “Home Alone” and its nearly-as-loved sequel “Home Alone 2: Lost in Upcoming York,” and both written by the late great John Hughes. If you can believe it, there have been six “Home Alone” movies in all, with the third one at least released in theaters and doing respectable box office numbers. The others are all TV movies or in the case of the most recent 2021 film “Home Sweet Home Alone,” a Disney+ streaming movie.

According to recent reports, the original two films though grossed $477 million and $358 million worldwide, respectively, and the original still gets tons of cable play and finds its way into the Nielsen streaming charts. It makes sense that a more serious sequel with Culkin back in the fold would be welcomed by audiences.

Sadly, “Home Alone” has been back on the minds of audiences of late after the recent passing of Catherine O’Hara, who played Kevin’s mom, and also Tim Curry, who had a small role as a hotel clerk in “Home Alone 2.” Joe Pesci and Daniel Stern as the Wet Bandits are still around, though Pesci has been mostly retired outside of his return in Scorsese’s “The Irishman” back in 2019 and his role in the Pete Davidson Peacock series “Bupkis” in 2023.

Culkin too has had a bit of a resurgence, making a cameo in the most recent season of “Fallout” and doing a voice in Disney’s “Zootopia 2.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing.
  • “That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire.
  • In a recent development, the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

“That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”.

In a recent development, the lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

“When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was notable to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “.

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

In a recent development, for Crawford, the major lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

It has been revealed that “The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”.

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”.

Recent findings suggest that this all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other significant studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

8 Thrillers That Become Masterpieces in the Last 30 Minutes

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1357 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Collider

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Audiences seek movies as a temporary escape from reality, yet they challenge their minds and send a tingle down their spines.
  • Some great thrillers start off strong but end with a whimper.
  • Directed by David Fincher and written by Gillian Flynn, Gone Girl became the definitive domestic psychological thriller.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Audiences seek movies as a temporary escape from reality, yet they challenge their minds and send a tingle down their spines. A good thriller triggers a cinematic fight-or-flight from the safety of your seat. They get to play along, becoming active participants as they try to outsmart the plot, crack the mystery, or guess the villain's motives before the reveal.

Some great thrillers start off strong but end with a whimper. Then there are those that become legendary masterpieces within the final 30 minutes. From shocking twists you never saw coming to terrifying revelations that reshape the entire narrative, these 10 thriller films leave a lasting impression long after the final credits roll.

Directed by David Fincher and written by Gillian Flynn, Gone Girl became the definitive domestic psychological thriller. The story follows Nick Dunne (Ben Affleck) as he becomes the prime suspect in the sudden disappearance of his wife, Amy (Rosamund Pike), on their fifth wedding anniversary. As the police and media circus close in, a series of dark twists reveals that neither spouse is who they appear to be, exposing a deeply toxic and manipulative marriage.

Rather than ending with a neat resolution, the climax traps the characters in a dark, satirical commentary on modern marriage and media manipulation. Amy’s return home isn't a relief; it is a life sentence for Nick. By using her pregnancy to lock him into the marriage, Amy ensures total control, turning the happy ending into a satire. Gone Girl's final minutes expose their marriage as a performance, with both partners actively playing a role for public consumption, while Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross' score provides a false sense of calm.

David Lynch's masterpiece Mulholland Drive is a gem from the start of the 21st century. The surreal thriller follows an aspiring actress, Betty (Naomi Watts), who helps an amnesiac woman, Rita (Laura Harring), piece together her identity after a car crash in Los Angeles. The story fractures into a dark, dreamlike puzzle that blurs the line between Hollywood fantasy and a tragic, guilt-ridden reality.

In the final 30 minutes, Lynch transforms the movie from a strange neo-noir mystery into a devastating psychological portrait, turning a surreal thriller into a raw, heartbreaking tragedy about loneliness and self-destruction. The pastel glamour is ripped away to reveal the raw, grim reality of Diane Selwyn, a depressed, failed actress consumed by jealousy, unrequited love, and crushing guilt. Lynch reframes the entire movie as a study of how people use romantic illusions, denial, and fantasy to escape personal failure and moral decay.

Directed and co-written by Park Chan-wook, the South Korean action thriller Oldboy follows Oh Dae-su (Choi Min-sik), who, after being mysteriously kidnapped and imprisoned in a single room for 15 years, is suddenly released and given five days to track down his captor and uncover the motive behind his torment. His quest for vengeance leads him down a dark path of shocking revelations and devastating secrets.

A truly diabolical story, Oldboy transforms a brutal revenge thriller into an epic tragedy, shifting the story from physical violence to total psychological devastation. Dae-su fights through conspiracies and brutal hand-to-hand corridors, expecting a typical action-hero resolution: the hero kills the villain and wins. Instead, we have something far more twisting and crueler. In the final snowy sequence, the lingering, ambiguous look on the protagonist's face reveals that trauma cannot simply be excised; instead, it's something one must learn to accept or else be consumed by it.

It has been revealed that in Prisoners, directed by Denis Villeneuve, the story follows Keller Dover (Hugh Jackman) as he desperately searches for his young daughter and her friend after they go missing on Thanksgiving. When Detective Loki (Jake Gyllenhaal) releases the prime suspect, Alex Jones (Paul Dano), for lack of evidence, Dover takes matters into his own hands, pushing moral boundaries as a dedicated detective races against time to solve the mystery.

The grim, gripping drama unravels as the complex moral framework builds to an intense, clock-ticking climax that recontextualizes everything that came before. After a series of wrong choices, Keller is trapped in the secret pit—the very place his daughter was kept, forced to face the literal and spiritual hole he dug for himself. Loki stands in the freezing cold, hearing the faint sound of Anna’s red whistle from the ground, leaving Keller’s rescue uncertain. With a perfectly ambiguous ending, we are left to decide whether he deserves salvation after the atrocities he committed.​​​​​​​.

According to recent reports, few films elicit guttural reactions quite like Se7en. Directed by David Fincher, the psychological crime drama follows two homicide detectives, William Somerset (Morgan Freeman), a veteran nearing retirement, and David Mills (Brad Pitt), his newly introduced, hot-headed partner, as they track a meticulous serial killer (Kevin Spacey), who uses the seven deadly sins as motifs for his gruesome murders.

Industry observers note that se7en becomes an exceptionally dark police procedural by subverting classic Hollywood tropes, shifting power psychologically, and delivering a devastatingly bleak moral conclusion. John Doe turns himself in, halting the “catch the killer” momentum. Thrust into a bright, vast, and barren desert landscape under harsh daylight, the protagonists are exposed as Doe dominates the action. The movie ends with the antagonist successfully completing his horrific masterpiece, leaving the audience with an overwhelming sense of dread.

In a recent development, scorsese’s crime thriller The Departed follows Billy Costigan Jr. (DiCaprio), an undercover cop who infiltrates an Irish gang, and Colin Sullivan (Matt Damon), a mole within the police department who secretly works for the gang's kingpin. Both sides eventually realize a traitor lurks in their ranks, sparking a deadly, high-stakes race for each man to uncover the other's identity before his own is exposed.

In the final thirty minutes, The Departed delivers a relentless, breathless cascade of subversion, consequences, and brutal payoffs. Right when audiences expect a traditional cinematic confrontation between Costigan and Sullivan, the movie pulls the rug out. Sergeant Dignam (Mark Wahlberg) acts as a silent instrument of pure karma, delivering a deeply satisfying yet bleakly cynical conclusion. The final, poetic shot of a literal rat scurrying across Sullivan's balcony acts as punctuation: corruption is foundational, the system is deeply broken, and the cycle of duplicity survives long after the players are dead.​​​​​​​.

The Prestige may be one of Christopher Nolan's most quintessential films. Set in 19th-century London, the story centers on two rival stage magicians, Robert Angier (Jackman) and Alfred Borden (Christian Bale), who engage in a bitter, obsessive feud to create the ultimate illusion. Their fierce competition escalates into a dangerous game of sabotage and deceit, costing them everything they hold dear.

Established as a magic trick, the film’s final act executes a perfect structural "Prestige"—the final stage of a magic trick where everything hidden is dramatically revealed. The opening monologue by Cutter (Michael Caine) explaining the Pledge, the Turn, and the Prestige is the blueprint for the entire film. Ultimately, as they try to destroy each other, Borden loses his brother and the woman he loved, while Angier loses his humanity entirely. The Prestige is a brilliant revenge thriller with an unforgettable gut-punch of an ending.

Industry observers note that directed by Bryan Singer, The Usual Suspects follows five criminals who meet during a routine police lineup and strategy a heist, only to be blackmailed by a mysterious, legendary crime lord named Keyser Söze. The entire story is told through the interrogation and flashbacks of the sole survivor of a subsequent, bloody boat explosion, Verbal Kint (Spacey).

Recent findings suggest that the final revelation remains one of cinema's greatest endings, reconfiguring the thriller into a masterclass in psychological manipulation and the malleability of truth. The final sequence reveals that Verbal fabricated the entire story on the spot using random objects sitting on Kujan's office bulletin board and desk. As Verbal walks out of the precinct, drops his limp, and lights a cigarette, the film cuts back through the previous 90 minutes. Every little aspect here is designed to mislead. Verbal played the part so effectively that the hunter sat across from the devil the whole time without ever noticing.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it’s been quite a year for Curry Barker.
  • Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest newly introduced director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.
  • “I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really promptly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a Fresh Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles.

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest newly introduced director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really promptly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”.

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

It has been revealed that “It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” remarked Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”.

Industry observers note that barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” stated Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”.

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”.

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” said Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”.

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how swiftly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”.

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

Industry observers note that what Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly states he fell short in “Obsession.”.

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”.

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”.

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

In a recent development, “I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”.

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”.

Crunchyroll Has A Latest #1 Anime, And It Blows One Piece Out Of The Water

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (749 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One Piece has grown accustomed to being at the top of charts, but Crunchyroll has unveiled a major competitor.
  • It has been revealed that while it's nothing unusual for anime to temporarily displace one of the greats of the Substantial Three, Frieren's dominance has been well above par.
  • This also isn't the first time that Frieren has dethroned One Piece, with Frieren and Jujutsu Kaisen outpacing One Piece's manga sales in 2026 per ORICON's midterm 2026 report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One Piece has grown accustomed to being at the top of charts, but Crunchyroll has unveiled a major competitor. Frieren: Beyond Journey's End is the most popular series on the streaming service, according to Crunchyroll's list of most popular anime. One Piece is trailing behind at number six, as of the time of writing.

It has been revealed that while it's nothing unusual for anime to temporarily displace one of the greats of the Substantial Three, Frieren's dominance has been well above par. Since the premiere of Frieren: Beyond Journey's End's anime back in 2023, the series has been constantly at the forefront of best-of lists and has regularly been the most popular anime on services like Netflix—in fact, the anime has retained a steady 100% on Rotten Tomatoes since its launch.

This also isn't the first time that Frieren has dethroned One Piece, with Frieren and Jujutsu Kaisen outpacing One Piece's manga sales in 2026 per ORICON's midterm 2026 report. All of these data points indicate something much larger than Frieren's individual quality; it represents Frieren's unique role within a broader cultural zeitgeist, and dethroning One Piece on Crunchyroll might just be the latest development that can prove that point.

On the surface, Frieren: Beyond Journey's End and One Piece might not seem to share much in common. One Piece's story hardly needs rehashing; the long-running shōnen juggernaut is an action-adventure series based on the scruffy pirate Luffy and the Straw Hat Crew as they travel the world in search of a mythical ultimate treasure called the One Piece so that Luffy can become King of the Pirates.

Frieren, on the other hand, chronicles the adventures of the elven mage Frieren, who sets off on a journey to collect spells after her party had once defeated the Demon King. The catch is that elves age particularly slowly in Frieren, living over 1000 years; her initial 50-year journey felt like a blip for her until she reunites with her party and sees them in old age. After the death of the party's hero Himmel, Frieren sets out on another journey and slowly assembles a new gang of friends, this time aiming to understand human emotions, experience, and mortality.

There isn't obvious connective tissue between the two series; to find it, one has to dig a bit deeper. One Piece's world-building is second to none, and it's inarguable that the shōnen massively raised the bar for what stories popular series could tell. One Piece didn't develop in a vacuum—its storytelling and worldbuilding are a continuation of predecessors like Hunter x Hunter and Dragon Ball.

Frieren didn't develop in a vacuum, either; its emotional resonances and character depth reflect conventions that One Piece played a massive role in making viable cornerstones of shōnen storytelling.

Perhaps there's no better example than One Piece's iconic Fan Letter special, in which the lives, environments, and consequences of the events taking place in One Piece's main story are intimately explored. That level of depth, retrospection, and introspection is precisely the motor powering Frieren under the hood, and it's the reason the series has become so successful. It's not so much that Frieren outshines One Piece; it's more that Frieren lovingly builds on the foundation One Piece has spent years laying.

One Piece, for all intents and purposes, has a long-standing, stable, and smoothly growing fanbase; in that sense, it's almost meaningless to directly compare the success of recent anime with punchier, more contained stories to it. Taking into account how the anime industry has boomed since the pandemic largely thanks to streaming libraries, it makes sense why tight, bingeable seasonal releases like Frieren might briefly overtake long-running episodic series like One Piece, which now numbers nearly 1200 episodes.

There's also something to be said about how a series like Frieren can ring true with some of One Piece's most satisfying emotional contrasts. Like One Piece, Frieren can be light and digestible, but it can also feel epic, dark, and all too human. What Frieren does very effectively is set them into a latest context. In a fun turn of events, series like Frieren can therefore turn into a thematic gateway for casual anime fans to try a series like One Piece—whose sheer length might otherwise intimidate them.

At any rate, one thing is for certain: for an absolute anime masterpiece like Frieren: Beyond Journey's End, taking over a giant like One Piece on Crunchyroll is a massive milestone to be celebrated.
