💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival.
  • Sources indicate that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness.
  • It has been revealed that when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.].

Sources indicate that world-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

It has been revealed that when he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he claims he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he stated through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

It has been revealed that but he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I noted, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”.

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”.

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”.

Sources indicate that his 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”.

Sources indicate that how’s his French? “Zero,” he noted. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”.

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” remarked Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”.

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” stated Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”.

Sources indicate that one serious problem for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”.

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”.

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”.

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he remarked. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”.

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”.

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he remarked, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

Industry observers note that one of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage.

Recent findings suggest that “With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler remarked. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”.

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he remarked. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the wonder of the movies is how they make us feel long after the final credits roll. No matter the genre, a great film that has a brilliant ending tends to be remembered for generations. Now, a great ending doesn’t always mean that it’s tied up neatly in a bow. Sometimes an open-ended conclusion is just as impactful as one that has a definitive answer. While some brilliant films have open endings, the ten on this list are among the best in film history.

From characters running off in a latest direction to the spinning top that still has audiences debating today, these open endings shape the entire film, sometimes reframing everything that came before. These stories that blur reality and illusion force audiences to confront their own desire for neat closure. How many of these monumental conclusions left your jaw on the floor or left you with an array of emotions?

Industry observers note that in Martin Scorsese’s neo-noir psychological thriller Shutter Island, U.S. Marshal Teddy Daniels (Leonardo DiCaprio) and his partner Chuck Aule (Mark Ruffalo) travel to a remote psychiatric facility for the criminally insane on Shutter Island to investigate the mysterious disappearance of a patient. As a massive storm cuts them off from the mainland, Teddy uncovers dark secrets about the hospital's experimental treatments while struggling with his own haunting past and deteriorating grip on reality. By the end of the film, audiences are taken for a ride when it’s revealed that Teddy is actually Andrew Laeddis, a long-term patient at Ashecliffe Hospital who murdered his wife, Dolores (Michelle Williams), after she drowned their three children. He created the persona to cope with the trauma and guilt. After briefly accepting the truth at the lighthouse, Andrew sits outside with Dr. Sheehan (Ruffalo) and slips back into calling him "Chuck," talking as if they need to escape the island. The final line of the film, as orderlies approach to take him away for a lobotomy, Andrew asks Dr. Sheehan: "Which would be worse: to live as a monster, or to die as a good man?".

The film’s ending stands out because it turns a psychological twist into a tragic moral choice. Rather than ending on a simple shock, its final exchange leaves room for debate over whether Andrew Laeddis/Teddy Daniels has relapsed into madness or is choosing a lobotomy to escape unbearable guilt. While Dennis Lehane’s book leans more clearly toward a relapse into delusion, Scorsese’s film leaves Andrew’s true state of mind more open to interpretation. Knowing the twist forces a second look at the clues, flashbacks, and performances throughout the movie. While other conclusions sparked more debate, Shutter Island made both sides feel their point was the ultimate conclusion. Was it a conscious decision? Is it a calculated choice to fake a relapse? Could it genuinely be ambiguous between insanity and manipulation? That’s the brilliance of the film’s ending.

David Lynch’s defining film of the 21st century is Mulholland Drive. In this surreal mystery, a bright-eyed aspiring actress named Betty Elms (Naomi Watts) arrives in Los Angeles and teams up with Rita (Laura Harring), an amnesiac woman who survived a violent car crash, to uncover her true identity. As they follow clues through a shadowy Hollywood filled with underworld interference and a mysterious blue box, the narrative abruptly fractures, revealing a tragic, guilt-ridden reality behind their glamorous illusions. After a massive twist is revealed, the film ends with Diane Selwyn, the real identity behind the earlier dream persona Betty Elms, dying by suicide in her apartment after a blue key confirms the hitman she hired has murdered her former lover, Camila Rhodes, the real-life inspiration for Rita. Following her death, the film cuts to surreal, overlapping imagery of Los Angeles and a blue-haired woman in the theater whispering "Silencio.”.

In a recent development, lynch left the film's exact meaning open to interpretation. It turns a traditional mystery into a psychological mirror that rewards repeated viewings. Instead of tying up loose ends, the final stretch fractures the earlier story and leaves viewers to piece together illusion, guilt, and desire. The shift from Betty Elms’s optimistic Hollywood adventure to Diane Selwyn’s bleak reality reframes what came before as a wish-fulfillment dream or nightmare. Because Lynch never locks in on a single literal explanation, the boundary between waking life, memory, and delusion stays alive. The film treats ambiguity as art, not a riddle. By letting the glamorous fairy tale collapse into rejection, obsession, and tragedy, the ending exposes the harsher side of ambition in Los Angeles. Of course, with much of his work, opinions are mixed, with some praising his conceptual, norm-defying storytelling and others viewing it as self-indulgent. Regardless, the ending operates as if that final piece is a stellar jigsaw puzzle. ​​​​​​​.

According to recent reports, even romantic comedies can have an open ending. Such is the case in Sofia Coppola’s stellar Lost in Translation. In the film, fading American movie star Bob Harris (Bill Murray) and neglected young newlywed Charlotte (Scarlett Johansson) cross paths at a luxury hotel in Tokyo as they both struggle with insomnia and personal disillusionment. Despite their age gap, the two lonely strangers form a deep, unconventional bond as they explore the foreign city together, finding brief solace from their isolating marriages and cultural displacement. At the end of the film, Bob spots Charlotte in a crowded Tokyo street while riding in his car to the airport, stops to catch up with her, hugs her, and whispers something inaudible in her ear. Charlotte replies softly, “okay,” kisses her, and departs as both walk away smiling.

In a recent development, so, what’s behind their glamorous illusions whisper? Coppola has noted that the whispered line was unscripted and left unvoiced, so the moment stays private between the characters and open to viewers. By keeping Bob’s whisper inaudible to the audience, the film preserves a private moment strictly between Bob and Charlotte. Instead of a tidy romantic cliché or a permanent life overhaul, the ending reflects how fleeting, melancholic connections in transit can quietly shift how two people see themselves going forward. The ending invites personal projection about longing, closure, and human connection. It’s the perfect ending because the mood, silence, and shared isolation carry more weight than traditional plot twists, making an ambiguous parting feel earned. ​​​​​​​.

Industry observers note that one of the greatest classic romantic comedies still today is The Graduate. Directed by Mike Nichols, the film follows recent college graduate Benjamin Braddock (Dustin Hoffman) as he returns to his parents' California home and is seduced into a secret affair by Mrs. Robinson (Anne Bancroft), the older married wife of his father's business partner (Murray Hamilton). Things turn chaotic when Benjamin genuinely falls in love with Mrs. Robinson's daughter, Elaine (Katharine Ross), forcing him to navigate a messy love triangle and confront generational expectations. In a dramatic conclusion, Benjamin crashes Elaine’s wedding to Carl Smith (Brian Avery) in Santa Barbara, fending off the guests with a large cross, and fleeing with Elaine on a city bus. After initial smiles of triumph, their expressions fade into uncertainty and quiet dread as the reality of their impulsive escape sets in.

The open ending of The Graduate is widely praised because it subverts the traditional romantic "happily ever after" and captures the sudden, quiet reality after a major act of rebellion. Their initial triumph and adrenaline fade into silence and uncertainty. Rather than giving Benjamin a neat transformation, the lingering shot on the bus highlights his continuing lack of direction and raises a "what now?" question once the rebellion ends. Nichols let the camera keep rolling past the expected celebratory beat, forcing audiences to reconcile with the less-than-perfect punchline. From a grander macro lens, by trading tidy Hollywood closure for ambiguity and psychological realism, the finale helped usher in the New Hollywood era. ​​​​​​​.

Though it may be strikingly different than Bret Easton Ellis’ masterpiece novel, American Psycho is a pitch-perfect horror comedy. In the Mary Harron-directed film, Patrick Bateman (Christian Bale) is a wealthy and narcissistic Wall Street investment banker who hides his psychopathic nature behind a superficial, status-obsessed exterior. As his violent impulses escalate into a string of brutal murders against colleagues and strangers, his sanity unravels, and his confessions go ignored in a hollow society indifferent to his crimes. By the bitter end, Patrick breaks down, leaves a frantic voicemail confessing to dozens of murders, including Paul Allen (Jared Leto), to his lawyer Harold Carnes (Stephen Bogaert), and then discovers no one believes him or cares. When he visits Paul Allen’s apartment to clean up the bodies, a real estate agent, Mrs. Wolfe (Patricia Gage), is showing the empty, freshly painted unit and orders him to leave. At a restaurant with colleagues, Bateman confronts Harold about the confession. Harold mistakes him for someone else, laughs the message off as a joke, and notes he recently had dinner with Paul Allen in London. Bateman returns to his superficial peer group, realizing in a final voice-over that his confession means nothing, and he will never face punishment or true recognition.

So what does it all mean? It’s not an exit but an existential metaphorical trap. It turns Patrick’s unreliability into a sharp critique of 1980s consumerism and elite indifference, leaving viewers to debate whether his crimes were real or imagined. In a status-obsessed world where everyone looks and acts alike, nobody pays close enough attention for accountability to matter. Bateman wants recognition, even as a monster, yet the world around him remains indifferent and unbothered. Because the ending refuses to lock in one literal answer, viewers keep re-evaluating every clue, from Bateman's shifting mask to whether the real-estate cover-up protected property values or exposed his psychosis. ​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that one of the most influential sci-fi thrillers of all time is Blade Runner. Directed by Ridley Scott, the film, set in a dystopian 2019 Los Angeles, follows retired cop Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford) as he is forced back into duty to hunt down and "retire" four rogue replicants, bioengineered humanoids who have escaped off-world slave labor to seek out their creator and extend their four-year lifespans. As Deckard pursues the fugitives and falls for an advanced replicant named Rachael (Sean Young), the neo-noir thriller explores deep philosophical questions about memory, empathy, and what truly defines humanity. At the end of the film, replicant leader Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer) saves Deckard from falling off a rooftop, delivers his famous "tears in rain" monologue reflecting on his fading memories, and dies as a white dove flies away. Deckard then returns to his apartment, finds the replicant Rachael, and leaves with her.

In a recent development, with two variations on the ending that evoke different feelings, the film turns its central mystery into an active question for the viewer rather than a solved puzzle. By ending on a quiet, unresolved note instead of a neat wrap-up, the film forces viewers to weigh what makes someone human: memory, empathy, or manufactured design. The ambiguity makes viewers rethink Deckard’s actions and his growing connection to Rachael and the replicants. Though the theatrical release added a studio-mandated drive through sunny mountains and narration that spelled things out. Cutting that return to a cleaner, open finish preserves the film's bleak, reflective tone. And we like that version much better!​​​​​​​.

If there’s one thing that No Country for Old Men’s got, it’s true grit! In Joel and Ethan Coen’s magnum opus, set in the 1980s West Texas, welder Llewelyn Moss (Josh Brolin) takes $2 million from a botched drug deal and is relentlessly hunted by hitman Anton Chigurh (Javier Bardem). Meanwhile, aging Sheriff Ed Tom Bell (Tommy Lee Jones) investigates the violence while struggling to understand a brutal world outpacing traditional law and order. What may come as a shock, No Country for Old Men ends without a traditional showdown. Moss dies off-screen, Anton Chigurh survives a car crash after killing Carla Jean Moss (Kelly Macdonald), and Sheriff Bell retires to share two dreams about his father before the film cuts to black.

Recent findings suggest that the film ends in masterpiece fashion by shifting the focus from thriller plot mechanics to existential reflection. Bell’s quiet monologue recounting two dreams to his wife, closing on the line, "And then I woke up,” is as The Wizard of Oz as it can get. Although the cat-and-mouse chase drives the action, the story's emotional weight belongs to Sheriff Bell confronting aging, retirement, and a changing, more brutal world he feels outmatched by. Bell's dreams leave no neat moral answer, ending instead as he wakes up to reality. The abrupt, elliptical finish follows Cormac McCarthy’s 2005 novel, turning a crime thriller into a somber meditation on time, fate, and mortality. Whether the closure feels too artsy for such a raw thriller, its ending is truly a genuinely raw conclusion because life is simply uncertain. ​​​​​​​.

One of the greatest and enduring sci-fi classics is Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind. Directed by Michel Gondry and written by Charlie Kaufman, the romantic drama documents the aftermath of a painful breakup, where Clementine Kruczynski (Kate Winslet) undergoes a medical procedure to erase her memories of Joel Barish (Jim Carrey), prompting heartbroken Joel to get the same treatment. As his memories fade, Joel realizes he still loves her and tries to hide her inside his mind to save their relationship from being forgotten. The film concludes in bittersweet fashion as Joel and Clementine reunite after erasing each other from their memories, discover the bitter truth of their past relationship on recorded tapes, and still choose to try again. Despite knowing the risks and potential heartbreak, they agree to give their relationship another chance, ending on a quiet "okay" as they run and laugh in the snow.

Rather than erasing pain to stay safe, the ending suggests that real connection requires accepting flaws and the risk of future hurt. Viewers read the final moments differently—some see a hopeful fresh start with eyes open, while others worry the couple is repeating a familiar cycle. Perhaps it depends on where your heart is when you watch. It forces audiences to confront an honest, recurring human choice: whether to love again, knowing pain is likely. Kaufman's writing and Gondry's direction blend melancholy, surrealism, and warmth without forcing a neat "happily ever after". Early ideas leaned more heavily toward a grim, inescapable cycle, whereas the finished scene leaves room for agency and connection. If you’re a cynic or a lover of love, Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind will no doubt task you with examining your own love choices from there on out. ​​​​​​​.

Sources indicate that hands down, the greatest sci-fi film of all time is the prolific 2001: A Space Odyssey. Directed by Stanley Kubrick, it follows humanity's evolutionary leaps triggered by mysterious black monoliths, from prehistoric apes learning to use tools to a voyage toward Jupiter where the sentient supercomputer HAL 9000 malfunctions. After confronting HAL, the surviving astronaut travels beyond space and time to undergo a transformative shift into the next stage of human existence. To finish the film, astronaut Dr. Dave Bowman (Keir Dullea) survives a showdown with the rogue computer HAL 9000, travels through a cosmic light vortex near Jupiter, ages rapidly in a surreal bedroom, and is reborn as a glowing fetus, the "Star Child,” floating near Earth.

Kubrick left the ending open to interpretation rather than spelling out a single literal explanation. Analyzing it, the monoliths are seen as tools or catalysts from an advanced intelligence that push human evolution forward—first nudging early hominids toward tool use and finally elevating Bowman into a higher stage of existence. By refusing to lock onto one literal explanation, the finale invites ongoing debate and personal meaning that remains a masterful timeless conclusion. It’s a mirror for the viewer as the ambiguity shifts the focus from chasing external answers to reflecting on human nature, technology, and what lies beyond the known. The film is framed as an evolutionary leap. It’s a powerfully surreal and richly philosophical conclusion that is utterly flawless. ​​​​​​​.

Recent findings suggest that yes, we’re still debating Inception’s ending and, chances are, it’s never ever going to stop. In Christopher Nolan’s masterclass in filmmaking, Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) is a skilled thief who steals valuable secrets by infiltrating his targets' subconscious minds while they dream. Offered a chance to clear his criminal record and return to his children, Cobb assembles a team of specialists to attempt the impossible reverse heist: planting an original idea into a business rival's mind while navigating a multi-layered dream world haunted by projections of his deceased wife, Mal (Marion Cotillard). The film ends on a profoundly ambiguous note as Dom returns home to his children after completing the dream heist, spinning his metal top totem before walking away from it to greet them. The camera lingers on the top as it begins to wobble, then cuts to black just before revealing whether it falls or keeps spinning.

Industry observers note that with a brilliant plot twist that lingers beyond the final frame, it serves as one last monumental character breakthrough. Throughout the film, Cobb’s fixation on proving reality and escaping guilt drives his pain. Walking away from the spinning top before seeing it fall reveals he chooses his children and his present life over needing absolute proof. Cobb’s indifference to whether he is dreaming or awake underscores the film's philosophical focus on personal reality over objective truth. Nolan’s design makes the ambiguity meaningful rather than frustrating, though those in the frustration camp, I see you. I feel you. I am you. Like the team planting an idea in Robert Fischer’s (Cillian Murphy) mind, the final cut plants a lingering question in the audience’s mind. Even after Nolan shared his thoughts on the scene, audiences remained free to interpret Cobb’s final moment on their own terms.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that looks like Hollywood could be heading into the newly introduced year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump mentioned. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Key Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he stated, “Hollywood would open again.”.

Recent findings suggest that trump stated his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors declared more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”.

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

According to recent reports, “Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she remarked in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”.

Recent findings suggest that A floor vote has yet to be declared, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff stated.

#131353. 5 Greatest YA Movie Franchises Of All Time, Ranked

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Screenrant ↗ Open Full Page

5 Greatest YA Movie Franchises Of All Time, Ranked

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Screenrant

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Young adult stories have always made for compelling movie adaptations, especially when you look at the massive YA movie boom that began in the early 2000s.
  • It has been revealed that the very best YA movie franchises turn relatable and familiar coming-of-age experiences into major cinematic experiences, balancing honoring the source material with offering newly introduced perspectives at the same time.
  • This ranking will consider a few different key factors, including overall quality, consistency, how well it adapts and expands the source material, world-building, and cultural impact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Young adult stories have always made for compelling movie adaptations, especially when you look at the massive YA movie boom that began in the early 2000s. Magical worlds, dystopian futures, complicated love triangles, and the supernatural surrounding various coming-of-age stories will always have strong entertainment potential, though some are better than others.

It has been revealed that the very best YA movie franchises turn relatable and familiar coming-of-age experiences into major cinematic experiences, balancing honoring the source material with offering newly introduced perspectives at the same time. As such, it's notable that our choices for the top five greatest YA movie franchises are all still ongoing with brand-new projects in some form or another, from Harry Potter to The Hunger Games.

This ranking will consider a few different key factors, including overall quality, consistency, how well it adapts and expands the source material, world-building, and cultural impact. Keeping that in mind, here are the five greatest YA movie franchises ranked from great to greatest.

Disney and 20th Century Fox's Chronicles of Narnia movies brought C.S. Lewis' beloved fantasy novels to life, starting with 2005's The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe. Audiences were introduced to the Pevensie children who discover the magical land of Narnia and ultimately join the fight against the White Witch.

In a recent development, without question, the first movie remains the peak of the franchise, though 2008's Prince Caspian offered a compelling darker journey with the Pevensies' return to a very different Narnia. 2010's Voyage of the Dawn Treader also adapted the source material fairly well. However, the franchise lost momentum and stalled after the third film, so much so that the rest of the books in Lewis' series were never adapted in this iteration of the franchise. That's a large reason why this ranks so low on this list, despite still being one of the GOATs.

Looking ahead, it will be very interesting to see how Netflix and Greta Gerwig's The Magician's Nephew fares next year, a brand-latest take on the franchise that looks to be incredibly unique.

DreamWorks' How to Train Your Dragon franchise is one of the most emotionally satisfying animated movie sagas ever made, with its focus on a young outcast Viking named Hiccup and a dragon named Toothless. Managing to change his entire village's hatred of dragons, the franchise gets better with every entry as Hiccup gradually evolves into a great leader and hero for his people.

There's an incredibly rich coming-of-age story baked into the entire franchise that is also full of some of the greatest dragon designs and animated action sequences of all time (not to mention one of the very best movie scores as well). Having expanded into television, short films, and most recently the start of a whole live-action adaptation, the enduring popularity and audience engagement are a clear testament to its GOAT status, though here's hoping the rest of the live-action franchise lives up to its animated counterparts as the first movie did.

It may not yet have the same cultural footprint as the top three from a live-action standpoint, but it still delivers one of the most satisfying and complete narratives on this list.

It has been revealed that few YA movie franchises have had quite the cultural impact of Twilight. Based on Stephenie Meyer's bestselling novels, the supernatural romance series follows Bella Swan as she moves to the rainy town of Forks, Washington, and falls in love with Edward Cullen, a vampire struggling to reconcile his feelings with his dangerous nature. Their relationship becomes increasingly complicated as werewolves, rival vampires, and ancient supernatural politics enter the picture.

Industry observers note that the five-film franchise, which began in 2008 and concluded with Breaking Dawn – Part 2 in 2012, became a defining pop culture phenomenon. Kristen Stewart, Robert Pattinson, and Taylor Lautner became household names, while the love triangle between Bella, Edward, and Jacob inspired years of passionate debate among fans. The movies also helped establish a newly introduced wave of supernatural YA adaptations, proving that romance could be just as powerful a theatrical draw as fantasy action.

It has been revealed that admittedly, the Twilight films are uneven, particularly when it comes to their pacing and melodramatic dialogue. Their critical reception and inconsistent quality prevent them from ranking higher, especially when compared with franchises that offer more consistently strong filmmaking. However, their distinctive atmosphere, memorable characters, and enormous cultural impact are difficult to dismiss. Few YA franchises have inspired such a devoted fanbase or remained such recognizable cultural touchstones more than a decade later. Twilight earns its place through its influence, even if its individual movies don't always match its popularity.

Suzanne Collins' The Hunger Games novels provided the foundation for one of the most compelling YA movie franchises of the 2010s. Set in the dystopian nation of Panem, the series follows Katniss Everdeen, a teenager who volunteers to take her younger sister's place in a televised fight to the death. What initially appears to be a survival story gradually becomes a much larger examination of propaganda, class inequality, political manipulation, and revolution.

Industry observers note that jennifer Lawrence's performance as Katniss is central to the franchise's success. She's a compelling protagonist precisely because she isn't a traditional action hero. Katniss is resourceful and courageous, but she's also frightened, emotionally complicated, and frequently overwhelmed by the expectations placed upon her. As the series progresses from the arena to an all-out rebellion, the movies increasingly explore the psychological consequences of turning a young person into a symbol of resistance.

Recent findings suggest that the original four films delivered a satisfying adaptation of Collins' trilogy, with Catching Fire standing out as a particularly strong sequel. The franchise has since continued with The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, a prequel exploring the younger years of future villain President Snow. That expansion demonstrates just how much storytelling potential remains in Panem, even without Katniss at the center. Its excellent world-building, strong central performance, increasingly ambitious themes, and relatively consistent filmmaking put it just below the top spot. The Hunger Games is arguably the strongest YA franchise, aside from one that absolutely takes the top spot.

It's difficult to imagine any YA movie franchise surpassing Harry Potter. Beginning with The Sorcerer's Stone, Warner Bros.' adaptation of J.K. Rowling's novels introduced audiences to a magical world hidden beneath the surface of everyday life. Following Harry, Ron, and Hermione through their years at Hogwarts, the eight-film saga gradually evolved from a whimsical fantasy adventure into a darker story about friendship, sacrifice, prejudice, and the fight against tyranny.

Industry observers note that one of the franchise's greatest strengths is how naturally its characters and world grow alongside its audience. The early movies capture the excitement of discovering Hogwarts, with moving staircases, Quidditch matches, enchanted objects, and countless magical surprises. As the characters get older, however, the stakes become increasingly serious. The introduction of Voldemort's return transforms the series into an epic conflict that challenges Harry and his friends in ways they could never have anticipated.

The eight movies also benefit from an unusually consistent cast, with Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, and Emma Watson growing up alongside their characters. Supporting performances from actors like Alan Rickman, Maggie Smith, and Ralph Fiennes further enrich the sprawling ensemble. While the adaptations occasionally sacrifice details from the books, they successfully preserve the emotional core of the story and deliver a genuinely satisfying cinematic journey.

According to recent reports, beyond the original saga, the Fantastic Beasts movies attempted to expand the Wizarding World with mixed results. Nevertheless, the original eight-film series remains a remarkable achievement, combining memorable fantasy, compelling character development, and an overarching story that builds toward an unforgettable conclusion. Its consistency, iconic world-building, memorable performances, faithful adaptation of the central story, and extraordinary cultural influence make it the most complete franchise on this list. More than any other YA series, Harry Potter made audiences feel as though they were growing up alongside its heroes, securing its place as the greatest young adult movie franchise of all time.

Tech Report: If There’s Generative AI in ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,’ It’s Not the First Time David Fincher’s Used It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path.
  • The criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films.
  • According to recent reports, at first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The uproar over the alleged use of generative AI imagery in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” has taken a familiar path. Early responses to the Netflix film penned by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher have pointed out egregious examples of generative video artifacts sticking out in key flashback moments in the film — including one shot from the trailer where it certainly looks like a video AI program rendered a wagon the wrong way around.

The criticism is of the use of generative AI in principle as a fundamental betrayal of the creative process — but it’s also of Fincher, as a director who, historically, has been meticulous with the level of detail and intention in every single shot of his films. In the early responses to Fincher’s latest, there’s been a lot of surprise and disappointment about this particular filmmaker being caught up in an AI controversy. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Vital Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

According to recent reports, at first blush, his approach seems at odds with using generative AI video, which relies on regurgitated (and, it bears repeating every time, stolen) data. But Fincher has defended his use of AI to the LA Times as a way to continue to innovate on an art form that is, after all, just over a hundred years old.

That defense really shouldn’t be surprising, given Fincher’s history with AI specifically. Although he’s been critical of generative tools in the past, Fincher admitted to using them (never publicly disclosing which) in the 4K remaster of “Se7en,” which the director described as a process of needing to remake the negative in order to battle the ravages of time (and the thousands of tiny scratches that would show up in 4K). “If you could see a 30-year-old negative and what it looks like even when immaculately stored — it was an enormous amount of fixing, just digs and scratches and cinch,” he told EW at the time.

In a recent development, that kind of image restoration technology was around long, long before the Anthropic IPO failed to save the stock market, but its level of precision has increased enormously in the past year. There were also sequences in the stored “Se7en,” though, where generative tech filled in gaps from the original. For one example, Fincher talked about a moment where a camera pan overshot the mark and changedh a shot. The performance had been good enough to use a technically flawed take — and, combined wit an unused take, allowed software to generate the missing information and restore the intended image.

Sources indicate that “It ends up being the most thrillingly stupid fix in the world because if you see it, we didn’t do our jobs. And you probably won’t see it. You probably won’t be aware that it’s happened. But you look at it, and you just think to yourself, ‘It’s so nice that we can fix that kind of stuff today,'” Fincher told Collider about that moment in “Se7en.”.

Industry observers note that by Fincher’s own lights, then, the problem with AI in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is that people are painfully aware of it. AI critics might make a distinction between video restoration tools that work on existing projects and those tools being used because they can more quickly and cheaply generate originals that would’ve otherwise needed to be crafted by human hands. Having something AI-generated isn’t necessarily better than nothing when it comes to art, and choosing to AI-generate a Western chase sequence inside of, say, 10 seconds isn’t a solution to all.

Still, Fincher knows what he’s doing. This past week, he emphasized to the LA Times that he’s not a Luddite when it comes to film: “We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old, and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’ Well, it exists. Should we not use it?”.

The answer is an emphatic “No!” to some And they can certainly be mad, or disappointed, or disheartened about Fincher’s decision to use AI tools. The one thing they shouldn’t be is surprised.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that yellowstone might have made Westerns cool again, but it’s not the only series that depicts the atrocities committed in the name of claiming American soil. Like Taylor Sheridan's landmark Western, Netflix’s American Primeval revolves around the fight for Native land. But instead of greedy corporations, the conflict involves Mormon militias, Indigenous communities, and white settlers all caught in the middle.

In a recent development, while men are often the ones framing these narratives, American Primeval indicates a different side of these conflicts, particularly through the women pulled into a world that disregards their value. Yellowstone might have shocked viewers with its relentless violence, but it doesn’t come close to American Primeval. The best part is that the miniseries only needs six episodes to expose the truth of America's colonial past, giving its female characters room to tell stories that Westerns have often left on the sidelines.

Set during the 1857 Utah War, American Primeval reimagines the Mormon Church’s expansion under Brigham Young (Kim Coates), rooted in deep religious fanaticism and historical violence committed in the name of faith. Young’s campaign to take control of Fort Bridger puts him in conflict with the U.S. Army officer Captain Edmund Dellinger (Lucas Neff), the fort’s owner Jim Bridger (Shea Whigham), and Red Feather (Derek Hinkey), the leader of a renegade group of Crow warriors known as the Wolf Clan.

At the center of the miniseries are mother and son Sara Rowell (Betty Gilpin) and Devin Rowell (Preston Mota), who have come a long way from Missouri to Fort Bridger, Wyoming, with the intention of reaching Devin’s father in Crooks Springs, Utah. However, getting there is easier said than done. With the treacherous terrain, bounty hunters scattered across the region, and wildlife that could kill them in an instant, their chances of making it are slim to none — and that's before they have to contend with the conflict brewing around Fort Bridger. Fortunately, the reluctant mountain man Isaac Reed (Taylor Kitsch) is willing to join Sara and Devin on their journey, but even that doesn't guarantee survival.

In a recent development, there’s no doubt that Yellowstone doesn’t shy away from violence. The series already has plenty of stomach-churning moments: a charging bull let loose inside a bar, Beth Dutton (Kelly Reilly) assaulted in her own office, and the controversial Monica (Kelsey Asbille) storyline, in which she puts herself in danger while trying to lure a predator. However, American Primeval arguably takes things much further, largely because of its historical setting. Unlike the more modern world of Yellowstone, where the Duttons still have to contend with law enforcement, government officials, and legal bureaucracy, the Utah Territory depicted in American Primeval is a largely lawless frontier where formal authority has little control over the men fighting for power and land.

In American Primeval, violence is normalized, with little regard for human life or legal consequences. Public hangings, the abduction of women, and the slaughter of entire groups of settlers are all part of the brutal reality of the frontier. The sequel represents a massive improvement on the opening of its predecessor, 2023’s “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes,” which bowed with $44 million, a franchise low. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the controversy surrounding its launch, there is no denying that Hogwarts Legacy dominated the gaming sphere in 2023, with the Harry Potter-inspired RPG even going on to become the best-selling game of the year.

As such, it was not long before a sequel was revealed, and over the past three years, Avalanche Software has been hard at work getting ready to send players back to Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.

It may have been the best-selling game of 2023, but Hogwarts Legacy did not come without its downfalls, especially as it did not receive any expansions or substantial post-game content drops. As such, fans are feeling mixed over a sequel. Will it expand on the open-world and offer long-term content, or will it be much of the same?

At the time of writing, Hogwarts Legacy 2 does not have a release date, or even a release window, despite previous rumors suggesting that it would coincide with the upcoming launch of the Harry Potter television show, which is set to debut on Christmas Day. However, it is unlikely that Hogwarts Legacy 2 is going to pop up over the next month, so we can safely assume that it will be 2027 at the earliest.

It was back in October that Warner Bros., the publishers behind Hogwarts Legacy, issued a statement on the game's progress, and after Paramount acquired Warner Bros. Discovery, it was confirmed that Warner Bros. Games would merge with Paramount Games Studio to create one giant gaming division.

Sources indicate that it will be this gaming division that works on Hogwarts Legacy 2, but, as mentioned, no further information has been revealed, and fans are yet to see any gameplay or substantial updates. As such, its potential cancellation has been a subject of worry for fans, but according to a letter to shareholders discussing WB's games division, WB's strategy will be to focus on its most successful franchises, with Harry Potter being one of them. "We expect Games to more meaningfully contribute to segment profitability going forward as our pipeline expands," the statement reads, "including the second installment of Hogwarts Legacy.".

With The Game Awards taking place on December 10, we can only hope that this next major gaming event will spare a moment for Hogwarts Legacy 2, and it would be perfect timing in the lead-up to the Harry Potter television show, especially as the two projects are rumored to be working together closely. However, this is mere speculation, and for now, we will have to wait with bated breath to see what comes next for the franchise.

Back in 2023, our very own William Cennamo awarded Hogwarts Legacy an almost perfect 9/10, with his review reading:.

According to recent reports, hogwarts Legacy is a wonderful game filled to the brim with adventures to be had, activities to engage in, and secrets to be found. The school and the surrounding areas have been recreated beautifully, and players will easily lose hours lost in the whimsical splendor of this wizarding world.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rian Johnson isn’t writing a Star Wars movie, but he isn’t ruling one out, either.

Responding to a question from IndieWire during an in-conversation event at the 23rd Marrakech International Film Festival, the writer/director of “Star Wars: The Last Jedi” was clear that his next project lies elsewhere: “I’m already writing the next thing I’m going to do, and it’s not a Star Wars thing, or in that genre,” he stated.

“I’m very much enjoying just making my own stuff, but I mean, if the opportunity presented itself,” Johnson noted, nodding. “It’s a world I deeply love. It’s also a group of people I love.”.

Industry observers note that “I love Star Wars more now than I ever have,” he added. “And it’s exciting to me that there are a lot of different voices now taking cracks at it.” The timing is hard to ignore. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Debuts to Mighty $120 Million, Reviving Lionsgate’s Most Important Franchise Box Office: A24’s ‘You Can See Everything’ Crosses $100 Million Globally.

In a recent development, johnson’s remarks land just as Lucasfilm appears to be turning back toward the corner of the saga he helped shape. Polygon reported that two long-gestating features, “Star Wars: New Jedi Order” and an untitled film from Dave Filoni, are still listed as in development by Production Weekly, despite months of silence and the soft box office performance of “The Mandalorian & Grogu.”.

“New Jedi Order” would theoretically bring back actress Daisy Ridley as Rey roughly 15 years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” rebuilding the Jedi Order that “The Last Jedi” so memorably called into question. Sharmeen Obaid-Chinoy is attached to direct, with George Nolfi now writing after earlier drafts from Damon Lindelof and Justin Britt-Gibson, and a stint by Bond 26 screenwriter Steven Knight. The film was pulled from its December 17, 2027 release date in May 2025. Meanwhile, “Star Wars: Starfighter,” the Shawn Levy-directed film starring Ryan Gosling and set five years after “The Rise of Skywalker,” remains the only Star Wars feature with a firm date: May 28, 2027.

Recent findings suggest that in 2017, the year “The Last Jedi” hit theaters, Lucasfilm announced that Johnson would create a new Star Wars trilogy. Those films have yet to materialize, but Johnson had warm words for Filoni, who took on the role of Lucasfilm’s president and chief creative officer in January: “Dave Filoni I got to know while making ‘The Last Jedi’, and he’s a wonderful guy who really has the spirit of Star Wars in him,” he stated. “All the Lucasfilm folks are awesome.”.

Later, answering questions from the audience, Johnson described “The Last Jedi” as “the most joyful process of any movie I’ve ever made”, despite the challenge of stepping from his own original films into what he called a contested mythology.

“I’m a huge, huge fan of George Lucas, and I’ve read a lot about when he was writing the original Star Wars, how personal it was for him,” Johnson continued. “I think especially with something that has a deep cultural impact, and that belongs to everybody, that makes it even more important… to make sure it’s coming from a personal perspective and something that’s deeply on fire inside you, as opposed to thinking, ‘what’s gonna please this person and this person and this person’. That leads to homogeneity, to repeating yourself and to something that feels dead on screen.”.

Recent findings suggest that as a middle chapter, “The Last Jedi” drew directly on Johnson’s childhood experience of “The Empire Strikes Back,” though not as something to copy. “I didn’t want to imitate ‘The Empire Strikes Back’,” Johnson said. “What I wanted to get to was the heart of what that movie has, which is this center part of life where your job is to fail, and your job is to learn from that and to get up and keep moving forward.”.

Industry observers note that he drew a distinction between a film having a moral compass and having a moral. The compass, he said, “comes from the entire mass of every single creative decision made by the writer, or director, or whole team.”.

Sources indicate that johnson also reflected on the only two composers he has worked with. His cousin Nathan Johnson has scored his films since the pair started making movies together at age ten: “Nathan is the first person to read the script; he’s on set for the entire shoot so it’s very much a collaboration.”.

John Williams, he said, is also “a miracle of a human being”, and working with him was the opposite experience. “You give him the movie and then the first time I hear any music is when we’re on the scoring stage, and there are 200 musicians playing it.”.

If Johnson does return to Star Wars, it seems he won’t be thinking about franchise strategy. “For me it’s not about thinking about IP, it’s about stories,” he remarked. “I deeply believe the only way to actually make a movie that matters and is worth something is to have your eyes nowhere else except on making that movie. What is the story we’re telling? Why are we telling it? Why do we care about it?”.

“Outside of that bubble,” Johnson added, “I’ll leave it to the executives.”.

With those executives now steering Star Wars back toward Rey and the post-“Rise of Skywalker” era, the bubble may be closer to his than it has been in years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nearly 20 years later, Danny Ocean is trying to get the gang back together for Ocean’s 14, which was expected to begin filming in 2026.

David Leitch, who is attached to direct the fourth installment in the heist film franchise, recently noted that George Clooney and his Smokehouse producing partner Grant Heslov have delivered a “great script,” but scheduling concerns stand in the way.

“Oh, I mean, there’s a great script and I think everybody’s excited about moving it forward,” he told People. “I think it’s always been about getting all those people together, and their schedules are always the problem.”.

Sources indicate that leitch added, “Look, there’s a lot of excitement around it and … George and Grant did incredible work on the script. So, yeah, a lot of motivation to make it happen.” Watch on Deadline.

Clooney starred as Danny Ocean in the 2001 Steven Soderbergh-helmed remake of the 1960 Rat Pack film, reprising the role in Ocean’s Twelve (2004) and Ocean’s Thirteen (2007).

In January 2025, Leitch was in early talks to direct the next installment. Last October, the 2x Oscar winner Warner Bros. approved the budget for Ocean’s 14, which he expected to begin filming this year.

Ocean’s 14 will mark the first installment in the main franchise not directed by Soderbergh, after Gary Ross helmed the 2018 female-led spin-off Ocean’s 8, starring Sandra Bullock as Danny’s sister Debbie Ocean.

Meanwhile, Bradley Cooper is attached direct an Ocean’s 11 prequel, which will star himself and Margot Robbie as Danny Ocean’s parents.

#131335. What China Gets From Its AI Honeypots and Smuggled Chips

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1277 w)

What China Gets From Its AI Honeypots and Smuggled Chips

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollingstone

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You could start casting the movie right now: Jensen Huang, the Taiwanese-American CEO of Nvidia, the most important tech company in the world, is sucked into an illicit affair with a Chinese spy.
  • Sources indicate that at least, that’s the simple version of the story.
  • Broadly speaking, there are two ways to think about AI, indicates Kyle Chan, an expert on Chinese technology development at the Brookings Institution.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You could start casting the movie right now: Jensen Huang, the Taiwanese-American CEO of Nvidia, the most important tech company in the world, is sucked into an illicit affair with a Chinese spy. The most valuable tech in the world — Huang’s super-powered computer chips — are smuggled into China or installed into data centers connected to America’s greatest rival. Above it all, the possibility of a super-intelligent AI, a true artificial mind, looms — and its creator will be positioned to rule the world.

Sources indicate that at least, that’s the simple version of the story. But the real picture of the great geopolitical AI race is both more complex and more unbelievable than the tale of spies and smuggling that’s playing out in the press right now. China wants the U.S.’s chips — that much is clear. But why? And what can our only real rival power actually do with them? To answer this, Rolling Stone spoke with two experts in the Chinese tech sector, who pulled back the curtain on what the superpower actually wants when it comes to AI — and why it’s willing to use sex, smuggling and lies to get there.

Broadly speaking, there are two ways to think about AI, indicates Kyle Chan, an expert on Chinese technology development at the Brookings Institution.

The first is as a straight race to one goal: creating a truly intelligent AI that surpasses human intelligence in all general tasks and can improve itself autonomously. In the industry, this is known as AGI, or Artificial General Intelligence. This point of view holds that the first country or organization to achieve true AGI will have an earth-shattering advantage over any competition in economics, war, medicine, and technology. Basically, it sets the world of AI up as a winner-take-all race. Many U.S. officials — including, at times, Trump himself — have made this argument, alongside many of the private sector CEOs actually working on the technology.

“If you start with that assumption, then the effort to slow down China is nearly existential,” Chan indicates. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

The biggest advantage the U.S. has is Nvidia’s chips. The most powerful computer chips in the world are made by one facility in Taiwan, using incredibly complex and rare machines manufactured by one organization in the Netherlands. It is a process so detailed and scientifically complex that it might as well be magic. Other companies can make chips, of course, but none of them can make chips as well as the single manufacturing company in Taiwan that Nvidia and most of the U.S. tech giants use. AI companies need these chips, and these chips alone, to run the most advanced AI models — which is why the U.S. has done a lot to limit China’s access to them, setting export controls on who Nvidia can sell their chips to and which countries they can be shipped into.

Recent findings suggest that because of this constraint, the Chinese don’t really see AI the same way as most of the U.S. industry does.

In a recent development, instead of an existential threat, Chan says, the second way to look at AI is a very powerful technology that will not necessarily lead to some massive strategic advantage for the first team past the AGI post. That makes the AI race a longer-term game, decided more by which power can holistically incorporate the advances of super-computing into its society and economy, which China has largely focused on doing.

Recent findings suggest that “What we’re kind of seeing unfold in the future is two different markets,” noted Kenton Thibaut, a China expert at the Atlantic Council’s Digital Forensic Research Lab. The U.S. is focused on “frontier” systems — the absolute cutting-edge AI, powered by their chip advantage — while China is supplying “near frontier” technology that hits different parts of the market for AI technology. In China, Thibaut said, AI is viewed as a “general purpose” technology that should be harnessed for practical use as promptly as possible, rather than a more conceptual race to the furthest frontier. Related Content Man Found Guilty of Igniting Blaze That Became the Devastating Palisades Fire Trump Says He ‘Can’t Speak To’ Whether Russia is a Friend to America Trump Got Played by Putin and Xi Your Favorite THC Drinks Are About to Be Illegal.

Recent findings suggest that “All of the [Chinese] policies and major policy pronouncements and planning around AI have to do with ‘How do we make this useful in society?’” Thibaut said. “I haven’t seen anything like that in the US.”.

“[China’s] version of winning is being able to benefit the most from AI,” Chan notes. “Integrate it in their economy, automate their factories, speed up drug discovery, et cetera. [They want it to] help them win across all these other domains, rather than this singular focus on achieving AGI.”.

According to recent reports, it’s a philosophical difference that is fueled by the physical constraints that the Chinese tech sector faces. The U.S. has access to more computing power than any other nation, allowing them to push the envelope. Companies like Anthropic have asked the U.S. government to regulate them more, fearful that their AI models will run out of control. In China, these discussions are scarce, Thibaut says, because the hardware they’re working with basically makes them moot — and the Chinese government is predisposed to prevent any societal disruptions. Instead, Chinese AI firms are usually focused on doing more with less — creating working, practical products and applications of AI that get the most out of whatever computing power they can harness.

And in some cases, that’s where the spies come in. The Nvidia honeypot scandal was largely controversial because it included a woman who ran a Singaporean front company that set up data centers in Southeast Asia stocked with Taiwan-made super-chips, and then leased the use of those chips to Chinese companies. Chan refers to this loophole, and the broader Chinese project of getting their hands on American tech, as a “bridge” to the country’s real goal: separating themselves from the Western “tech stack,” while still retaining competitive computing power. Eventually, Chan claims, China wants to have its own version of the super-manufacturers in Taiwan, its own version of the very best chips — but until then, it has to use more subtle methods to get what it wants.

“If they want to keep pace today, they do still need access to Nvidia chips now,” Chan says. Trending Stories Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Marry at Palm Springs Wedding Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Princess of Wales Reflects on Cancer Battle in 'Heal' Documentary Special Boy George on His Israel Trip: 'I Wasn't Able to Not Say Something'.

Some parts of the U.S. government may be helping them achieve that. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik had been very lax with Nvidia and Huang personally, allowing the organization to continue selling to companies that the U.S. knew were linked with China. While Trump has remarked he views AI as a winner-take-all race, Reuters reported that his administration also signed off on the sale of 900,000 AI chips to Chinese companies in one six-month period, and his own AI Czar David Sacks has explicitly advocated for selling more chips directly to China.

China, then, has allies to go along with its spies — and it seems that one way or another, it’s getting all the chips it needs.

Latest Update: This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • According to recent reports, in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • Industry observers note that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first confirmed. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

According to recent reports, in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

Industry observers note that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you remarked) to your “Notes to self” note.

According to recent reports, to take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

According to recent reports, all the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

According to recent reports, it’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

According to recent reports, there’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can initiative them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

It has been revealed that I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I mentioned it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Las Vegas Raiders owner Mark Davis, whose father Al recruited Madden to coach for the NFL team when they were located in Oakland in 1967, criticized David O.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As John Madden‘s life gets the biopic treatment, his longtime colleague and friend Al Davis‘ family is not pleased with their late patriarch’s portrayal.

Las Vegas Raiders owner Mark Davis, whose father Al recruited Madden to coach for the NFL team when they were located in Oakland in 1967, criticized David O. Russell‘s Madden for its “totally unfair” depiction his father (portrayed by Christian Bale), who died at age 82 in 2011.

“It was full of turducken,” he told USA Today of the movie, referencing the Thanksgiving dish Madden popularized.

Mark continued, “As far as representations of my dad, yeah, that hurts, and I did the best I could to protect him. It’s absolutely a crime that they’re able to treat people that have passed away and characterize them in ways that are unfair, and there’s nobody around to protect their legacies. It’s just unfair. I don’t know what the purpose of the movie was to be real honest.” Watch on Deadline.

He doesn’t consider his father “a pimp like Christian Bale played him, but that’s fine,” noting, “And I don’t blame Christian Bale. I don’t blame Nicolas Cage. All they did was what the director and the writers told them to do.”.

Having screened the film two weeks before its release, Mark was surprised by a scene depicting the 1978 preseason game that paralyzed New England Patriots wide receiver Darryl Stingley, in which Al discourages Madden (Nicolas Cage) from seeing the player in the hospital.

Industry observers note that “One of the main legacies of my father was how much he took care of people, whether it was on the Raiders or other teams,” said Mark. “People that were ill or needed help or whatever. He helped so many players on other teams that it’s incredible. And he did it quietly.

“And for them to put in the Darryl Stingley incident, that my dad was trying to talk John out of going to see him – that was just such a hurt to me personally, because that’s my father’s legacy, is how he treated people. No matter whether they were Raiders or not, he cared about people. That’s one of the redeeming qualities of my father throughout his life. And I just thought it was totally unfair for them to portray it that way,” added Mark.

Sources indicate that while he said that scene “hurt” him, Mark added, “All the other crap, I could take all that (stuff). I don’t care if they talk about my haircuts and stuff like that. I don’t know what it had to do with anything, but I don’t mind that. They can do that to me. But to do that to somebody that’s passed away, that can’t defend himself, is totally unfair. And I’m sure that there’s gonna be thousands of people that could contradict what that clip portrayed my father as.”.

Mark added that the portrayal of his mother Carol Davis (played by Sienna Miller) and John’s wife Virginia Madden (Kathryn Hahn) is “all made up stuff too,” conceding, “But there are some, you know, elements of them in that. I will say that, but not much.”.

Co-written by Russell and Cambron Clark, Madden charts John Madden’s career from Raiders coach to TV broadcaster to the namesake of the Madden NFL video game franchise.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Catherine, the Princess of Wales will discuss her cancer battle in an upcoming documentary special that will raise money for the hospital that treated her.

Heal: A Princess of Wales Story will air November 30 on NBC, a day after it premieres on the BBC. The documentary follows Kate Middleton as she reflects on her cancer battle while completing the Three Peaks Challenge — climbing the tallest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in the span of 24 hours — this past June in support of the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, the hospital where she was treated; proceeds from the distribution of Heal will also benefit Royal Marsden.

Industry observers note that “Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. But there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you,” the Princess of Wales says in the trailer.

“It’s clear we’re not meant to carry life’s challenges alone. Things can renew and grow. After it is through pain that we realize there’s a greater beauty that lies beyond that.”.

The news of Middleton’s initial diagnosis was disclosed to the public in March 2024, following an abdominal surgery in January. In a video statement, Middleton said, “At the time, it was thought that my condition was non-cancerous,” referring to her surgery. “The surgery was successful, however, tests after the operation on cancer had been present,” she added. In January 2025, Middleton declared, “It is a relief to now be in remission and I remain focused on recovery.”.
