📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the wake of Lionsgate‘s last Hunger Games: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes hitting a franchise low at the box office, the Santa Monica, CA based studio got very serious — serious about marketing and reaching the younger audience segemts that the conglomerate built their brand upon with franchises such as Twilight and, of course, Suzanne Collins’ Hunger Games.

In a recent development, three years ago, it looked like the Hunger Games series petered out with a $44.6M domestic, and $100.8M WW opening and final of $166.3M domestic and $363.9M WW. But this weekend in a death-defying act worthy of Katniss Everdeen herself, Lionsgate completely resuscitated the franchise from its rock bottom. Prequel Hunger Games: Sunrise of the Reaping rose like a phoenix, leaving behoind the previous installment’s box office ashes with a great $120M domestic, $225M global opening. Among prequels at the domestic B.O., Sunrise on the Reaping‘s opening was second only to Rogue One: A Star Wars Story‘s $155M start.

Sources indicate that that worldwide B.O. on Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes was worse than any installment in another popular YA franchise; the Harry Potter prequel/spinoff series Fantastic Beasts hit a low wih the last film, 2022’s The Secrets of Dumbledore, at $407.1M. Songbirds & Snakes repped the first time that Collins had written an origins story about one of the core characters, specifically, its villain Coriolanus Snow in a mentorship love story with District 12 tribute Lucy Gray Baird. There was a big bluegrass music element in the film, with Olivia Rodrigo on the soundtrack. Lacking, however, was an OG cast member from the first four films, given that it took place 64 years before the events of the initial Hunger Games novel. Watch on Deadline.

In a recent development, the novel was flat out rejected by fans, some pointing to Covid as an easy reason, others to the fact that it was about the bad guy, with 500K first week copies sold and final reported figure of 2.5M. Complicating business further was the fact that Songbirds & Snakes opened at the box office shortly after the actors strike ended. Even though Lionsgate, as an indie studio, had a SAG-AFTRA waiver for the cast to promote, it was still a challenge to prop up a tentpole during such times.

Industry observers note that collins marched on and figured out what her fanbase needed, crafting her next novel, Sunrise on the Reaping about the rise of Katniss and Peeta mentor Haymitch Abernathy (played by Woody Harrelson in the first four films). There was an epilogue in the book, not just with the older Haymitch, but Peeta and Katniss as well. It was the novel that fans wanted and they demonstrated their love by snapping up 4.4 million copies around the globe. It was also a good enough roux for filmmaker Francis Lawrence, director on films 2-5, to work from. In a complete one-up from Songbirds & Snakes, Lionsgate brought back the original 2012 pic’s screenwriter, Oscar-nominated Billy Ray, to adapt Collins’ latest.

RELATED: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Album Boasts 29 Songs; Releases Ahead Of Film.

In July 2025, Lionsgate saw a changeover in their marketing and publicity with then EVP Strategy and Chief of Staff Amanda Kozlowski, EVP Worldwide Publicity Nasim Cambron and EVP Global Creative Advertising Jack Teed stepping up. Such exec maneuvers ultimately left Lionsgate all the richer with a female tentpole in last Christmas’ Sydney Sweeney and Amanda Seyfriend thriller The Housemaid ($400.4M, first weekend turnout of 18-34 was 63%) fueled by a dish plate smashing social media meme, and of course, the studio’s first billion-dollar grossing movie last summer, the Michael Jackson biopic, Michael.

Kozlowski was promoted to Worldwide Marketing President in May shortly after Michael‘s $218.8M global opening, in addition to Cambron being elevated to EVP, Worldwide Marketing & Publicity and Teed to EVP, Worldwide Marketing & Creative Advertising. Chris Daniel, SVP, Global Creative Marketing and other members of the Lionsgate Marketing team also get shoutouts here for this weekend’s B.O. success.

“There is a new generation of marketing brains who understand how people are communicating with one another and how marketing messages can make an impact. The leaders of our marketing group, digital, media, publicity and creative teams are going 14 months strong with The Long Walk, Now You See Me, Now You Dont, Housemaid, Michael, and they’re not doing things in traditional ways. They’re creating moments that permeate popular culture and get audiences excited and want to share them with their friends,” stated Lionsgate Motion Picture Chairman Adam Fogelson today in celebration of Sunrise on the Reaping.

Previously at a Deadline Regal event over the summer, Fogelson told us that, “All of the things when I was growing up in marketing that were sort of held to be certain and true about how you reach an audience, those things, especially for the generations we’re talking about, have changed.” Case in point: Don’t overshare too much in a trailer; if you do, “you’re going to get flat-out rejected,” he added at the time.

RELATED: 13 Changes Made In ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’ Film From Suzanne Collins’ Novel“Some of the movies that are succeeding that are coming from this generation, they’re telling [a] story in a very different way,” mentioned Fogelson.

The overarching strategy for Sunrise on the Reaping was to make the sixth installment of the 14-year old franchise feel like the biggest games yet, not only reigniting the passion of longtime fans with a fave character in Haymitch, but also introducing a latest generation to Panem.

Industry observers note that A longtime motion picture marketing exec going back to Universal, Fogelson’s campaigns were always known for being anchored in character. Sources say Kozlowski has a similar philosophy, but also that the exec knows how to sell story and how to sell to a fanbase. At the center of this Hunger Games promo was Joseph Zada nailing a portrayal of a younger Haymitch.

Sources indicate that kozlowski tells Deadline, “From the beginning, Sunrise on the Reaping had a lot to offer Hunger Games fans — a fan-favorite character whose backstory many had long been asking for, the scale and spectacle of the biggest Games ever and a throughline that connected Haymitch’s tragedy to the rise of the revolution that culminated with Katniss. The marketing team combined those elements with a fan-forward campaign rooted in Gen Z and Gen Alpha online culture, peak Millennial nostalgia, activations that brought the world of Panem into our own and a wealth of unforgettable cast and filmmaker moments. As fans ourselves, it’s been gratifying to see moviegoers responding to the campaign with as much enthusiasm as we have for the world that Suzanne, Francis and Nina (Jacobson) have so lovingly created.”.

RELATED: ‘Sunrise On The Reaping’ Epilogue Scene Explained: How Everything Ties Together.

Industry observers note that the drumroll for Sunrise on the Reaping began a year ago when Lionsgate dropped the first teaser to 109 million global views in 24 hours, which became the studio’s second-most-watched trailer ever after Michael, which they had just debuted a few days prior. At the time, that trailer traffic for Sunrise was +48% ahead of Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, an excellent sign.

From there, Lionsgate created a card stacking (to use a Sunrise word) of high-impact reveals and cultural moments all the way up to release. The studio turned the casting announcements into a pop culture even with 16 individual announcements that generated 541 million views and 35.2 million engagements.

It has been revealed that when it came to the late campaign unveiling of the 29-song soundtrack, the studio executed a staggered, artist driven rollout with such performers as Noah Kahan, The Smashing Pumpkins, Ella Langley and Gigi Perez. Altogether this part of the pic’s marketing, which sought to expand beyond the franchise’s core, yielded 40 million+ social views and 186 playlist placements.

Sources indicate that A glittery part of the pic’s push was bringing Panem into the real world with immersive activations, fashion and lifestyle partnerships, and cultural integrations. Lionsgate set up Sunrise Gardens installations across 30 countries and six continents including Peru, Sweden, Brazil, South Africa, Denmark, Belgium, Singapore, Finland, London and more, which was picked up across social media.

The marketing also leaned into the pic’s themes of Capitol Propaganda with a customized Election Day activation, spearheaded by Lionsgate EVP Global Paid Media & Analytics, Dani Otero, across CNN and Fox News generating 79M+ social impressions and repping 31% of the Sunrise social conversation the following day.

Timed to Paris Fashion Week, there was the Elegance Is Authority exhibition at the Musée Rodin attracted 10,000+ registrations in 24 hours.

According to recent reports, also, there were beauty and fashion partnerships with Stila Cosmetics and Depop. Stila’s collaboration reached 1,500+ Ulta stores and generating 50 million+ press and organic social impressions.

In appealing to Gen Z and Gen Alpha, Lionsgate embraced creators, platforms, humor and content creators, inviting them to participate in the franchise rather than simply consume its marketing. Specifically, the studio teamed with a 16-year-old viral editor on the franchise’s first official fan-edit trailer, which pulled in 60.3 million+ views on TikTok. A global fan casting contest inspired 7,500+ submissions and 195.6 million+ views on fan-created videos, with participation extending beyond the core fandom to KATSEYE, Zooey Deschanel and Disney’s Stitch.

In a recent development, toward the end, Sunrise on the Reaping‘s propaganda built to a crescendo of peak nostalgia by paying homage to the old in the new. Lionsgate made a point to rope in OG cast members Harrelson, Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson with bookings on The Tonight Show and Bravo’s Watch What Happens Live.

In a recent development, the result was a great report card of stats for Sunrise‘s push: 1 billion+ owned-social views, 691M TikTok views, and 74 billion+ views of fan-generated content across relevant Hunger Games TikTok hashtags; 1.5 million newly introduced followers across the pic’s official social channels with a massive turnout by the 18-34 at 72% in PostTrak exits. The movie was the No. 2 pic on TikTok’s Trending Chart, behind only Avengers: Doomsday. Conversation volume on X was more than 4x than Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes at the comparable point in its campaign. The digital campaign was overseen by Lionsgate EVP, Head of Worldwide Digital Marketing, Briana McElroy.

The campaign for Sunrise on the Reaping generated renewed enthusiasm among women 17-34 who gave it a 36% first choice versus 24% for Ballad of Songbirds and Snake. Women under 25 showed up at 38% for Sunrise on the Reaping per PostTrak exits.

Overall, the media and social reach for the Sunrise push clocked 2.7 billion+ paid media impressions with heavy play on the NFL, NBA, World Series, and highlights such as Saturday Night Live, The Voice, Abbott Elementary, The Traitors and the Real Housewives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple could see iPhone shipments rise 7% next year, giving it a 26% share of global smartphone shipments, according to a latest report. Here are the details.

As detailed by AppleInsider, a new Morgan Stanley research report claims Apple is poised to ship approximately 270 million iPhones in 2027, a 7% bump from 2026.

The forecast comes amid a change of pace for Apple, which released only the iPhone 18 Pro models and iPhone Duo this fall, with the rest of its iPhone lineup reportedly set to arrive early next year.

Morgan Stanley notes that this could push some purchases from late 2026 into 2027, contributing to the projected shipment growth without necessarily reflecting an increase in underlying demand.

The report also comes as Apple and the rest of the smartphone industry continue to grapple with rising memory and storage prices, though previous reports have suggested that Apple is better positioned than many of its competitors to absorb those costs.

Recent findings suggest that apple raised iPhone prices in September, after keeping them stable for much of the year while competitors had already introduced price hikes. In some cases, they raised prices more than once within a matter of months.

It has been revealed that back to the report, it notes that global smartphone shipments are expected to drop 5% next year, compared with a previous forecast of 3.6% growth. That said, it’s still an improvement over the estimated 13.8% decline in 2026.

According to recent reports, when it comes to Apple and the iPhone specifically, Morgan Stanley notes that consumer interest in upgrading has remained largely unchanged year over year, with 37% of iPhone owners saying they are extremely likely to upgrade within the next 12 months. That’s compared with 41% of smartphone owners overall, a figure that dropped by 2 percentage points year over year.

As for the market’s reaction to the iPhone Duo, Morgan Stanley found that 22% of non-iPhone users surveyed expressed interest in switching to Apple’s foldable device, with that figure reaching 34% in China.

Importantly, Morgan Stanley’s survey was conducted after the iPhone Duo was announced, but before it launched, so these figures reflect consumer interest rather than actual purchasing behavior.

Apple Intelligence was another factor examined in the survey, with Morgan Stanley concluding that AI features are becoming less crucial in driving iPhone upgrades, while factors such as battery life and upgrade eligibility are gaining importance.

Finally, Morgan Stanley found that Apple’s customer retention rate increased three percentage points to a record 93%, while its net switching rate improved to 12%.

Huawei was the only other major smartphone brand to show a positive and improving net switching rate, while Samsung and Google remained relatively neutral, and Xiaomi, Motorola, Honor, Oppo, and Vivo recorded negative rates.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud.
  • A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.
  • At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid looks for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Select WhatsApp beta testers on iOS are now seeing an option to use the app’s own backup service as an alternative to iCloud. Here are the details.

A few months ago, WABetaInfo reported that WhatsApp was working on its own backup service as an alternative to the current method of backing up chats, which relies on Apple’s iCloud.

At the time, the feature wasn’t available even to beta testers, but WABetaInfo’s report provided details on how it would work, including 2GB of free storage, optional paid looks for larger backups, and mandatory end-to-end encryption for backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers.

Now, the site reports that some WhatsApp people running the latest TestFlight build are seeing the option to switch from iCloud to WhatsApp’s own backup service, suggesting that a wider rollout may not be too far off.

Consumers can switch to WhatsApp cloud storage from the Chat backup screen. Here, users will have to choose the backup provider they want to use. If they choose WhatsApp, they will have to secure their backups using end-to-end encryption. Since encryption is mandatory, users cannot skip this step. However, they can choose a different method to encrypt their backups. For example, users can secure their backups using a 64-digit encryption key. Users who do not know what to choose can opt for the passkey, which is the default method WhatsApp recommends. After users complete the setup, they can back up their chat history on WhatsApp’s servers. WhatsApp keeps the backup on its servers for four months after a subscription expires. If users do not renew their subscription, WhatsApp deletes the backup permanently.

Importantly, the site notes that backups stored on WhatsApp’s servers cannot right now be used to restore chats across platforms, meaning users switching from iPhone to Android, or vice versa, will still need to rely on WhatsApp’s built-in chat transfer feature.

Although the feature appears to be rolling out to beta testers first, the report notes that “the latest version available on the App Store is also compatible with this functionality,” meaning WhatsApp could theoretically enable it for users running the public version without requiring another app update.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that iFixit’s teardown of the new Apple HomeView is now up, revealing a device that seems nearly impossible to take apart and repair. Watch it below.

Following last week’s launch of the Apple HomeView, iFixit today published its teardown of the device.

Contrary to recent teardowns, which found significant repairability improvements with greater component modularity and easier access to internal components, the HomeView put up a fight nearly all the way through.

With heavily glued or adhesive-bonded components, including the display, speakers, antennas, and logic board, the teardown proved particularly challenging, even after the adhesive securing the display’s speakers was soaked in isopropyl alcohol.

At one point, one of them broke apart during removal, while the logic board required considerable force to separate from the chassis due to the thermal adhesive holding it in place.

iFixit’s teardown covered the two HomeView variants: the tabletop model and the wall-mounted version. Interestingly, there are some internal differences between them, as the wall-mounted model has a slightly wider logic board to accommodate capacitors that are housed in the base of the tabletop version.

As a result, the wall-mounted HomeView also has smaller internal speakers, which helps explain the differences in their audio systems that Apple had already acknowledged at launch.

Back to the tabletop model, iFixit’s teardown also indicated that separating the display from the base requires either specialized tools or extensive, potentially destructive disassembly of the display assembly, thanks to the way Apple routed the connecting cables through the pivot mechanism.

Once iFixit was in the base, however, there was some good news: the USB-C port is modular and relatively easy to access, as are the passive radiators and the board powering the lower assembly.

Still, an extremely short cable connecting the woofer to the board underneath made disassembly difficult, with iFixit questioning how anyone would be able to reconnect it during reassembly.

Industry observers note that percentage of Apple owners who are interested in repairing their device. 0.000001%.

Percentage of Apple owners who will actually try and repair their device. 0.00000001%.

Given all these repairability challenges, Shahram Mokhtari joked that while iFixit doesn’t have an official repairability scorecard for this category of device, he would give the Apple HomeView a “BEEP this thing” out of 10.

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4’s fourth episode.

George Russell’s gunshot wound is coming back to haunt him in a way as Season 4 of The Gilded Age reaches its midpoint.

As has been building since last season when George survived an assassination attempt in his home, a troubling laudanum addiction has come to light for the railroad tycoon, whose behavior early on in the season has grown more and more unpredictable.

“I think it is fairly easy, when you have a long-term injury, and you do have lingering pain, to fall into opiate addiction. I think that is a real thing, but I also think George is someone with a really indomitable will. And I think for someone like him, in our story, to slip into the situation, I think there’s something else going on in his life,” Spector told Deadline. “I think that something else is the destabilization of his relationship with Bertha. I don’t think that’s entirely it. I think, after the shooting last season, he’s really having a gigantic midlife crisis. He’s built this enormous empire, and he’s suddenly realized he doesn’t really know who he is anymore, what his values are, and if and if he wants to keep living his life the way he has been, so I think the laudanum comes along at just exactly the wrong time for him.”.

George is under extra pressure this season with President Grover Cleveland (Jim Gaffigan) in town and working on antitrust legislature, which would threaten the railroad monopoly he has worked so hard to construct and protect. Add J.D. Rockefeller (Neal Huff) into the equation wanting to cut back prices he pays Russell Industries to transport his oil, and George feels very cornered in business. Spector had hinted that his character was already having a “crisis of conflict” in Season 3. Watch on Deadline.

In a recent development, “Rockefeller was this really interesting character, and so we learned more about him from the research. I’m from Cleveland, and he’s originally from Cleveland. And he basically bankrupted Toledo or some city. He ripped them off, but he was also really pious, and he did do the price fixing,” co-showrunner Sonja Warfield told Deadline. “That’s something he did do. He was ruthless in business, but in church all the time. I love to put characters under pressure. I think it’s where the magic happens, and George and the laudanum —Doctor [Erica] Dunbar had actually suggested that last season.”.

It has been revealed that the tincture of opium was prescribed by the white doctor who attended to George’s gunshot wound after Dr. William Kirkland (Jordan Donica) saved Mr. Russell’s life in Season 3.

“She did say, ‘You know that you can get addicted to it,’ and so we planted that last season, and what I love is that, Morgan plays it just so deftly and just beautifully — this vulnerable side of George. And in the first season we see George, there’s a character who gets down on his knees and begs him, ‘Spare us,’ and now George is is really at his knees [on this],” Warfield said.

RELATED: RELATED: ‘The Gilded Age’ Producers Address George’s Shocking Decision In Season 3 Finale: “He Feels Bertha Made Him Act Against His Instincts”.

Will Morris (Will Pullen) turned out to be the man responsible for the attempt on George’s life, and there is history between the two, because Will is the son of Patrick Morris, the business partner of George’s who took his own life in Season 1 after a deal he made with railroad magnate went bad.

A meeting with Daniel Manning, Secretary of the Treasury during the first two years of Grover Cleveland’s presidency is one of the last instinces of Season 4 in which George exhibits normal behavior despite his substance abuse. It’s explicitly established during that chat that President Cleveland thinks “monopolies threaten our way of government.” George wants to meet with the president, and also Rockefeller, to convince the United States leader that he could gain him political backing in Newly introduced York for re-election, which George things is iffy for Cleveland. Vieweres can’t help but notice similarities with the merger taking place between Paramount and Warner Bros.

“About the merger thing, Julian and Sonia have a really fantastic record of being a little clairvoyant in terms of the things that they choose to take on in these seasons, and I think partly that’s because there are just so many structural parallels between the era at the end of the 19th century and the era we’re living in now in terms of wealth inequality and concentration of monopoly power,” Spector said. “And what’s fascinating is that those structural similarities create really similar consequences, and that’s because of the way capitalism works. These are systemic dynamics, and they play out in similar ways, no matter what time you’re living in. So yeah, I think either Julian is Nostradamus or maybe there are some structural issues with our political economic system.”.

George also confronts Rockefeller at the gentleman’s club they both frequent for business and social life, displaying increasingly erratic behavior and raised voice, as he communicates to the oil baron his plan to get President Cleveland on their side.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple today announced that App Store prices for apps and In-App Purchases will be adjusted in five countries starting December 3, following changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates. Here are the details.

In a new post published on its developer portal, Apple today confirmed a series of changes to App Store pricing, as well as updates to tax rules affecting developers and customers in several countries, including the US.

According to the tech giant, developers’ proceeds from eligible app and In-App Purchase sales have been adjusted in four countries, reflecting the following tax updates:.

Specific to Botswana and Rwanda, Apple said that “Exhibit B of the Paid Applications Agreement will be updated to indicate that Apple collects and remits applicable taxes.”.

Apple added that a fresh “Software as a Service (SaaS)” attribute is now available for several App Store tax categories, including App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting. Developers can review and update their tax category selections in App Store Connect.

Additionally, starting December 3, developers who rely on Apple’s automatic pricing adjustments will see changes to app and In-App Purchase prices in:.

Apple usually makes these adjustments to account for changes in taxes and foreign exchange rates, and notes that prices won’t change in countries selected as the base storefront, for auto-renewable subscriptions, or in storefronts where developers manually manage their prices.

The announcement does not go into detail about how much prices will change in each country, or whether they will increase or decrease.

Finally, starting January 1, 2027, apps and In-App Purchases in the SaaS, App Store Software, Software Training Material, Dating, and Boosting categories will become subject to sales and use taxes in California.

Apple noted that “prices on the United States storefront are displayed to customers exclusive of taxes, so the tax change will not affect them,” but added that while developers’ proceeds will remain unchanged, “the total amount customers are charged, inclusive of tax, may increase.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4’s fourth episode.
  • As if a new house and husband weren’t enough, Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), now Mrs.
  • The recognition for her novel could be seen as the cherry on top of a wonderful latest chapter for the journalist, writer and now wife, whose wedding unfolded in episode 403.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SPOILER ALERT: This post contains spoilers for The Gilded Age Season 4’s fourth episode.

As if a new house and husband weren’t enough, Peggy Scott (Denée Benton), now Mrs. Dr. William Kirkland, receives a letter from journalist Ida B. Wells about her newly published book in the fourth episode of Season 4 of The Gilded Age.

The recognition for her novel could be seen as the cherry on top of a wonderful latest chapter for the journalist, writer and now wife, whose wedding unfolded in episode 403.

Sources indicate that “It’s really fun to see Peggy step into her Renaissance woman era. She’s striving so much for the first few seasons. It’s very ‘Don’t believe me? Just watch’ like everything that she’s getting to do in Season 4,” Benton told Deadline. “Since Season 1, she’s like, ‘I told y’all, you didn’t believe me, but it’s okay.’ And now it’s nice to see her do her victory lap.” Watch on Deadline.

In a recent development, peggy is now part of a union, though, and while her star is on the rise, her husband isn’t currently satisfied at his job. An old colleague of his, Dr. Harris (Dennis Haysbert) pinpoints this with William and suggests he look out for an opening back at Friedman’s Hospital, where Dr. Harris practices in Washington D.C. After discussing it with William, Dr. Harris brings it up with Peggy and both sets of parents of the newlyweds present, where he unintentionally causes some ripples.

“It’s also really nice to play with the ambitious tension that I recognize in Bertha, where there [are] these blinders on, and I was really thankful for how radical it was to see her completely lose sight for a time that she was in a pair and in a family,” Benton added. “It’s fun that the audience won’t always agree with [Peggy]. I think it adds a lot of dynamic texture to her not just having to be this moral gold star for the show, which is very limiting, but to have her lose sight of the fact that William is facing his own challenges, like the limitations of racism, not being able to practice surgery in Latest York and having a patient die because the white doctor didn’t tend to him. It’s not just as limited as a man having trouble with her ambitions. It’s ‘How do they really balance both of their dreams?’”.

A very representative moment of such “ambitious tension’ between husband and wife arrives when one of Peggy’s colleagues, Mr. Simms, mistakenly calls her husband Mr. Scott instead of Dr. Kirkland at a reading and signing for her book. This scene stemmed from a real-life incident co-showrunner Sonja Warfield experienced at a writing event.

“I wasn’t even that much of an established writer, but I have always used my maiden name, even when I was married, and he got referred to as Mr. Warfield. And so I thought, what if that happened in 1885? What’s the impact of that? Especially if the parents are around to witness that, and what does that do to your masculinity then?” Warfield told Deadline. “Because men felt, probably, still to an extent, proprietary over their wives, right? Women really were barely dealing with their career versus family back then, and women worked, and a lot of Black women worked or expected to work and had to work.”.

In a recent development, during a carriage ride home after the book signing, Dr. Kirkland tries to address the idea of moving to Washington D.C. with Peggy, who holds firm and wonders why they have to uproot at that exact moment. She doubles back and gives William recognition for his work, but she isn’t quite sold on them moving yet.

In a recent development, “Marriage is really about coming together and becoming one, and Peggy has lived a long time as an individual, and she was an only child, and so she got to do what she wanted,” Warfield noted. “So, again, like with Enid and Oscar, marriage will be an eye opener for Peggy and William as well about gender roles, to an extent, because he’s the man, and so he’s supposed to have the last word about their lives, and that was what was expected back then. She would have no say.”.

Industry observers note that peggy does holds her own when the discussion of children comes up — as it has now multiple times this season before and after she got married via her husband or his mother when she refers to grandchildren. This is, in addition to the lavender marriage aspect of Enid (Kelly Curran) and Oscar’s (Blake Ritson) union, what sets the women on different paths, since Enid keeps poking at the idea of having a child with Oscar, especially after Agnes van Rhijn (Christine Baranski) indicates she sees a glow about Enid signalling she could be with child in this latest episode.

“It’s cool to watch this power couple trailblaze and navigate what power looked like for them and her. Even seeing a woman at that time decide when or if she wants children, even now there’s still a little taboo for those of us who will admit out loud that we are not sure,” Benton noted. “And so for a woman at that time to say, “We’ll see,” is wild, and then it’s really cool to see the ways Mrs. Kirkland is kind of right, where she’s like, ‘Listen, Peggy’s a great woman, but is she going to be a great wife to you?’ And what it means to run a household at that time is basically a full time job. lIt’s cool ike that [Peggy’s] getting to represent so many textures of womanhood and femininity.”.

Warfield agreed with Benton’s assessment of the character.

“I think Peggy’s character does surprise us, as Denee noted in her reaction to things. I think people think will think a lot of things,” the co-showrunner said. “People might get a little bit upset because Dr. Kirkland is a catch, and I’m sure there are going to be women out there who are saying, ‘Girl, if you don’t want him, then… [I’ll take him!]’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB blueprint to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances ….

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud intends.

Recent findings suggest that however, tucked away in the small print in the organization’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries.

Sources indicate that siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust complications. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:.

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:.

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The organization may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

#131290. Tech Report: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2889 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he indicates he has identified the next major shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his firm Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big problems in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Industry observers note that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Industry observers note that andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having noted that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Sources indicate that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having stated that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing firm with millions of owners.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

In a recent development, “In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and stated, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and mentioned, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that highlighted up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from significant data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

According to recent reports, when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand fresh model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

It has been revealed that ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having mentioned that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

It has been revealed that for example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very rapidly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Industry observers note that ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an crucial piece of the puzzle.

It has been revealed that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is vital, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention rapidly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

Sources indicate that for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

According to recent reports, ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

In a recent development, “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion people. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these challenges more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a firm approaches Landing AI and claims it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Recent findings suggest that ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

According to recent reports, how do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

In a recent development, ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift problem. I find it really notable to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and patch the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

Recent findings suggest that in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion consumers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

In a recent development, ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent newly introduced neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Industry observers note that ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print matter as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

Steinfeld appeared in Marvel’s Hawkeye limited series as Kate Bishop, the character who takes up the Hawkeye mantle from Jeremy Renner’s Clint. She also appeared as Bishop in The Marvels.

Sources indicate that if you’re going to commit to an Amazon Prime membership, you might as well squeeze as much as you can out of the deal. And there's a good amount of juice to squeeze there. If you're on the fence about signing up, consider that Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale is underway, and the firm is hosting some amazing tech deals. It's a great time to sell your soul—or take advantage of the 30-day free trial—and there's a lot more to your membership than just deals and free shipping.

The standard Prime membership costs $14.99 per month or $139 per year, but there are other tiers that some people might qualify for. For example, the Amazon Prime for Young Adults program allows young adults between the ages of 18 and 24 to get all of the Prime perks for half the cost—$7.49 per month or $69 annually.

In a recent development, I'll be the first to admit I didn't know all of the benefits that Amazon Prime offers to its members. There are a lot more perks than people think. Here are the most impressive ones (and check out the full list):.

Fast free shipping on millions of items: Depending on where you live, shipping can take one or two days, and some even come on the same day for orders of $25 or more in most areas—and it’s always free (if being shipped by the Amazon store).

Select pre-ordered items can be delivered on their release date for free (for most areas).

The option to have items delivered inside your garage with a smart garage device (depending on where you live) for $1.99 per order, or for free if you combine it with Amazon Day delivery.

Earn rewards for future purchases when you select free no-rush shipping.

The option to have all your weekly orders delivered on a specific day, to reduce waste from boxes.

Amazon Prime Visa card: Cardholders get 5% back on Amazon, Whole Foods, Chase Travel, and other purchases. Prime members who use this card extensively can earn rewards that offset the cost of membership.

Industry observers note that A Grubhub+ and Uber Eats membership, normally $9.99 per month, which gets you free delivery on eligible orders, lower service fees, exclusive deals, and other perks as long as you remain a Prime Member (it used to be only for a year). The Uber Eats membership gets you free delivery on eligible restaurants of $25 or more.

Industry observers note that sharing with family or friends: Amazon Family is the existing program for sharing Prime benefits, and it allows you to add separate profiles for one other adult who lives in the same household as the primary account holder, up to four teens, and up to four child accounts. This grants access to all the standard benefits, such as free delivery, Prime Video with ads, Prime Reading, third-party benefits like Grubhub, and access to audiobooks, e-books, certain games, and Amazon Music.

Amazon Health: Prime owners get One Medical access for an additional $9 per month or $99 per year. Through your devices, you’ll have 24/7 access to on-demand virtual care, plus real-life access to primary care offices in a number of U.S. cities. It accepts most major health insurance looks, too.

Amazon Pharmacy: Access to free two-day delivery and other savings on medications.

Prime Video: Prime includes unlimited streaming of movies, TV shows, and Amazon Originals with ads, which normally costs $9 per month.

Amazon Music Prime: Access to Amazon's Spotify-esque music streaming service (not to be confused with Amazon's other music streaming subscriptions).

Amazon Luna: A cloud gaming platform that offers latest free games every month, free downloadable PC games, content, a monthly Twitch channel subscription, and a free channel subscription on Twitch each month for Prime Members.

Amazon Photos: Unlimited photo storage plus 5 GBs for videos and other files (which extends to members of your Family Vault).

Prime Reading: Free access to a rotating selection of e-books and magazines for Kindle or Fire tablets and Kindle apps.

Amazon's First Reads: You get up to two free e-books every month from a curated list of books handpicked by editors.

It aims to lift the industry with its aircraft, motors, batteries, and charging network.

Beta Technologies, one of the top three U.S. electric aircraft makers, is aiming first at regional cargo and medical transport, before pursuing the passenger market. Shown here is Beta’s Alia A250, for vertical takeoffs and landings.

In the cockpit of Beta Technologies’ Alia CX300, pilot Chris Caputo steers onto Runway 33 at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in Vermont. Cleared for takeoff, he releases the brakes and nudges the throttle forward.

At the back of the aircraft, the five-blade pusher propeller snaps awake, and the Alia bolts forward. There’s no shriek of a turbofan spooling up, no shudder of a piston engine, and no wait for thrust. Just the low hum of an electric motor and a shove of instant acceleration.

Within a few seconds, we’re at 85 knots (almost 160 kilometers per hour), and Caputo rotates the nose upward. The runway drops abruptly away as we climb. Gaining speed and altitude, we head northwest over Lake Champlain. Through the wraparound canopy, I watch the hunched shoulders of Vermont’s Green Mountains shrink under the right wing, with Upcoming York’s taller Adirondacks to the left.

Caputo, a former Air Force fighter pilot, flicks the control stick hard left, then right. Despite its 15-meter wingspan, the Alia feels snappy, its fly-by-wire system automatically coordinating aileron and rudder inputs. The machine, he claims, is much simpler to manage than the Cessna 182 I flew around Australia in my student-pilot days.

Recent findings suggest that what’s more, our half-hour flight in the Alia will consume only about US $9 worth of electricity. The same flight in a comparable Cessna 208 Caravan would burn roughly 25 to 30 gallons of Jet A fuel, costing about $210 to $255 at press time. “Even at full throttle, we’re not burning any fuel up here,” claims Caputo, as he takes the Alia into a sweeping left turn and heads south over the lake. “We’re not polluting the environment. [There’s] no noise pollution.”.

In a recent development, at Beta’s South Burlington, Vt., facility, workers assemble the body of an Alia A250. The company notes it has an order and option-to-buy backlog of nearly 1,000 aircraft.Beta Technologies.

This ride is happening during an unusually lively time for electric aviation. The promise of lower operating costs and cleaner flight has pushed electric aircraft from a fringe experiment to one of the aviation industry’s most closely watched frontiers. After years of renderings, prototypes, and overly optimistic timetables, companies are now flying full-size aircraft, submitting hardware to regulators for certification, building factories, and testing routes with prospective customers.

Among the top three U.S. developers of electric planes, Archer Aviation and Joby Aviation are concentrating on piloted vertical-takeoff-and-landing air taxis, otherwise known as eVTOLs. Beta Technologies is taking a broader—and in some ways more innovative—path into the market. Rather than betting first on air taxis, Beta is looking to enter electric aviation through short-haul freight planes that use conventional runways, fed by an open charging network that’s designed to make electric aircraft—both Beta’s and its competitors’—part of a working transportation system.

Recent findings suggest that to that end, the manufacturer is developing two variants of its Alia airframe: the runway-based CX300 I’m flying in and the A250, which adds four lift propellers for vertical takeoff and landing. Beta states its test pilots have flown the Alia family more than 300,000 kilometers, including doing multiple U.S. crossings and overseas demonstrations. The company claims an order and option-to-buy backlog of 991 aircraft.

Sources indicate that “We’re taking a pragmatic stepwise approach for both certification and market entry,” says Beta’s CEO and founder Kyle Clark. “We’re ready to go today with medical and cargo aircraft that fly from airport to airport.” Next up, he says, will be passenger aircraft with conventional takeoff and landing, followed by cargo eVTOLs, and finally passenger eVTOLs.

Industry observers note that beta’s 17,500-square-meter production facility sits beside the Burlington airport and looks more like a giant sunlit workshop than a conventional airplane factory. Geothermal heat pumps help heat and cool the structure. The roof will eventually hold a megawatt of solar panels. On the floor, technicians make composite structures and join aircraft sections beneath American and Pride flags.

The company says Midnight is in Phase 4 of the FAA certification process and has completed trial flights.Beta Technologies’ piloted Alia aircraft comes in two flavors: The A250 eVTOL has separate vertical-lift rotors and a rear cruise propeller, while the CX300 is a conventional-takeoff fixed-wing plane. The two models use the same pusher motor, battery pack, flight control computer, and fixed-pitch propeller. The company is initially focusing on cargo and medical transport, regional logistics, and airport-to-airport operations, with passenger service later. Beta expects FAA certification for the CX300 in 2027 and for the A250 a year later.Kyle Clark, a native of Vermont, founded Beta in 2017 to realize his long-held dream of building a hybrid-electric aircraft. (For his bachelor’s thesis at Harvard University, he designed a flight-control system for such an aircraft.) Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech company United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.The company has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. But it also means the company must be competent at several businesses simultaneously: airframes, electric motors, inverters, batteries, software, chargers, and aircraft production.The production line can build both the fixed-wing CX300 and the vertical-lift A250, which share the same fuselage, wings, pusher motor (for horizontal propulsion), batteries, avionics, and much of the tooling. This results in some one-size-fits-all decisions: The CX300’s twin booms, which connect the wing to the tail surfaces, look superfluous until you see the A250’s four lift propellers mounted on similar structures.On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the company is bringing the runway version forward first. It’s certifying the motor, batteries, fly-by-wire controls, and much of the airframe in the simpler aircraft; it will then reuse evidence and manufacturing experience when it certifies the A250.The other significant reason to start with the CX300 is logistical: The United States has more than 5,000 public-use airports, so the CX300 can operate from infrastructure that already exists. The cargo and medical flights that the aircraft will initially tackle offer tightly defined missions in which lower energy and maintenance costs matter more than cabin amenities. Hence the company’s decision to leave cabin air-conditioning off the CX300, at least for now. “Things that don’t exist on an airplane don’t weigh anything,” Clark says. “They can’t break. You don’t have to service them…. You don’t have to certify them.”“This strategy, at the beginning, was seen as a failure of their VTOL,” says analyst Sergio Cecutta, a managing partner at SMG Consulting. “But I think a lot of people were very myopic. It was a way for [Beta] to break up the certification in two pieces, and so they have retired a lot of the risk. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”How Redundancy Enhances SafetyA decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. In some ways, an electric car has more complicated power-engineering requirements than an electric aircraft. An electric car’s power demands change constantly, while an electric aircraft operates in a narrower set of power regimes: takeoff, level flight, and descent.But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.“You could lose an entire half of the system, and it would still function the same,” says Adam Lowe, Beta’s flight operations lead.The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.Beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the company’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.Innovation in eVTOLsBeta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.“One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” says Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.Electric propulsion also lets designers break up the work with multiple motors. The weight of an electric motor is tied closely to its torque. If you spread that torque among several motors, each of the motors can shrink, meaning that their combined weight is less than would be needed for one big engine. This is one reason why so many electric aircraft designs appear to have sprouted propellers wherever an engineer found a place to put one.There is a downside to using multiple smaller motors: If one of the motors quits, the rotor it’s driving has little stored energy compared to the inertia in a conventional helicopter’s one large rotor. This inertia can come in handy if the engine dies, because the rotor will continue to spin and allow the pilot to descend under control, in an emergency technique known as autorotation. And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company presently employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.As befits an aviation company, Beta offers flying lessons for all employees—a perk that is intended to give engineers, software developers, pilots, and mechanics a common language. The company also operates a health clinic for employees and their families and is building a day care center. Those programs have an idealistic Vermont flavor that is shaped by Clark and his wife, Katie Clark, who is Beta’s head of brand, creative, culture and spaces. But they also serve a practical purpose: attracting and retaining the best people in a small labor market. —T.C.

3 Competing Paths to Electric Aviation.

Industry observers note that the top three U.S. electric-aircraft makers are taking different approaches to the same challenge: how to make short-hop flight cleaner, quieter, and commercially useful.

Martine Rothblatt, CEO of the biotech organization United Therapeutics and cofounder of SiriusXM satellite radio, invested $48 million in Beta to fund its first prototype, with the eventual goal of using the aircraft to transport organs for transplantation.

The organization has kept much of its design and manufacturing in-house, partly because the pieces are closely coupled and partly because suitable aviation components didn’t exist when development began. Vertical integration gives Beta’s engineers control over the interfaces and any failure data. On the CX300, those booms add weight and drag even though they serve no lift function. But the trade-off—a simpler overall design—is part of Beta’s central strategy: Rather than applying for FAA certification for the more novel and complex eVTOL A250, with its multiple lift systems and transitions between hover and wing-borne flight, the manufacturer is bringing the runway version forward first. [A majority] of the [CX300’s] parts are shared with the VTOL, and that means that a lot of the documentation for certification can be easily reused on the VTOL side when that certification starts.”.

A decade and a half after electric cars began making significant inroads into the automotive market, electric airplane technology is advancing rapidly. But if your car’s drivetrain fails, you can just pull over to the side of the road. That’s not an option for a pilot 1,000 meters up. The hurdle isn’t that electric motors are inherently fragile; it’s that aviation safety standards are extraordinarily demanding. Catastrophic failure conditions generally must be held to roughly one chance in a billion flight hours or less.

Because individual electrical components cannot meet that standard on their own, electric aircraft rely on layered redundancy: duplicate power paths, independent inverters, fault isolation, monitoring, and backup capacity. Each layer helps close the safety gap, but each also adds weight and complexity.

To close the reliability gap and satisfy regulators who have little experience with electric aircraft, Beta engineers have built redundancy into the motor itself. When I visit the company’s motor shop, technicians are assembling the H500A pusher motor, which splits up critical components like the inverters and stator sections.

The H500A’s broad diameter gives the magnetic forces greater leverage, producing high torque at low rotational speed, a useful trait when turning large propellers. The H500A weighs about 75 kilograms and produces about 640 kilowatts of power. The motor achieves 97.5 percent efficiency, based on internal testing; typical conventional turboprops have an efficiency range of 25 to 35 percent.

Sources indicate that beta had aimed to have its motor certified in the first half of 2026, a deadline that passed without a public announcement. Although the tech giant’s certification strategy is aimed at streamlining the process, getting clearance to fly from the Federal Aviation Administration is probably still its biggest obstacle. For Beta, and any company trying to bring an electric aircraft into service, the FAA must sign off first on the propeller, then the motor, then the aircraft. After that, the manufacturer must pursue a production certificate from the FAA, proving that the company can build the same approved aircraft again and again, with the right tools, records, inspections, quality controls, supplier oversight, training, calibration, and parts tracking.

Beta has found a narrow on-ramp to get the A250 flying before full certification. Under the FAA’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program, companies and public agencies can run FAA-supervised, real-world trials to test how advanced air-mobility aircraft might operate in the national airspace. For Beta, that included July flights of the CX300 across a Virginia-to-Maryland corridor carrying, among other things, a manufactured transplantable organ in a medical containment system. Beta has also been chosen for six other FAA-backed trials.

For the fixed-wing Alia CX300, customer trials are moving in parallel. In March, Beta’s CX300 successfully completed 23 flights over 10 days on Loganair routes linking six Scottish cities. The airline has since signed a term sheet for five Beta aircraft, with options for five more and service expected to start in 2029.

In a recent development, beta is pushing so hard for the A250 because the case for electric flight gets even more interesting with vertical-lift aircraft. Helicopters and other VTOLs have a less orderly life than fixed-wing planes do. They must hover, sidestep, turn in place, settle, climb, and hold themselves in the air by main force. But conventional helicopters are built around a rotor speed that varies only a few percent because the engine, transmission, and rotor system are all designed around one narrow operating point.

Sources indicate that “One of the dreams of vertical flight has been to vary the rotor rpm,” states Anubhav Datta, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of Maryland, College Park, who studies electric propulsion and vertical flight. Electric motors, he argues, have advanced enough to make that practical. A rotor that can slow down or speed up as conditions change can waste less energy, make less noise, and better match the odd assortment of tasks that vertical flight demands.

And you say, ‘You can actually live here and have a high-paying job in a mission-driven business, doing something that you care about with great people.’ ” The company right now employs about 1,500 people, most of them in South Burlington, Vt., and is actively hiring for its engineering, manufacturing, software, flight operations, and commercial teams.
