Recent findings suggest that electric-aircraft makers compensate with redundant motors and electrical channels, but most leading designs also have wings to allow gliding. In Beta’s A250, that means that if all else fails, the pilot still has a shot at reaching a suitable landing spot.

In a recent development, that helps explain the convergence in today’s eVTOL designs. Joby Aviation’s S4 uses six propellers that tilt between lift and cruise. Archer Aviation’s Midnight has six tilting propellers and six dedicated lift props. Beta’s A250 keeps its four lift propellers horizontal and uses a separate pusher motor for forward flight.

In Beta’s home state of Vermont, the electricity produced in the state comes almost entirely from renewable sources. Of course, electric aviation’s climate advantage depends not only on how clean the power grid is, but on how efficiently the aircraft uses energy. The turbines in conventional jet engines are marvelous machines, but they throw away a lot of energy as heat. Plus they need to carry the hardware to manage that heat—inlets, ducts, radiators, oil coolers—and the drag that comes with pulling air through all of it.

It has been revealed that kyle Clark [in cockpit], founder and CEO of Beta Technologies, pilots the manufacturer’s Alia CX300, an electric plane that Beta expects to receive FAA certification in 2027. Clark began designing a hybrid electric plane while still in college.Beta Technologies.

According to recent reports, by contrast, an electric design, with no combustion, gearbox, or oil circuits, avoids much of that energy burden. The result is an aircraft that is more than twice as “slippery” in terms of its lift-to-drag ratio. Batteries will never come close to the fuel density of petroleum fuels. But because electric drivetrains are much more efficient than combustion engines, a battery doesn’t necessarily need to match the energy density of petroleum fuel to be useful.

While the motors on an electric aircraft provide the drama at takeoff and landing, the batteries set nearly every boundary: the range, payload, charge time, cooling load, reserve energy, and, ultimately, useful life. For now, the hardest limit on electric aviation is not imagination, software, or even motors. It is the stubborn weight of stored energy.

“One thing you notice about [electric] airplanes is that they are all small,” says Cecutta, the aviation analyst. “They are not small because someone has done a market study and decided that is the optimal size. They are small because you cannot make them substantial. This limitation is from the batteries.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a conventional aircraft, fuel accounts for a significant percentage of the takeoff weight. But that weight gradually disappears during flight. In an electric plane, the battery packs also account for a lot of the weight; in Beta’s CX300, they’re close to half the aircraft’s mass. But a drained battery at landing weighs the same as a fully charged one at takeoff. That means the rest of the aircraft must be light enough to lift a power source that never gets lighter, yet strong enough to endure vibration, turbulence, hard landings, and years of fatigue. The more engineers push to save weight, Datta notes, the more flexible the airframe becomes, making the wings and other structures more prone to bending, twisting, and vibration. In that sense, the battery problem becomes a structural problem, too.

Beta’s CX300 carries five liquid-cooled battery packs of about 45 kilowatt-hours each, giving the aircraft roughly 225 kWh of rated capacity, though not all of that may be usable in flight. Each pack weighs 255 kg and contains 2,772 cylindrical cells. Altogether, about 14,000 cells sit beneath the occupied cabin, each one a tiny storehouse of energy, heat, and potential trouble.

The burden of the battery explains much of what I see elsewhere in Beta’s aircraft: the 15-meter wingspan, the composite structure, and the almost doctrinal effort to leave out every piece of hardware and creature comfort that’s not essential to the mission. The CX300 even does without flaps, which most aircraft use to generate extra lift at low speeds, so it must take off and land unusually fast for an aircraft of its size.

Industry observers note that on Beta’s battery line, commercially supplied standard 21-millimeter-diameter, 70-mm-long cells are tested and assembled. Cells become modules, modules become subpacks, and eleven subpacks become a 45-kWh pack. Cooling plates manage heat during normal operation, while passive barriers and electrical isolation are designed to contain the ugly edge cases that Beta’s testing process intentionally triggers.

Industry observers note that the modular design of the packs will give Beta’s planes a path to better batteries as the cells and battery chemistry improve. Caputo tells me that the company is already evaluating higher-density cells at its battery testing facility in nearby St. Albans, Vt. More watt-hours per kilogram could eventually mean more range, more payload, or both.

What sets Beta Technologies apart from its competitors is the breadth of its ambitions: It’s not just building electric aircraft. It’s also cultivating a broader ecosystem to nurture the growth of electric aviation.

In a recent development, for instance, Beta intends its motor business to extend beyond its own aircraft. The firm has delivered lift motors for Eve Air Mobility’s proof-of-concept aircraft and has a contract to supply up to $1 billion in pusher motors as Eve’s program develops. In addition, Beta is selling flight-control computers and software to Horizon Aircraft. It is also producing propulsion systems for the military, as well as the MV250, a hybrid-electric autonomous aircraft for defense missions.

It has been revealed that beta’s fast-charging stations [left] have been installed at 138 locations. The thermal-management station [right] keeps the battery from overheating during charging. The tech giant uses the open-standard Combined Charging System (CCS) so that other aircraft can use its chargers. Beta Technologies.

Further evidence of Beta’s far-ranging aims is visible near the battery line in the South Burlington facility, where workers are readying a few of the organization’s 1.5-meter-tall Charge Cubes for shipping. Intended for installation at airports, each cube takes 480-volt AC from the grid and can deliver up to 320 kW at as much as 1,000 volts DC. According to Beta, charging either model of its Alia aircraft takes about 35 minutes, from the minimum charge required under visual flight rules to full state. A separate thermal-management cube circulates water-glycol coolant through the aircraft to keep the batteries from overheating during charging.

The charge cubes use the Combined Charging System (CCS), an open standard increasingly shared across the electric transportation industry. Beta’s strategy resembles Tesla’s decision to treat charging as part of the vehicle business, with one notable difference: Beta is courting other aircraft makers, airports, and operators to use its technology. Archer, Atlantic Aviation, Signature Aviation, and government agencies have purchased or installed Beta’s charging equipment. As of October, Beta has 138 fast-charge locations, with additional sites in permitting or construction.

Recent findings suggest that for charging beyond the fixed network, Beta offers a wheeled 40-kW Mini Cube and a 65-kW Mini Cube+ that can ride inside an Alia and plug into more modest electrical service. The Mini Cube can also charge cars, buses, and trucks—any vehicle that uses the CCS standard.

In a recent development, back above Lake Champlain, the CX300 levels off, and the motor recedes to a faint hum. Then Caputo switches it off, and there’s nothing but the rush of wind around the canopy. The aircraft glides on its long wings while the coasting propeller turns the motor into a generator, feeding about 9 kW back to the battery.

Sources indicate that then we turn to the east and slip into the landing queue behind a National Guard C-130 Hercules, and Caputo powers and slides the throttle forward. The motor springs to life again, pushing the airplane, and perhaps aviation itself, into the future.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today.
  • When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its upcoming app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.
  • In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its upcoming app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”.

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Consumers can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that highlights where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the organization says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”.

Sources indicate that unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets consumers quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

Sources indicate that as MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”.

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:.

Sources indicate that “When we debuted Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”.

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.

#131283. These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1482 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

These 14 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1482 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov.
  • Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program.
  • Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially introduces the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 upcoming features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger complications. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

Sources indicate that the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this new feature here.

Industry observers note that iOS 27.3 also comes with a upcoming setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Right now, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the substantial screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the manufacturer is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally declared with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,.

Industry observers note that the tech giant generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company indicates Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing upcoming abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you proposal a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These newly introduced actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its upcoming Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Sources indicate that continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training proposal. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Recent findings suggest that apple is also testing a upcoming Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Industry observers note that vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

It has been revealed that another newly introduced Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Industry observers note that apple is also testing newly introduced StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

Industry observers note that "Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with massive iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability at the moment works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

According to recent reports, apple is also rolling out newly introduced languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

If you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the latest updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.).

According to recent reports, its intelligent AI sensing algorithm drastically improves reliability by reducing false triggers caused by environmental factors like pets, airflow, and robotic vacuums. A built-in ambient light sensor also helps trigger smart home scenes based on both human activity and lighting conditions.

  • VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.
  • VWFNDR + MBL debuted on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out.
  • The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VWFNDR + MBL, an Android camera app that doesn’t overprocess and delivers high-quality DNG (RAW) files, is getting a 2.0 release with improved color grading and an expansion to the iPhone.

VWFNDR + MBL debuted on Android in May 2026 with a few points that stood out. A unique UI that adapts to the shot, minimal processing for a natural look, and support for DNG files at a level that only Google’s Pixel Camera app can truly compete with.

The app has been downloaded over 300,000 times since then, and is now getting a pretty substantial update.

It has been revealed that on Android, this comes in the form of new color grading profiles built into the app. “NATURAL,” “NIHON,” or “B+W.” The app still saves an unprocessed DNG alongside the JPG and the grading adapts across the frame rather than having a fixed result, keeping highlights and shadows in place.

Industry observers note that colour grades: MBL still records unprocessed Bayer RAW DNG, and the JPG it renders alongside now uses one of three grades: NATURAL, NIHON, or B+W. Grading happens on VWFNDR’s own spatial engine. Instead of applying a fixed LUT, it adapts across the frame, much like a raw editor, so highlights and shadows keep their detail. The DNG stays untouched.

Here’s what the output looks like:.

The rest of VWFNDR + MBL 2.0 takes place off of Android.

Sources indicate that in a rare case of the tables turning, MBL was released first on Android, and only on Android for the first several months. But VWFNDR is now bringing the app to iPhone with support for variable aperture on iPhone 18 Pro and Content Credentials, Apple’s version of the C2PA standard that’s meant to prove a photo is real and not AI-generated.

Recent findings suggest that we’re expecting Apple to use a combination of ultra-thin bezels and curved glass to create the illusion of no bezels at all – a more sophisticated version of the effect seen on the Apple Watch. Today’s report says the bezels are around 1mm thick.

The curved edges on the quad-curved version are approximately 1mm wide. However, because the glass curves around all sides, when viewed straight on from the front, the bezel becomes nearly invisible, creating a near‑borderless appearance. The actual visual effect could be quite stunning.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea.
  • Samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses.
  • Sources indicate that sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung said in a newsroom statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Samsung Electronics’ Digital City campus in Suwon, South Korea.

Samsung Electronics has named new heads for its memory chip and smartphone businesses. The changes came in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules. The manufacturer confirmed the changes on Friday in Korea.

Sources indicate that sang Joon Hwang will run the memory business, and Won-Joon Choi takes over Mobile eXperience, the unit behind Galaxy phones, Samsung said in a newsroom statement. Co-chief executives Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles.

Industry observers note that samsung promoted Hwang to president. He previously led memory development, including DRAM and the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in AI chips. Samsung remarked it expects him to strengthen its memory products for the AI era. It reportedly plans to make HBM parts for AMD and Nvidia at a second Texas fab.

It has been revealed that sangyeun Cho, who ran Samsung’s chip business in the Americas, becomes president of System LSI, its chip design unit. Jong Myeong Lee, the former head of process development, becomes chief technology officer of the Device Solutions division, which makes Samsung’s chips.

Choi has been chief operating officer of the mobile unit since March 2025 and led the rolls out of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Roh had run the mobile business for most of the last seven years, 9to5Google noted. He stays in charge of the Device eXperience division, which includes phones and TVs.

In a recent development, earlier this week, the Financial Times reported that Samsung and TSMC had suspended some shipments to Chinese customers. Both are applying for licences from the US Commerce Department under upcoming rules, the FT reported.

The rules close a route that let Chinese designers order advanced chips through third-party packaging and testing firms. They also remove an exemption for chips not meant for AI, according to the FT. They arrived in the same week as US limits on Chinese remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres.

Recent findings suggest that samsung’s Chinese customers include ByteDance and Baidu’s chip unit Kunlun, while TSMC makes phone chips for Xiaomi, the FT reported. It is unclear which customers have been told to wait. An industry insider told the FT that Washington will likely approve licences for consumer smartphone chips. The process could still cause delays. TNW has not independently verified the report.

Industry observers note that chinese firms have already warned about the curbs. Tencent and Alibaba noted this week the rules will slow growth in AI.

In a recent development, some data centre operators that serve China have also been hit. Shares in Japan’s Datasection have fallen 47% since Monday, and it warned annual revenue could be up to 89% below its forecast, The Telegraph reported.

Recent findings suggest that samsung did not link its leadership changes to the export rules. Its statement notes it wants the fresh team to strengthen its future competitiveness in semiconductors.

Etsy will revise its AI training terms after sellers close their shops

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (420 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the newly introduced terms take effect on 16 December.
  • Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”.
  • Several sellers who had run shops for years said they were leaving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the newly introduced terms take effect on 16 December. They let Etsy and its partners use sellers’ content to build and train AI. The previous version had no clause about AI, the Times reported. The key line reads:.

Etsy and its “third party partners and vendors” may use sellers’ content to “develop, train, test and improve artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies.”.

Several sellers who had run shops for years said they were leaving. Illustrator Aaron Millard said on Instagram he was deleting the shop he had run for nearly a decade. He wrote that sellers had no way to opt out.

It has been revealed that kristen and Geoff Zephyrus deleted their shop too. They have sold home goods and stationery on Etsy for 13 years as Cognitive Surplus.

“For Etsy to be helping to train algorithms with our human content is just unimaginably awful,” Kristen Zephyrus told the Times.

James Ossman, Etsy’s vice president for customer operations, answered sellers in a post on Etsy’s website this week.

Sources indicate that etsy will not “use your content to train A.I. models designed to copy your original work or replace your creativity,” Ossman wrote.

He said third parties get access to sellers’ content for uses such as fraud detection and advertising. In a statement to the Times, he said Etsy would send sellers the revised terms soon. Sellers’ creative work belongs to them, he added.

According to recent reports, some critics doubt the reassurance. Tyler Wilde, PC Gamer’s US editor-in-chief, wrote an opinion piece on the clause. To him, it reads like blanket permission to train AI on user content for any purpose. He argued that Etsy should leave every seller out of AI training by default.

In a recent development, etsy has faced seller protests before. In 2022, more than 20,000 sellers went on strike over a fee rise. Etsy had raised its basic sales fee from 5% to 6.5%. In October, it tightened its rules on low-quality AI content after consumers complained, the Times reported.

The company cut 12% of its staff in August. The dispute also lands amid wider pushback against AI. Donald Trump Jr told Axios this week that investors had underestimated the AI backlash. Elton John urged Australia to protect artists from AI at the Aria awards.

Apple only launched high-end ‘Pro’ and ‘Duo’ iPhones this fall, marking a departure from previous years when more affordable models debuted too. But iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 are still coming, and a new report offers an update on release timing.

A new report from Kim Yeong-ho at ETNews provides a fresh update on timing for the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2.

Rumors have indicated for well over a year that Apple planned to push these models out of the typical fall launch window and introduce them in early 2027 instead.

Per ETNews, Samsung and LG are providing the display panels for the latest models, with Samsung the sole supplier for iPhone Air 2 and both companies splitting orders for iPhone 18. And their mass production plans signal a March release for the products.

Kim Yeong-ho, writing at ETNews:.

Samsung Display intends to begin mass production in January, while LG Display will start late this year…The Korean panel makers appear to be aligning their production plans with an expected March launch.

A March launch window lines up well with when Apple tends to ramp up product introductions following a slower winter. Earlier this year, iPhone 17e debuted in March alongside fresh Macs and the iPad Air.

The year before, however, the iPhone 16e arrived in February instead.

With Apple shaking up its normal iPhone rollout schedule, it was anyone’s guess how soon the new models would debut. But a March launch makes sense and gives Apple a trio of new iPhones every six months—three unveiled in September, and another three in March.

Are you holding out for an iPhone 18 or iPhone Air 2? Let us know in the comments.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (465 w)

SK Hynix will become Kioxia’s largest shareholder through a bond swap

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (465 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference.
  • SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares.
  • Bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SK hynix’s exhibition booth at the Supercomputing 2026 (SC26) conference.

SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder in Kioxia, its Japanese rival in flash memory, by converting bonds it has held since 2018 into shares. It will hold an indirect stake of about 14.1%, it said in a filing on Friday.

Bloomberg’s Yoolim Lee first reported the filing. The move puts SK Hynix ahead of Toshiba, Kioxia’s former parent, which held 10.46% in early November, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

In a recent development, SPC2 is a special-purpose organization set up for the 2018 deal. SK Hynix will convert 129bn yen ($810m) of its bonds into 129,000 shares. It will also buy Bain Capital’s remaining 1,001 SPC2 shares for 100m yen. The steps close in December, leaving SK Hynix as SPC2’s sole owner.

Apart from the payment to Bain, the deal adds no new money, MoneyToday reported, citing the manufacturer. SK Hynix called it a follow-up step after it sold out of a separate Kioxia fund in June. Gains from that sale funded about 7tn won ($5.2bn) of special dividends in the third quarter.

It has been revealed that SK Hynix joined the Bain-led group that bought Kioxia, then Toshiba Memory, in 2018. It put in 395bn yen at the time.

Both companies make NAND, the chips used for storage in phones and AI servers. SK Hynix held 19% of the global NAND market in the second quarter and Kioxia 14%, according to Counterpoint figures cited by Bloomberg. Together that tops market leader Samsung’s 28%.

The 2018 deal caps SK Hynix at 15% of Kioxia’s voting shares until 2028, unless Kioxia agrees otherwise. Kioxia lists the stake as a risk factor in its annual report, citing a possible conflict of interest, Bloomberg reported.

According to recent reports, both sides say nothing changes in how Kioxia is run. A Kioxia spokesperson mentioned its management will stay independent.

In a recent development, “We at the moment have no looks to further buy or sell shares in Kioxia. We will continue to respect Kioxia’s independent management going forward,” an SK Hynix official said.

Masahiro Wakasugi of Bloomberg Intelligence sees little change in the short run.

The move is “unlikely to materially change near-term NAND competition,” Wakasugi wrote.

Sources indicate that the stake still gives SK Hynix some say over substantial decisions, he added. That includes the power to oppose a possible deal between Kioxia and Sandisk.

In a recent development, separately, SoftBank’s Masayoshi Son reportedly explored a buyout of SK Hynix itself. The Korean firm reported a 632% profit jump in October, even as memory stocks slid.

  • iOS 27.3 debuts next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.
  • Apple is granting iPhone Duo consumers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.
  • Recent findings suggest that face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27.3 debuts next month and includes several exciting changes for iPhone Duo, here’s what’s new for Apple’s foldable model.

Apple is granting iPhone Duo consumers one of their biggest feature requests: face unlock is coming with iOS 27.3.

Recent findings suggest that face unlock isn’t a full-fledged Face ID, and it doesn’t work for features like Apple Pay, but it is a convenient new option for unlocking your iPhone Duo just by looking at it. Per Apple:.

According to recent reports, use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it’s closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device.

Recent findings suggest that if your iPhone Duo has gone unused for 45 minutes or more, face unlock won’t work and you’ll need to authenticate with Touch ID or your passcode. But for most customers, that probably just means using Touch ID first thing in the morning, then relying on face unlock the rest of the day.

In a recent development, on a related note, you can also enable Attention Aware features in iOS 27.3. These are available whether you use the face unlock feature or not, but are limited to the outer display. Once enabled, they can automatically lower the volume of alarms and timers, keep the display from dimming, and more.

Read more: iOS 27.3 adds latest face unlock feature for iPhone Duo.

Sources indicate that reachability is available on other iPhone models to move onscreen content down vertically, closer to your thumb. But on iPhone Duo with iOS 27.3, Apple has a unique twist on the feature.

Instead of helping you reach content vertically, Reachability on iPhone Duo works horizontally.

If you’re using the outer screen and find that buttons or other UI elements are out of reach, you can swipe from the side to have onscreen content shift closer to your thumb.

Sources indicate that you can always disable Reachability if you find yourself accidentally triggering it too often. But if one-handed iPhone Duo use gives you trouble, Reachability is a great upcoming option to have.

Read more: iOS 27.3 introduces newly introduced iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use.

In a recent development, what should happen when you close your iPhone Duo’s folding screen? Apple has found that people have different preferences. Some want the iPhone to stay unlocked for continued use, while others prefer that it automatically locks when closed.

In iOS 27.3, Apple adds a fresh setting so people can enable whichever behavior they prefer.

Recent findings suggest that by default, iPhone Duo will work as it always has, staying unlocked after being closed. But inside Settings ⇾ Display & Brightness, iOS 27.3 provides the option of automatically locking upon being closed instead. You could achieve something similar before with Shortcuts, but now there’s a built-in setting too.

Industry observers note that it’s not exactly a “latest feature,” but iPhone Duo users will also find that the system keyboard has changed in iOS 27.3. Apple tweaked the outer display keyboard to push keys closer together and make one-handed use easier.

Here’s a comparison of the old and new keyboards via Beta Profiles on X:.

It has been revealed that iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z.

Read more: iOS 27.3 changes the iPhone Duo keyboard, here’s how.

#131262. Industry News: OpenAI notes its agents now finish nearly half of 2 to 4-hour research tasks

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (714 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thenextweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: OpenAI notes its agents now finish nearly half of 2 to 4-hour research tasks

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that openAI states its coding agents now complete 46% of research tasks that would take a person two to four hours, with no human help.
  • It has been revealed that the figures come from Research acceleration: The jagged frontier, a report OpenAI published on Wednesday.
  • According to recent reports, at API list prices, the median OpenAI researcher used about $2,400 of agent time a day in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that openAI states its coding agents now complete 46% of research tasks that would take a person two to four hours, with no human help. In March the figure was 23%. For tasks of four to eight hours, success rose from 13% to 35%.

It has been revealed that the figures come from Research acceleration: The jagged frontier, a report OpenAI published on Wednesday. It is the firm’s second on how AI speeds up its own research, after its first such report in September. OpenAI says labs should be required to track and publicly report signs of recursive self-improvement, where AI speeds up the building of future AI. It adds that the reporting does not mean it intends to pursue full self-improvement.

According to recent reports, at API list prices, the median OpenAI researcher used about $2,400 of agent time a day in October. That is up 62% from $1,500 in September. At the 90th percentile, daily use reached about $23,000, more than double September’s $11,000.

Measured in time, agent use per researcher rose elevenfold, from 0.5 to 5.7 “agent workdays” a day. OpenAI counts every eight hours of agent running time as one workday. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of researchers ran at least four agents at once at their daily peak. More than 10% ran at least 16.

In September, the value of agent use in OpenAI’s research organisation was about twice its pay bill for researchers. That excludes equity, which OpenAI states makes up 70 to 80% of their target pay. Internal use still took only 2% of research compute.

Results for OpenAI research agents vary widely by task, which is why the company calls the gains jagged. Agents succeeded alone 79% of the time when monitoring training runs, and 72% when answering technical questions. They managed 25% when writing code for inference and serving systems, and 29% when building evaluation and training environments.

OpenAI flags a caveat in its own numbers. As agents improved, researchers may have changed which tasks they handed over, so the success rates track those choices as well as the models.

According to recent reports, in a survey of 101 research staff, OpenAI asked what each would give up to keep frontier coding agents for three months. The median answer was 40% of team headcount, or 30% of team compute. The company warns that self-reports may be inaccurate and that it sampled staff in an ad hoc way.

According to recent reports, openAI also asked key researchers where the main ideas behind GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra came from. Post-training and safety researchers credited people with all of them, with models helping to build them. For GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers noted they developed ideas in conversation with Codex, and one credited it with key insights.

Industry observers note that in interviews, researchers mentioned agents still have poor taste in research ideas, code, data and writing, and need close oversight. One pretraining researcher doubted the human edge would last.

“I do think I have more taste in terms of the ideas. But I have no confidence that will continue to be true for any significant period of time,” the researcher told OpenAI.

In a recent development, safety and Alignment saw the largest rise in researcher time of any area, OpenAI says, with documented workweeks up 77% from January to September. Growth picked up after the Hugging Face breakout in July, when its own research agents hacked the AI platform.

Sources indicate that openAI is not alone in publishing such data. It cites three reports from Anthropic, which notes it has met its own threshold for AI-accelerated research. The same day, OpenAI mentioned its models had found gains in AMD’s GPU design.

Recent findings suggest that to see whether AI is speeding up progress itself, OpenAI tracks an internal version of Epoch AI’s capabilities index. Its frontier has risen 16.4 points a year since August 2025, against the 14 a year Epoch found since late 2024. OpenAI notes that its models score higher on its own index than on Epoch’s.

The Microsoft chief executive spoke to Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.

He apologised for Microsoft’s own outage, which he mentioned had no direct link to that problem.

“This was a latent bug that was there. It got invoked and, you know, it’s one of those perfect storms,” Nadella said.

Later that day, he told Jim Cramer on CNBC’s Mad Money that Microsoft could have done more to prevent it.

It has been revealed that “Of course, we should have done the testing before. We should have figured out how to have the bulkheads such that you didn’t have a global outage,” Nadella told Cramer.

The bigger risk comes from AI tools that find vulnerabilities, Nadella noted. A fix for a critical bank system used to get a week of testing. Now attackers exploit flaws as soon as they surface, so fixes go straight into production. On the day he spoke, he said, three critical patches had landed for open-source packages.

Recent findings suggest that “The patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create its instability,” he noted.

Banks and the NSA have reportedly blamed this week’s US outages on rushed patches for AI-found flaws. Nadella also stated the “floor of cyberattacks has fallen”. With AI models, anyone can now run what amounts to a persistent, nation-state-level attacker, he said.

Sorkin asked whether this was a passing phase. Nadella compared it to the Y2K bug, but noted he had no view yet, because models keep getting more capable. Much critical infrastructure runs firmware that nobody can patch, he added. He named chillers, heating and cooling systems, and transport networks that sit on the internet.

Sources indicate that last month, Nadella told 20VC that alignment would not come from scale alone. Sorkin remarked Sam Altman, who spoke earlier at the summit, disagreed with that premise.

Nadella said he learned about scaling laws from OpenAI’s founders, and that scaling had worked. Alignment, and a real way to debug models, had not followed, he said. He hoped Altman and Greg Brockman were right.

“I mean, if it doesn’t happen, we are in a world of hurt,” Nadella remarked.

In a recent development, his answer is what he called a trust architecture. He would ban models that reason in neuralese, an internal shorthand people cannot read. Every model’s reasoning needs tamper-proof logs that other models can inspect, he remarked, because models will try to hide what they are doing. He praised OpenAI for monitoring its models during training runs.

For now, whoever deploys an AI system is liable for what it does, Nadella noted. He expects insurers to price that risk and to ask for the logs.

Sorkin asked what happens to OpenAI and Anthropic, in which Microsoft holds stakes, if cheaper models can do the same work. Nadella stated everyday office work no longer needs frontier models. Copilot already chooses between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Microsoft’s own MAI models, he said. He added that his bigger stake is in Microsoft.

“Arguing for some massive pricing power of tokens is betting against somehow US GDP,” he said.

In a recent development, microsoft’s deal with OpenAI gives it royalty-free access to a frontier model until 2032, Nadella said. That lets Microsoft build MAI models three to six months behind the frontier, using 5% to 20% of the computing power. Anthropic and OpenAI play “a vertical stack game”, he said, while Microsoft plays “a model system game”.

Sources indicate that AI agents will reshuffle who pays whom on the web, as the move from Yahoo to search once did, Nadella remarked. Sites that live off ads from human visitors will have to change. Asked about sites that keep agents out, such as Amazon, he said rivals would take the business.

“If you don’t accept the agent, somebody else will. If Amazon doesn’t, Shopify will,” Nadella remarked.

It has been revealed that the staff buyouts Microsoft offered 60,000 people were meant to give everyone agency, he mentioned. Software engineering is “very much alive”, but the work has changed. The team behind Microsoft’s Cowork agent is 11 developers who build “a software factory that builds the product”. That shift will take longer than anyone expects, Nadella said.

Sorkin noted that Nadella has kept his distance from the Trump administration. Nadella said his job is to earn Microsoft’s permission to operate through its products.

According to recent reports, “I just don’t want to be in Washington. I just want to be in Redmond, Washington,” he remarked.

Dan Hendrycks calls for a pause on frontier AI, Max Hodak pushes back

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, at TechCrunch Disrupt in October 2025.
  • According to recent reports, dan Hendrycks used the DealBook Summit to call for an indefinite pause on frontier AI training runs.
  • Industry observers note that they spoke on the DealBook AGI panel, which Michael Barbaro of The Daily moderated at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dan Hendrycks, director of the Center for AI Safety, at TechCrunch Disrupt in October 2025.

According to recent reports, dan Hendrycks used the DealBook Summit to call for an indefinite pause on frontier AI training runs. Max Hodak, on the same panel, stated enforcing one would take a surveillance state.

Industry observers note that they spoke on the DealBook AGI panel, which Michael Barbaro of The Daily moderated at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit in New York on Wednesday. Hendrycks runs the Center for AI Safety, and Barbaro said he had been a safety adviser to several AI companies until hours earlier. Hodak co-founded Neuralink and now runs Science Corporation. Lila Ibrahim of Google DeepMind and Mati Staniszewski of ElevenLabs also joined. Clem Delangue of Hugging Face arrived late, with 18 minutes left.

In a recent development, hendrycks said the US midterms showed how strongly voters feel about AI. That gives politicians room, he said, and they can now discuss ideas such as pausing AI development openly in Washington. He expects 2027 to be a very interesting year for regulation.

He said he used to favour narrow technical rules, but the companies blocked them for years.

“So now it’s, we’re going to need a more blunt intervention. That’s how it is,” Hendrycks remarked.

In a recent development, he described an indefinite pause on the biggest training runs, with carve-outs for narrow models such as DeepMind’s AlphaFold and voice models. Labs could still sell inference, he said. In the meantime, they could make models more reliable and secure, close jailbreaks and backdoors, and help patch critical infrastructure.

Hendrycks also said the frontier labs, Google aside, put few people on healthcare, because their revenue comes from coding. At some of them, he said, the healthcare team is zero or one person.

Recent findings suggest that barbaro put to the panel the objection Jensen Huang would raise: China would not observe a moratorium. Staniszewski agreed a pause could work with global alignment, but said whether anyone can get it “is the big question mark”. Without it, Barbaro added, a pause would be a waste of time.

Recent findings suggest that hodak noted people have spent the past eight months patching critical infrastructure anyway, running their code through AI tools that hunt for new flaws. The regime needed to enforce a training ban, he said, would be as draconian as anything people fear from the labs.

“You’re setting up like an exhaustive surveillance state on the internet to enforce this,” Hodak said.

He mentioned today’s top models already meet his definition of AGI, naming Mythos, Fable, Astra and Sol. He expects governments to keep a superintelligence frontier for themselves, with an “industrial intelligence frontier” open to everyone else.

“I don’t think that the genie is going to be put back in the bottle,” Hodak mentioned.

It has been revealed that his answer is antitrust law. Frontier labs should only sell intelligence, he stated, and not move into drugs, cars and other products. He called AI the inverse of nuclear weapons, where safety came from stopping their spread. With AI, he said, safety comes from spreading it widely, and the futures that worry him most involve a few actors holding all of it.

Ibrahim, Google DeepMind’s chief AI readiness officer, noted it was not an either-or. Safety is not something a organization can “bolt on to the end”, she said. In 35 years in tech, she added, she had never seen global trust in technology as low as it is now.

Sources indicate that anthropic was due to start trading the next day. Hendrycks repeated the charges of the statement his group organised against the company, and added a latest one. Several safety organisations agreed with the statement privately, he stated, but would not sign it for fear of losing funding or access.

It has been revealed that “What they’re doing is reckless and they don’t have a safety initiative. They know it,” Hendrycks remarked.

Anthropic was not on the panel. In its IPO filing, it stated it does not expect to let Claude fully build its successors without meaningful human supervision.

Delangue stated his main worry is that AI concentrates talent, computing power and wealth. Barbaro asked how credible he was on that, given that Nvidia is buying Hugging Face. Delangue said Nvidia and Hugging Face both push AI outwards to more builders. He said Hugging Face never held sale talks with Anthropic, because their missions were too misaligned.

In a recent development, barbaro closed by asking Delangue about the Hugging Face breach by OpenAI’s research agents. Delangue said the four-day attack left Hugging Face more optimistic about AI, not less. It used an open-source Chinese model to analyse the attack logs, because the volume was so big that it needed AI to defend itself.

“People only see that we got attacked by AI and they rarely see that we defended ourselves with AI,” Delangue said.

Barbaro summed up the table as no moratorium and less concentration of power, with Hendrycks the exception. Hodak had the last word: antitrust law, he stated, could get most of the way there without a fresh regulator.

Why a Mathematician Is Chasing Eclipses With Algorithms and Cameras

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.
  • According to recent reports, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated.
  • The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With custom-built gear, his team seeks to solve a long-standing solar mystery.

According to recent reports, advanced image-processing software developed by Miloslav Druckmüller combines scores of individual images, captured during a total solar eclipse and painstakingly calibrated. The techniques reveal fine details in the sun’s corona, which is white in this image. The tiny pink shapes seen along portions of the edge of the blacked-out solar disk are prominences, which are extensions of relatively cool plasma that can jut out hundreds of thousands of kilometers into space.

The sun hangs low over the plains of Castile and León, in the north-central region of Spain. But from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza, it appears that a few puffy white clouds have started to block the sun. That’s vexing.

A group of researchers, some wearing cardboard eclipse glasses, is clustered around sets of portable telescopes and cameras connected to laptops. All this gear is scattered on tabletops perched on the mountainside. On the computer screens, the sun’s disk looks like a deep orange crescent that is slowly waning. That’s because the moon began to crawl across it about half an hour ago. In 25 minutes, it will obscure the sun completely, producing an eerie and wondrous phenomenon—a total solar eclipse.

Sources indicate that in the late-summer, late-afternoon heat, the researchers watch anxiously as those fluffy clouds linger around the sun. From an abandoned hut on the slope a few meters above, where the researchers have set up camp, one of the grad students emerges and nods toward the cloud formation. “Do you think it will dissolve?” he blurts out.

“It will.” Miloslav Druckmüller glances calmly at his group of doctoral candidates, now making final checks of the equipment in preparation for totality. Here in Spain, on this 12th day of August, Druckmüller is getting ready for his 19th solar eclipse. He knows from long experience that weather can turn promptly when the moon’s shadow suddenly pushes the temperature down. Plus, there’s no sense in riling up the grad students any more than they already are.

Miloslav Druckmüller led the design and construction of a unique optical instrument that incorporates eight astrocameras. Each is equipped with a spectral filter for sensing and recording specific emission spectra from the solar corona. Each of those spectra, in turn, is associated with a particular ionic species of iron atoms. Because the temperature needed to ionize iron varies depending on the ionic species, analyzing the locations and relative abundance of these ionic species offers valuable insights into the distribution of heat in the corona.Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that during totality, the moon blocks the overwhelming glare of the solar disk, revealing delicate structures in the sun’s outer atmosphere, the corona. Using custom-built telescope systems and image-processing techniques that Druckmüller has spent decades developing, the researchers aim to gain insights into the processes in this enigmatic region that is otherwise hard to study. In addition to imaging the visible coronal light, the team will try to track the dispersal of superhot ions of iron into interplanetary space, which could give rare insights into the pattern of heat emanating from the corona.

And they’ll have 107 seconds to do all that.

In a recent development, druckmüller is a professor of mathematics and image processing at the Brno University of Technology in the Czech Republic and a leading figure in the Solar Wind Sherpas, an international team that studies the sun’s corona during total eclipses. In the solar eclipse world, he is nothing short of a legend, albeit a reluctant one.

An image from Miloslav Druckmüller’s first solar-eclipse expedition, to Hungary, vividly indicates Baily’s Beads. These elongated white lights along a piece of the left edge of the blacked-out solar disk are caused by beams of sunlight shining through gaps in the irregular lunar surface during the eclipse. The pink shapes are solar prominences, which are jets of plasma extending out into space and held in place by the sun’s intense magnetic field.

According to recent reports, he photographed his first solar eclipse in 1999, in what he thought would be a one-off lark. During that eclipse, the moon’s deep shadow missed Druckmüller’s native Czechia by just a few tens of kilometers, so he chased it to Hungary with a 30-year-old Soviet MTO 1,000-millimeter lens. All he remembers from that day is the rush of adrenaline he felt while trying to find the sun in the sky with the lens’s minuscule field of view and keep it in focus for the two minutes of the eclipse.

He insists that he has never enjoyed any of the eclipses he has photographed. “In fact, I have never properly seen any of those eclipses. You are just watching the screens, making sure that it’s all doing what it’s supposed to do. There are so many things that can go wrong and you can’t redo it.”.

A composite sequence of photographs shows the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse as seen from a slope of the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain.

Václav Široký and Miloslav Druckmüller.

Industry observers note that despite Druckmüller’s outward tranquility on this Spanish hillside, the stakes are high. Just 45 minutes ago, his group heard from their colleagues in Iceland, where viewing conditions had promised to be better than in Spain. But a vast low-pressure system had clouded the entire sky, leaving all three Iceland teams without a view.

On the Pico Trigaza mountain in Spain, two postgraduate researchers used a laser to get a rough, initial alignment for the tracking mount of an optical instrument. The alignment was necessary to precisely compensate for the Earth’s motion.

The corona has been a mystery for centuries. Though dimmer—by a factor of a million—than the sun’s visible surface, the corona is nevertheless extremely hot: about a million degrees Celsius compared to 5,500 degrees on the surface. Because the sun’s nuclear fusion engine churns at the star’s heart, it might seem that temperatures should fall farther from the core.

To observe the faint corona in visible light, researchers must block the sun’s ferocious glare. Specialized telescopes called coronagraphs do this with an opaque disk called an occulter. But because light bends around the occulter’s edges in an effect called diffraction, it must block an area much larger than that of the solar disk to prevent light from spilling over and ruining the images. But doing so means obstructing the inner part of the corona, which harbors the most important processes that underpin the puzzling phenomena of the sun’s upper atmosphere.

Sources indicate that that’s why total eclipses matter so much to solar physicists. By sheer chance, the moon is exactly the right size and at just the right distance to completely cover the sun during a total solar eclipse. Because the moon is so far away from Earth, the view is not marred by diffraction, and the corona reveals itself nearly all the way down to the sun’s surface.

As astrocameras recorded spectral data about the sun’s corona, a laptop computer [on table, at left] displayed the phase of the eclipse.

Industry observers note that space probes can image the solar surface in other wavelengths, but those views have limitations, too. Spacecraft such as NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory do see the innermost parts of the corona in extreme ultraviolet light, explains Shadia Habbal, a solar physicist at the University of Hawaii and leader of the Solar Wind Sherpas project. “But it cuts off very swiftly, so you don’t see its extension into space as well as we can see it in the visible emission lines” during an eclipse. “That’s the biggest advantage,” she says, of solar eclipse photography.

Recent findings suggest that the European Proba-3 mission, launched in 2024, simulates total solar eclipses by flying two spacecraft in a formation 150 meters apart with one acting as an occulter and the other as the telescope. The instruments aboard that satellite, however, have limitations compared to the equipment used by the Solar Wind Sherpas team.

According to recent reports, when Druckmüller developed the film from his 1999 eclipse expedition, the photographs didn’t do justice to the event’s eerie beauty. He spent countless evenings applying his expertise in numerical image processing in an attempt to re-create in his photographs the sights he witnessed in that Hungarian corn field.

Recent findings suggest that it took two years, but eventually he succeeded. Where before there were dull views of the blackened lunar disk surrounded by the blunt wisps of the corona, Druckmüller revealed the subtlest details of the magnetic field lines stretching from the sun far into space. As his photographs circulated among solar physicists, invitations to eclipse expeditions began to arrive.

Solar researchers Miloslav Druckmüller and Shadia Habbal have been collaborating for two decades and 15 eclipses.

Sources indicate that habbal learned about the images from a Ph.D. student who had seen them at a conference presentation that didn’t credit Druckmüller. When Habbal’s team later published the images in a paper, they misattributed them to another researcher. Druckmüller found out through an astrophysicist friend. “I wrote her a rather disappointed email and she responded within 10 minutes,” Druckmüller recalls. “She really didn’t have a clue.”.

The error was corrected, and within weeks, Habbal and Druckmüller began a collaboration that grew into a friendship. “Milos’s processing brings out details that nobody has seen before, and they tell you a lot about very tiny features in the corona that you don’t see otherwise,” says Habbal.

Industry observers note that capturing the corona’s delicate structures means finding a way to show its brightest and faintest features in the same image. “During the solar eclipse, the contrast between the darkest and brightest parts of the corona is enormous, possibly one to a million,” Druckmüller explains. “But a computer monitor only allows you to display a contrast ratio of one to about 800.” (Some modern monitors, particularly OLED ones, can deliver higher contrast ratios.).

Recent findings suggest that the human eye can adjust to this enormous range of brightness, allowing an observer to see both the bright corona and the faint stars and planets that briefly emerge in the darkened sky. To bring those details together in a photograph, Druckmüller uses custom image-processing algorithms to combine exposures that capture different parts of that range.

Researchers Martin Šebek and Peter Urgoš make fine adjustments to the focus and alignment of the astrocameras on a key optical instrument before the 12 August solar eclipse.

Industry observers note that to create a single image, Druckmüller’s teams need to take 200 individual frames during the eclipse at exposure times ranging from 0.001 second to two seconds. The data must then be calibrated against a vast number of reference images to filter out noise and imperfections. Flat fields, which depict a uniform light background, help correct for defects caused by telescope optics, dust spots, and variations in pixel sensitivity. Dark frames, taken with light blocked from the sensor, help correct for artifacts created by the camera’s image sensor itself. “It takes the computer more than two days to process one image,” Druckmüller states. Including the calibration data, a single finished image requires about 3,000 input frames.

Recent findings suggest that since 2008, teams directed by Habbal and Druckmüller have traveled to every total solar eclipse, spreading out across multiple locations to hedge against bad weather. About half of the teams return with usable data. For the others, it’s just a short and stressful voyage. For the 12 August eclipse, three groups deployed to Iceland and two to Spain.

The teams seek sites close to the center of the band of totality, where the moon blocks the sun for longest. In Spain, the 12 August band of totality cut across the north of the country; the center line of the shadow passed within 11 kilometers of Pico Trigaza, promising Druckmüller and his colleagues a precious 107 seconds of totality.

But duration is only part of the calculation. Totality on Pico Trigaza will commence 51 minutes before sunset, with the sun just 8 degrees above the horizon. That low, the rays must pass through a much thicker layer of the atmosphere than when the sun is higher in the sky, increasing the light distortion that complicates photography. At the researchers’ camp on Pico Trigaza, 1,600 meters above sea level, the thinner air should help a bit.

An abandoned hut on the mountain Pico Trigaza in Spain was spruced up so that it could serve as a home base for the research team recording the 12 August solar eclipse.

“Iceland would have been a much better place for us than Spain because the sun was higher up, some 25 degrees above the horizon,” Druckmüller notes wistfully. But Iceland’s notoriously unpredictable weather made Spain an essential backup.

In a recent development, if you pack a van with thousands of dollars’ worth of cameras and optical gear and then set out on a 2,351-kilometer journey, you shouldn’t be surprised if you finish the trip with a few striking photographs [top]. The sleeping arrangements for the grad students at the Pico Trigaza hut [bottom] were spartan, but the views were first-rate.Top: Martin Šebek; Bottom: Václav Široký.

In a recent development, on the mountain, locals have spruced up a rustic, long-unused hut for the researchers, running power cables from a nearby telecommunication outpost and bringing in a water tank. Five Ph.D. students drove more than 2,000 kilometers from Brno and have spent nearly a week preparing the equipment. Druckmüller and his wife joined them two days before the eclipse. They cook on a small propane grill and sleep in sleeping bags on yoga mats. “We have plenty of space here to set up our telescopes, beautiful views, and a roof over our heads,” Druckmüller says with a grin. “It’s perfect.”.

In a recent development, but even the best equipment and a carefully chosen site count for nothing if the clouds roll in. “So much work goes into the preparations and then, if you end up with nothing, you just feel terrible sadness,” says Jana Hoderová, an assistant professor of mathematics at Brno University of Technology and one of Druckmüller’s key collaborators.

As the moon continues to slide in front of the solar disk, the pesky cumulus cloud that kept everybody on edge begins to dissolve. It’s 10 minutes to totality. The relief is palpable.

The countdown on the computers that control the cameras has begun. The screens are now showing only a tiny orange sliver, and the evening is becoming perceptibly less bright.

Twenty astrophotography cameras, most of them drawing power from a car battery that was also buffering the cameras from any grid instabilities, are pointed at the sun. Alongside equipment capturing the corona’s visible light, the team has built an assembly of eight cameras to detect light emitted by various iron ions that arise in the corona.

Among the optical gear assembled at Pico Trigaza to capture the 12 August solar eclipse was a unique instrument designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona [at left]. Václav Široký.

Those instruments looking for iron ions have been put together with resourcefulness and thrift. A colleague of Druckmüller’s laser-cut the aluminum plates holding the carefully aligned lenses in exchange “for two bottles of whisky.” The brackets and attachments were 3D-printed at Brno University of Technology. The lenses, produced for the defunct camera maker Contax, were bought at steep discounts on eBay. By far the most expensive elements are interference filters that isolate the wavelengths emitted by the iron ions.

It has been revealed that around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still.

According to recent reports, “That’s something nobody else in the world can do,” Druckmüller notes with visible satisfaction. The unique technology, codeveloped with Habbal’s Hawaii team, has already enabled researchers to map the distribution of temperatures across the entire corona and to discover previously unseen structures, dubbed “smoke rings,” in the coronal plasma. The photographs also revealed the boundary region where the solar plasma becomes so thin that its ions stop colliding.

Industry observers note that the optical assembly designed to record the distributions of iron ions in the corona is outfitted with astrocameras, each of which captures spectra from a different ionic species. To do that, each astrocamera is equipped with a spectral filter whose bandwidth is so narrow—one nanometer—that the filter appears as a mirror.Martin Fornůsek.

Industry observers note that “Iron is the most abundant of the heavy elements that we see in the solar corona,” states Habbal. “And because the corona is so hot, the iron atoms lose electrons and get ionized. The larger the loss, the higher the temperature.”.

In a recent development, for example, a temperature of around 1.6 million °C is necessary to produce an iron ion that has lost 12 electrons. But only 1.4 million °C is needed to strip an iron atom of 11 electrons. Once it’s in a particular electrical state, the ion retains its specific ionization, even as it travels outward with the solar wind. Each of those ions, whether +11 or +12, emits a different wavelength of light, allowing the researchers to map not just temperatures within the corona, but also how those iron ions spread into interplanetary space and distribute heat. Habbal and her colleagues had long been trying to image those iron ions during solar eclipses. But it wasn’t until Druckmüller entered the picture that they were able to develop the gear and the mathematical techniques to do it.

With just a minute to go to totality, the researchers begin removing protective filters from the lenses. It’s 50 minutes to sunset, and the waning sun has just begun to light up the clouds above the horizon with the first tinge of orange. Then, suddenly, the evening begins a rapid and premature descent into darkness. Along the edge of the fantastically thin solar crescent, the brilliant orange points known as Baily’s Beads flash and disappear—the last fragments of photospheric light visible through deep lunar valleys. As totality begins, observers remove their glasses. The hot air cools. The graduate students remain quietly and intently focused on their gear.

Sources indicate that druckmüller looks up from his camera toward the darkened plains. Around the blackened solar disk rises the magnificent golden halo of the corona. In the hush on the mountainside, it seems that even the birds have gone still. The sky is ablaze with fiery colors all along the horizon where the deep lunar shadow drops off. Venus burns brilliantly in the southwest, a sharp white pinpoint in the darkened sky. The sound of camera shutters suddenly fills the air. Then, as quickly as it fell, the darkness begins to recede, bid farewell with another handful of golden Baily’s Beads.

In a recent development, the crowd erupts in cheers. The Ph.D. students throw themselves at each other and hug like they mean it.

“The students did most of the work this time, so I actually allowed myself to really look at it,” Druckmüller notes. “It was beautiful. Pico Trigaza may not have been the best for science photography, but from the aesthetic point of view, it was extraordinary.”.

The 2026 solar-eclipse team at Pico Trigaza in Spain included [from left] Magdalena Šrotířová, Peter Urgoš, Martin Fornůsek, Miloslav Druckmüller, Václav Široký, and Martin Šebek.Václav Široký.

Recent findings suggest that but for Druckmüller, this is just the beginning. While other eclipse chasers will race to release their images, he will take his time. He expects to publish the first visible-light images of the corona in about two weeks. Processing the iron-ion images, and uncovering whatever insights they may hold, will take months—maybe even a whole year.

“Probably until the next eclipse in 2027” in North Africa, Druckmüller indicates.

Sources indicate that who knows? Maybe he’ll even enjoy that one, too.
